sources.full_text_concat:
Vācaspatimiśraviracitaṭīkāsaṃvalitavyāsabhāṣyasametāni Pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi. tathā
            bhojadevaviracitarājamārtaṇḍābhidhavṛttisametāni pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi.
            sūtrapāṭhasūtravarṇānukramasūcībhyāṃ ca sanāthīkṛtāni ... Kāśinātha Śāstrī Āgāśe ity
            etaiḥ saṃśodhitam.
          Kāśinātha Śāstrī Āgāśe
          Ānandāśramamudraṇālaye
          Punyākhyapattane
          1904
          Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series no. 47
          The transcription below excludes the commentary of Bhojadeva, the sūtrapāṭha and
            indexes.

content.value:
The transcription below excludes the commentary of Bhojadeva, the sūtrapāṭha and
            indexes.

Pātañjalayogaśāstra (Yogasūtra with Bhāṣya) transcribed by Philipp Maas from the Āgāśe
          1904 Ānandāśrama edition.

The edition from which this e-text was transcribed was printed in the Devanāgarī script.
        The electronic text below is in a lossless transliteration using the Latin alphabet. The
        transliteration scheme used is the IAST (
The International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration

Word division is marked with a space, where sandhi allows, not with sandhi-akṣaras or
        conjunct glyphs as in Devanāgarī (i.e., "ity evam" not "ityevam".)

Initial vowel elision for avagraha is reversed and marked with a + sign: e.g.,
        "prathamo+adhyāyaḥ"

children.translated_text: Auspicious Invocation

children.text: yas tyaktvā rūpam ādyaṃ prabhavati jagato+anekadhānugrahāya
children.translated_text: He who, having abandoned the primordial form, exerts himself in manifold ways for the world’s beneficence,
whose mass of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) is worn away, who bears the poison that is harmful, possessing many mouths, well-hooded;
from whom the production of all knowledge proceeds, and whose retinue is of serpents, for whose delight always,

children.text: devo+ahīśaḥ sa vo+avyāt sitavimalatanur yogado yogayuktaḥ //1//
children.translated_text: may that god, the lord of serpents, protect you, he of white and stainless body, bestower of <s>Yoga</s> (<s>yoga</s>) and himself joined to <s>Yoga</s> //1//
Section on <s>Samādhi</s> (<s>Samādhi</s>-pāda)
Now, the instruction in <s>Yoga</s> (<s>yogānuśāsana</s>)

children.text:
athety ayam adhikārārthaḥ. yogānuśāsanaṃ śāstram adhikṛtaṃ veditavyam. yogaḥ samādhiḥ.
            sa ca sārvabhaumaś cittasya dharmaḥ. kṣiptaṃ mūḍhaṃ vikṣiptam ekāgraṃ niruddham iti
            cittabhūmayaḥ. tatra vikṣipte cetasi vikṣepopasarjanībhūtaḥ samādhir na yogapakṣe
            vartate.
children.translated_text: The word “now” has the sense of qualification for study; it should be understood that the treatise on the instruction in <s>Yoga</s> is undertaken. <s>Yoga</s> is <s>samādhi</s> (enstasis), and this is a universal property of the mind (<s>citta</s>). The states of mind are: scattered, stupefied, distracted, one-pointed, and restrained. There, when the mind is distracted, <s>samādhi</s> being subordinate to distraction does not belong on the side of <s>Yoga</s>

children.text:
yas tv ekāgre cetasi sadbhūtam arthaṃ pradyotayati kṣiṇoti ca kleśān karmabandhanāni
            ślathayati nirodham abhimukhaṃ karoti sa saṃprajñāto yoga ity ākhyāyate. sa ca
            vitarkānugato vicārānugata ānandānugato 'smitānugata ity upariṣṭān nivedayiṣyāmaḥ.
            sarvavṛttinirodhe tv asaṃprajñātaḥ samādhiḥ.
children.translated_text: But that which, when the mind is one-pointed, illumines a real object, also diminishes the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), loosens the bonds of <s>karma</s> (action), and makes for restraint—this is termed discriminative (<s>saṃprajñāta</s>) <s>Yoga</s>; and it is accompanied by deliberation (<s>vitarka</s>), accompanied by reflection (<s>vicāra</s>), accompanied by bliss (<s>ānanda</s>), and accompanied by the sense of I-ness (<s>asmitā</s>), as we shall explain below. But when all the modifications are restrained, then it is non-discriminative (<s>asaṃprajñāta</s>) <s>samādhi</s>
Desiring to state its definition, this sūtra was set forth —
<s>Yoga</s> is the cessation of the modifications of the mind

children.text:
sarvaśabdāgrahaṇāt saṃprajñāto 'pi yoga ity ākhyāyate. cittaṃ hi
            prakhyāpravṛttisthitiśīlatvāt triguṇam.
children.translated_text: Because the term “all” is not employed, even discriminative <s>Yoga</s> is also so called. For the mind (<s>citta</s>), by reason of its nature of manifestation, activity, and stability, is of the three <s>guṇas</s> (constituents)

children.text:
prakhyārūpaṃ hi cittasattvaṃ rajastamobhyāṃ saṃsṛṣṭam aiśvaryaviṣayapriyaṃ bhavati. tad
            eva tamasānuviddham adharmājñānāvairāgyānaiśvaryopagaṃ bhavati. tad eva
            prakṣīṇamohāvaraṇaṃ sarvataḥ pradyotamānam anuviddhaṃ rajomātrayā
            dharmajñānavairāgyaiśvaryopagaṃ bhavati.
children.translated_text: The sattva-aspect of the mind, being of the nature of manifestation, when commingled with rajas and tamas, becomes fond of dominion and objects; that very mind, when pierced by tamas, becomes associated with non-dharma, ignorance, non-dispassion, and non-lordliness; that very mind, when the veil of delusion is worn thin, shining forth on all sides, and penetrated by mere rajas, becomes associated with dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and lordliness

children.text:
tad eva rajoleśamalāpetaṃ svarūpapratiṣṭhaṃ sattvapuruṣānyatākhyātimātraṃ
            dharmameghadhyānopagaṃ bhavati. tat paraṃ prasaṃkhyānam ity ācakṣate dhyāyinaḥ.
            citiśaktir apariṇāminy apratisaṃkramā darśitaviṣayā śuddhā cānantā ca sattvaguṇātmikā
            ceyam ato viparītā vivekakhyātir iti. atas tasyāṃ viraktaṃ cittaṃ tām api khyātiṃ
            niruṇaddhi. tadavasthaṃ saṃskāropagaṃ bhavati. sa nirbījaḥ samādhiḥ. na tatra kiṃcit
            saṃprajñāyata ity asaṃprajñātaḥ. dvividhaḥ sa yogaś cittavṛttinirodha iti.
children.translated_text: That very mind, when free from the slight stain of rajas, established in its own nature, consisting only of the cognition of the otherness of sattva and <s>puruṣa</s> (<s>sattva</s>-<s>puruṣa</s> otherness-cognition), becomes associated with the meditation called the cloud of dharma (<s>dharmamegha</s>); that supreme is what meditators call discriminative knowledge (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>). The power of consciousness (<s>citi-śakti</s>), unchanging, not passing over to another, having shown its object, is pure and infinite, and is of the nature of the sattva-<s>guṇa</s>; and the discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>) is the opposite of this. Therefore, the mind, dispassionate even towards that knowledge, restrains that very cognition. In that state it becomes associated with latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>); that is seedless <s>samādhi</s>. There, nothing is cognized; therefore it is non-discriminative (<s>asaṃprajñāta</s>). Thus that <s>Yoga</s> is twofold, as the cessation of the modifications of the mind

children.text: tadavasthe cetasi viṣayābhāvād buddhibodhātmā puruṣaḥ kiṃsvabhāva iti ---
children.translated_text: When the mind is in that condition, in the absence of objects, what is the nature of the <s>puruṣa</s>, whose essence is the illumination of the intellect? —
Then there is abiding in the seer’s own nature

children.text:
svarūpapratiṣṭhā tadānīṃ citiśaktir yathā kaivalye. vyutthānacitte tu sati tathāpi
            bhavantī na tathā.
children.translated_text: Abiding in one’s own nature—then the power of consciousness is as in isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>); but when the mind has arisen again, although it still exists in that way, it is not thus
How then? Because it presents an object —
Elsewhere there is conformity with the modifications

children.text:
vyutthāne yāś cittavṛttayas tadaviśiṣṭavṛttiḥ puruṣaḥ. tathā ca sūtram ekam eva
            darśanaṃ khyātir eva darśanam iti. cittam ayaskāntamaṇikalpaṃ saṃnidhimātropakāri
            dṛśyatvena svaṃ bhavati puruṣasya svāminaḥ. tasmāc cittavṛttibodhe puruṣasyānādiḥ
            saṃbandho hetuḥ.
children.translated_text: In emergence, the modifications of the mind are those whose function the <s>puruṣa</s> does not differ from; and thus there is one sūtra only: “seeing is just recognition; recognition is just seeing.” The mind (<s>citta</s>), like a loadstone, is helpful merely by proximity, and, being the seen, becomes one’s own—of the <s>puruṣa</s>, the master; therefore, the beginningless relation of the <s>puruṣa</s> is the cause in the cognition of the mind’s modifications

children.text: tāḥ punar niroddhavyā bahutve sati cittasya ---
children.translated_text: Now those, on the other hand, are to be restrained, the mind having a multiplicity [of them] —
The modifications are of five kinds, afflicted and non-afflicted

children.text:
kleśahetukāḥ karmāśayapracaye kṣetrībhūtāḥ kliṣṭāḥ. khyātiviṣayā guṇādhikāravirodhinyo
            'kliṣṭāḥ. kliṣṭapravāhapatitā apy akliṣṭāḥ. kliṣṭacchidreṣv apy akliṣṭā bhavanti.
            akliṣṭacchideṣu kliṣṭā iti. tathājātīyakāḥ saṃskārā vṛttibhir eva kriyante. saṃskāraiś
            ca vṛttaya iti. evaṃ vṛttisaṃskāracakram aniśam āvartate. tad evaṃbhūtaṃ cittam
            avasitādhikāram ātmakalpena vyavatiṣṭhate pralayaṃ vā gacchatīti. tāḥ kliṣṭāś cākliṣṭāś
            ca pañcadhā vṛttayaḥ.
children.translated_text: Afflicted are those whose cause is the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), which, becoming a field, lead to the accumulation of the deposit of <s>karma</s> (<s>karmāśaya</s>); non-afflicted are those whose object is recognition (<s>khyāti</s>) and which are opposed to dominion of the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents). Even [modifications] fallen into an afflicted stream are [sometimes] non-afflicted; even in the fissures of the afflicted they become non-afflicted; in the fissures of the non-afflicted, they are afflicted. Thus, impressions (<s>saṃskāras</s>) of the same kind are produced precisely by the modifications; and through the impressions, the modifications [arise]. In this way, the wheel of modifications and impressions revolves incessantly. Such being the case, the mind, its function exhausted, remains as if of the nature of its own self, or goes to dissolution; thus the modifications, afflicted and non-afflicted, are fivefold
Right knowledge, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory
Perception, inference, and authoritative testimony are means of right knowledge

children.text:
indriyapraṇālikayā cittasya bāhyavastūparāgāt tadviṣayā sāmānyaviśeṣātmano 'rthasya
            viśeṣāvadhāraṇapradhānā vṛttiḥ pratyakṣaṃ pramāṇam. phalam aviśiṣṭaḥ pauruṣeyaś
            cittavṛttibodhaḥ. pratisaṃvedī puruṣa ity upariṣṭād upapādayiṣyāmaḥ.
children.translated_text: Perception is the modification of the mind, chiefly a determination of the particular of an object whose nature is both general and particular, having that as its object, due to the tinging of the mind by an external thing through the channel of the senses; the result is the undifferentiated, personal cognition that is a modification of the mind; that the <s>puruṣa</s> experiences [that cognition] we shall establish below

children.text:
anumeyasya tulyajātīyeṣv anuvṛtto bhinnajātīyebhyo vyāvṛttaḥ saṃbandho yas tadviṣayā
            sāmānyāvadhāraṇapradhānā vṛttir anumānam. yathā deśāntaraprāpter gatimac candratārakaṃ
            caitravat, vindhyaś cāprāptir agatiḥ. āptena dṛṣṭo 'numito vārthaḥ paratra
            svabodhasaṃkrāntaye śabdenopadiśyate, śabdāt tadarthaviṣayā vṛttiḥ śrotur āgamaḥ.
            yasyāśraddheyārtho vaktā na dṛṣṭānumitārthaḥ sa āgamaḥ plavate. mūlavaktari tu
            dṛṣṭānumitārthe nirviplavaḥ syāt.
children.translated_text: Inference is that modification whose object is the relation—continuant among those of the same kind as what is to be inferred, and excluded from those of a different kind—being chiefly a determination of the general pertaining to that; for example, as motion to another place implies that the moon and stars move, like <s>Caitra</s>, while the <s>Vindhya</s> does not move, implying non-motion; what is seen or inferred by a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>) is taught elsewhere by a word, for the transmission of his own cognition, and from the word there arises in the hearer the modification whose object is that thing—this is authoritative testimony (<s>āgama</s>). But if the speaker is not trustworthy regarding the matter, not having seen or inferred it, that <s>āgama</s> wavers; whereas when the original teacher has seen or inferred the matter, it would be unwavering
Error is false cognition, established in a form other than that [of the object]

children.text:
sa kasmān na pramāṇam. yataḥ pramāṇena bādhyate. bhūtārthaviṣayatvāt pramāṇasya. tatra
            pramāṇena bādhanam apramāṇasya dṛṣṭam. tadyathā dvicandradarśanaṃ
            sadviṣayeṇaikacandradarśanena bādhyata iti. seyaṃ pañcaparvā bhavaty avidyā.
            avidyāsmitārāgadveṣābhiniveśāḥ kleśā iti. eta eva svasaṃjñābhis tamo moho mahāmohas
            tāmisro 'ndhatāmisra iti. ete cittamalaprasaṅgenābhidhāsyante.
children.translated_text: Why is that not a means of right knowledge? Because it is sublated by right knowledge, since a means of right knowledge has real things as its object; there, the sublation of a non-means of right knowledge by a means of right knowledge is observed—just as the seeing of two moons is sublated by the seeing of a single moon whose object is real. This is five-limbed ignorance; the afflictions are ignorance, I-ness, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life. These very [afflictions], with their own names, are darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, and utter gloom; these will be spoken of in connection with the impurity of the mind
Conceptual construction is a modification devoid of a real object, following upon verbal cognition

children.text:
sa na pramāṇopārohī. na viparyayopārohī ca. vastuśūnyatve+api
            śabdajñānamāhātmyanibandhano vyavahāro dṛśyate. tad yathā caitanyaṃ puruṣasya svarūpam
            iti. yadā citir eva puruṣas tadā kim atra kena vyapadiśyate.
children.translated_text: It does not admit of being superimposed as a means of right knowledge, nor as error; although devoid of a real object, a conventional usage grounded in the potency of verbal cognition is seen—for instance, “consciousness is the very nature of the <s>puruṣa</s>.” When consciousness itself is the <s>puruṣa</s>, then what here is designated by what and by whom?

children.text:
bhavati ca vyapadeśe vṛttiḥ. yathā caitrasya gaur iti. tathā pratiṣiddhavastudharmo
            niṣkriyaḥ puruṣaḥ, tiṣṭhati bāṇaḥ sthāsyati sthita iti. gatinivṛttau dhātvarthamātraṃ
            gamyate. tathānutpattidharmā puruṣa iti, utpattidharmasyābhāvamātram avagamyate na
            puruṣānvayī dharmaḥ. tasmād vikalpitaḥ sa dharmas tena cāsti vyavahāra iti.
children.translated_text: And a modification occurs in designation—just as “Caitra’s is the cow.” Likewise, [we say] “the <s>puruṣa</s>, whose property is that of the negated object, is inactive,” “the arrow stands,” “it will stand,” “it stood”—upon the cessation of motion, only the verbal root-meaning is apprehended; likewise, [when one says] “the <s>puruṣa</s> is of the property of non-arising,” only the absence of the property of arising is apprehended, not a property inhering in the <s>puruṣa</s>. Therefore that property is conceptualized, and yet there is usage
Sleep is the modification having as its support a cognition of absence

children.text:
sā ca saṃprabodhe pratyavamarśāt pratyayaviśeṣaḥ. katham, sukham aham asvāpsam.
            prasannaṃ me manaḥ. prajñāṃ me viśāradīkaroti. duḥkham aham asvāpsam. styānaṃ me mano
            bhramaty anavasthitam gāḍhaṃ mūḍho 'ham asvāpsam. gurūṇi me gātrāṇi. klāntaṃ me cittam.
            alasaṃ muṣitam iva tiṣṭhatīti. sa khalv ayaṃ prabuddhasya pratyavamarśo na syād asati
            pratyayānubhave tadāśritāḥ smṛtayś ca tadviṣayā na syuḥ. tasmāt pratyayaviśeṣo nidrā. sā
            ca samādhāv itarapratyayavan niroddhavyeti.
children.translated_text: And this, upon waking, is a specific cognition discerned by reflective awareness; how so? “I slept happily; my mind is clear; it makes my discernment skillful; I slept unhappily; my mind is torpid; it wanders, unsettled; I slept in deep stupefaction; my limbs are heavy; my mind is weary; it stands as if sluggish and robbed,” yet indeed this reflective awareness would not occur for one who is awakened if there were no prior experience of a cognition, and the memories that rely on that, having that as their object, would not exist; therefore sleep is a specific cognition, and it too, like the other-cognitions, is to be restrained in <s>samādhi</s> (enstasis)
Memory is the non-loss of what has been experienced as an object

children.text:
kiṃ pratyayasya cittaṃ smaraty āhosvid viṣayasyeti. grāhyoparaktaḥ pratyayo
            grāhyagrahaṇobhayākāranirbhāsas tajjātīyakaṃ saṃskāram ārabhate. sa saṃskāraḥ
            svavyañjakāñjanas tadākārām eva grāhyagrahaṇobhayātmikāṃ smṛtiṃ janayati.
children.translated_text: Is it the mind’s cognition that remembers, or is it the object? The cognition, tinged by the graspable, shining forth in the dual form of graspable and grasping, initiates an impression of its own kind; that impression, being its own revealer, produces a memory of precisely that form, having the dual nature of graspable and grasping

children.text:
tatra grahaṇākārapūrvā buddhiḥ. grāhyākārapūrvā smṛtiḥ. sā ca dvayī ---
            bhāvitasmartavyā cābhāvitasmartavyā ca. svapne bhāvitasmartavyā. jāgratsamaye tv
            abhāvitasmartavyeti. sarvāḥ smṛtayaḥ pramāṇaviparyayavikalpanidrāsmṛtīnām anubhavāt
            prabhavanti. sarvāś caitā vṛttayaḥ sukhaduḥkhamohātmikāḥ. sukhaduḥkhamohāś ca kleśeṣu
            vyākhyeyāḥ. sukhānuśayī rāgaḥ. duḥkhānuśayī dveṣaḥ. mohaḥ punar avidyeti.
children.translated_text: Therein, understanding is preceded by the form of grasping; memory is preceded by the form of the graspable; and it is twofold—both cultivated-to-be-remembered and uncultivated-to-be-remembered; in dream it is cultivated-to-be-remembered, whereas in the waking time it is uncultivated-to-be-remembered; all memories arise from the experience of right knowledge, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory; and all these modifications are of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion; and pleasure, pain, and delusion should be explained among the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions): attachment (<s>rāga</s>) accompanies pleasure, aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) accompanies pain, and delusion is in fact ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>)

children.text:
etāḥ sarvā vṛttayo niroddhavyāḥ. āsāṃ nirodhe saṃprajñāto vā samādhir bhavaty
            asaṃprajñāto veti.
children.translated_text: All these modifications are to be restrained; upon their restraint, <s>samādhi</s> is either discriminative (<s>saṃprajñāta</s>) or non-discriminative (<s>asaṃprajñāta</s>)
Now, as to the means for their restraint—
By practice and dispassion is their restraint

children.text:
cittanadī nāmobhayatovāhinī vahati kalyāṇāya vahati pāpāya ca. yā tu kaivalyaprāgbhārā
            vivekaviṣayanimnā sā kalyāṇavahā. saṃsāraprāgbhārāvivekaviṣayaniṃnā pāpavahā. tatra
            vairāgyeṇa viṣayasrotaḥ khilīkriyate. vivekadarśanābhyāsena vivekasrota udghāṭyata ity
            ubhayādhīnaś cittavṛttinirodhaḥ.
children.translated_text: The river of mind, so called, flows both ways; it flows toward the auspicious and it flows toward the inauspicious; that which slopes toward the field of <s>viveka</s> (discriminative insight), weighted in advance toward <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation), that carries the auspicious; weighted in advance toward saṃsāra and sloping toward non-<s>viveka</s>, it carries the inauspicious; there, by dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) the current toward objects is dammed up, and by practice of the vision of <s>viveka</s> the current of <s>viveka</s> is opened—thus the restraint of the mind’s modifications depends on both
There, effort toward steadiness is practice

children.text:
cittasyāvṛttikasya praśāntavāhitā sthitiḥ. tadarthaḥ prayatno vīryam utsāhaḥ. tat
            saṃpipādayiṣayā tat sādhanānuṣṭhānam abhyāsaḥ.
children.translated_text: The steadiness is the tranquil, even flow of a mind devoid of modifications; the effort for that—energy, vigor, zeal—for the desire to mature that, the undertaking of the means to accomplish it is practice
And this, practiced for a long time, without interruption, and with reverence, becomes well-founded

children.text:
dīrghakālāsevito nirantarāsevitaḥ satkārāsevitaḥ. tapasā brahmacaryeṇa vidyayā
            śraddhayā ca saṃpāditaḥ satkāravān dṛḍhabhūmir bhavati. vyutthānasaṃskāreṇa drāg ity
            evānabhibhūtaviṣaya ity arthaḥ.
children.translated_text: Practiced for a long time, practiced without interruption, practiced with reverence; brought to completion by austerity (<s>tapas</s>), celibate conduct (<s>brahmacarya</s>), knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>), and faith (<s>śraddhā</s>), endowed with reverence, it becomes well-founded; “quickly” means “not overpowered by the impression of emergence,” that is, not overmastered by the domain of distraction
Dispassion is the mastery-designated state of one who is without thirst for objects seen and heard-about

children.text:
striyo+annapānam aiśvaryam iti dṛṣṭaviṣaye vitṛṣṇasya
            svargavaidehyaprakṛtilayatvaprāptāv ānuśravikaviṣaye vitṛṣṇasya
            divyādivyaviṣayasaṃprayoge+api cittasya viṣayadoṣadarśinaḥ prasaṃkhyānabalād
            anābhogātmikā heyopādeyaśūnyā vaśīkārasaṃjñā vairāgyam.
children.translated_text: For one without thirst for visible objects—women, food and drink, lordly power—and for one without thirst for heard-about objects—attainment of heaven, disembodiment, and dissolution into <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature)—even in contact with divine and non-divine objects, for a mind that, through the power of discriminative contemplation (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), sees the defects of objects, dispassion, called mastery, is of the nature of non-indulgence, devoid of what is to be shunned and what is to be taken up
That which is higher is indifference to the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents) through knowledge of the <s>puruṣa</s> (person)

children.text:
dṛṣṭānuśravikaviṣayadoṣadarśī viraktaḥ puruṣadarśanābhyāsāt
            tacchuddhipravivekāpyāyitabuddhir guṇebhyo vyaktāvyaktadharmakebhyo virakta iti. tad
            dvayaṃ vairāgyam. tatra yad uttaraṃ taj jñānaprasādamātram. yasyodaye sati yogī
            pratyuditakhyātir evaṃ manyate --- prāptaṃ prāpaṇīyaṃ, kṣīṇāḥ kṣetavyāḥ kleśāḥ, chinnaḥ
            śliṣṭaparvā bhavasaṃkramaḥ, yasyāvicchedāj janitvā mriyate mṛtvā ca jāyata iti.
            jñānasyaiva parā kāṣṭhā vairāgyam. etasyaiva hi nāntarīyakaṃ kaivalyam iti.
children.translated_text: He who sees the faults in objects seen and heard-about, being dispassionate, through the practice of the vision of the <s>puruṣa</s> (person), whose intellect, nourished by purity and discriminative discernment (<s>praviveka</s>), becomes dispassionate toward the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents), which possess the properties of manifest and unmanifest—this twofold is dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>). Of these, that which is higher is nothing but the lucidity of knowledge; when this arises, the yogin, with recognition newly arisen, thinks thus—“what was to be attained has been attained, the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) that were to be eradicated are exhausted, the course of becoming, whose joints are interlinked, is cut; because of the non-break [of this state], one, having been born, dies, and dying is born”—dispassion is the very highest limit of knowledge; indeed, for this very one, isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>) is immediate

children.text: athopāyadvayena niruddhacittavṛtteḥ katham ucyate saṃprajñātaḥ samādhir iti ---
children.translated_text: Now, by the two means, when the modifications of the mind have been restrained, how is it said that <s>samādhi</s> (enstasis) is discriminative (<s>saṃprajñāta</s>),—
By following upon the forms of vitarka (discursive examination), vicāra (subtle reflection), bliss (<s>ānanda</s>), and I-am-ness (<s>asmitā</s>) there is discriminative <s>samādhi</s>

children.text:
vitarkaś cittasyālambane sthūla ābhogaḥ. sūkṣmo vicāraḥ. ānando hlādaḥ. ekātmikā saṃvid
            asmitā. tatra prathamaś catuṣṭayānugataḥ samādhiḥ savitarkaḥ. dvitīyo vitarkavikalaḥ
            savicāraḥ. tṛtīyo vicāravikalaḥ sānandaḥ. caturthas tadvikalo 'smitāmātra iti. sarva ete
            sālambanāḥ samādhayaḥ.
children.translated_text: Vitarka is the gross engagement of the mind with a support; subtle is vicāra; <s>ānanda</s> is delight; <s>asmitā</s> is a cognition that is of one essence [with its object]. Therein, the first <s>samādhi</s>, accompanied by the first four, is with vitarka; the second, lacking vitarka, is with vicāra; the third, lacking vicāra, is with bliss; the fourth, lacking that, is mere I-am-ness—thus all these <s>samādhis</s> are with a support
Now, as for non-discriminative <s>samādhi</s> (<s>asaṃprajñāta</s>): what is its means and what its nature?—
Another [<s>samādhi</s>] preceded by the practice whose idea is cessation, with only impressions remaining

children.text:
sarvavṛttipratyastamaye saṃskāraśeṣo nirodhaś cittasya samādhir asaṃprajñātaḥ. tasya
            paraṃ vairāgyam upāyaḥ. sālambano hy abhyāsas tatsādhanāya na kalpata iti virāmapratyayo
            nirvastuka ālambanīkriyate. sa cārthaśūnyaḥ. tadabhyāsapūrvakaṃ hi cittaṃ nirālambanam
            abhāvaprāptam iva bhavatīty eṣa nirbījaḥ samādhir asaṃprajñātaḥ.
children.translated_text: When all modifications have subsided, the restraint of the mind, with only impressions remaining, is non-discriminative <s>samādhi</s>; for that the supreme dispassion is the means. For practice with a support is not suitable for accomplishing that; therefore the idea of cessation, being without a real object, is made the support; and that is devoid of content. Indeed, preceded by the practice of that, the mind becomes supportless, as if it had attained non-existence—this is seedless <s>samādhi</s>, non-discriminative

children.text:
sa khalv ayaṃ dvividhaḥ --- upāyapratyayo bhavapratyayaś ca. tatropāyapratyayo yogināṃ
            bhavati ---
children.translated_text: Now this indeed is twofold—having the [meditative] means as its basis, and having becoming as its basis. Of these, the one having means as its basis belongs to yogins—
The one having becoming as its basis belongs to the disembodied and to those dissolved into <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature)

children.text:
videhānāṃ devānāṃ bhavapratyayaḥ. te hi svasaṃskāramātropayogena cittena kaivalyapadam
            ivānubhavantaḥ svasaṃskāravipākaṃ tathājātīyakam ativāhayanti. tathā prakṛtilayāḥ
            sādhikāre cetasi prakṛtilīne kaivalyapadam ivānubhavanti, yāvan na punar
            āvartate+adhikāravaśāc cittam iti.
children.translated_text: For the disembodied gods it is the one based on becoming; for they, with a mind making use only of their own latent impressions, experiencing as it were the state of isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>), carry over into the ripening of their own impressions that which is of the same kind; likewise, those dissolved into <s>Prakṛti</s>, while the mind, along with its sphere of operation, is merged into <s>Prakṛti</s>, experience as it were the state of isolation, until the mind returns again by force of the residual claim to activity
For others, it is preceded by faith (<s>śraddhā</s>), vigor (<s>vīrya</s>), memory (<s>smṛti</s>), <s>samādhi</s>, and insight (<s>prajñā</s>)

children.text:
upāyapratyayo yogināṃ bhavati. śraddhā cetasaḥ saṃprasādaḥ. sā hi jananīva kalyāṇī
            yoginaṃ pāti. tasya hi śraddadhānasya vivekārthino vīryam upajāyate. samupajātavīryasya
            smṛtir upatiṣṭhate. smṛtyupasthāne ca cittam anākulaṃ samādhīyate. samāhitacittasya
            prajñāviveka upāvartate. yena yathārthaṃ vastu jānāti. tadabhyāsāt tattadviṣayāc ca
            vairāgyād asaṃprajñātaḥ samādhir bhavati.
children.translated_text: The one based on means belongs to yogins. Faith is the serenity of the mind; for she, auspicious like a mother, protects the yogin. For him who has faith and desires <s>viveka</s> (discriminative insight), vigor arises; when vigor has arisen, memory is established; when memory is established, the mind, undisturbed, becomes enstatically collected; for the one whose mind is collected, insight-as-discrimination (<s>prajñā-viveka</s>) returns, by which he knows a thing as it really is; from the practice of that and from dispassion toward each respective object, there is non-discriminative <s>samādhi</s>

children.text:
te khalu nava yogino mṛdumadhyādhimātropāyā bhavanti. tadyathā --- mṛdūpāyo
            madhyopāyo+adhimātropāya iti. tatra mṛdūpāyas trividhaḥ --- mṛdusaṃvego madhyasaṃvegas
            tīvrasaṃvega iti. tathā madhyopāyas tathādhimātropāya iti. tatrādhimātropāyānām ---
children.translated_text: Now these yogins are nine, having mild, middling, and excessive measures of the means. Namely—mild means, middling means, and excessively strong means. Therein the mild means is threefold—mildly impelled, moderately impelled, intensely impelled; so too the middling means, and so too the excessively strong means. Among those of excessively strong means—
For those intensely impelled it is near at hand
Both the attainment of <s>samādhi</s> and the fruit of <s>samādhi</s> occur
From mildness, middlingness, and excessiveness, there is yet further distinction

children.text:
mṛdutīvro madhyatīvro+adhimātratīvra iti. tato 'pi viśeṣaḥ. tadviśeṣād api
            mṛdutīvrasaṃvegasyāsannaḥ tato madhyatīvrasaṃvegasyāsannataraḥ, tasmād
            adhimātratīvrasaṃvegasyādhimātropāyasyāpy āsannatamaḥ samādhilābhaḥ samādhiphalaṃ
            ceti.
children.translated_text: Mild-intense, middling-intense, and supremely-intense—that is the classification. Even beyond that there is a distinction. From that very distinction too: for one with mild-intense impulsion it is near at hand; from that, for one with middling-intense impulsion it is nearer; than that, for one with supremely-intense impulsion, even with a supremely-great means, the attainment of <s>samādhi</s> (enstasis) and the fruit of <s>samādhi</s> are nearest

children.text:
kim etasmād evāsannatamaḥ samādhir bhavati. athāsya lābhe bhavaty anyo 'pi kaścid upāyo
            na veti ---
children.translated_text: Is it only from this that <s>samādhi</s> becomes nearest? Or, upon its attainment, is there perhaps some other means as well, or not—
Or by devotion to <s>Īśvara</s>

children.text:
praṇidhānād bhaktiviśeṣād āvarjita īśvaras tam anugṛhṇāty abhidhyānamātreṇa.
            tadabhidhyānamātrād api yogina āsannatamaḥ samādhilābhaḥ samādhiphalaṃ ca bhavatīti.
children.translated_text: By devotion, by a distinctive form of bhakti, <s>Īśvara</s>, being drawn toward him, favors him by mere contemplation; and even from that mere contemplation, for the yogin the attainment of <s>samādhi</s>, nearest of all, and the fruit of <s>samādhi</s> arise
Now, is this <s>Īśvara</s>, distinct from <s>Pradhāna</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, who or what is he, or not—
<s>Īśvara</s> is a special <s>puruṣa</s> untouched by the afflictions, actions, fruition, and deposits of latent impressions

children.text:
avidyādayaḥ kleśāḥ. kuśalākuśalāni karmāṇi. tatphalaṃ vipākaḥ. tadanuguṇā vāsanā
            āśayāḥ. te ca manasi vartamānāḥ puruṣe vyapadiśyante, sa hi tatphalasya bhokteti. yathā
            jayaḥ parājayo vā yoddhṛṣu vartamānaḥ svāmini vyapadiśyate. yo hy anena
            bhogenāparāmṛṣṭaḥ sa puruṣaviśeṣa īśvaraḥ.
children.translated_text: The afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>) are ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) and the rest. The actions are meritorious and demeritorious. Their fruit is fruition (<s>vipāka</s>). The dispositions (<s>vāsanā</s>), corresponding to those, are the deposits (<s>āśayas</s>). And these, while occurring in the mind, are imputed to the <s>puruṣa</s>, for he is the enjoyer of that fruit; just as victory or defeat, though occurring among the fighters, is imputed to the lord. He who is not touched by this enjoyment is the special <s>puruṣa</s>, <s>Īśvara</s>

children.text:
kaivalyaṃ prāptās tarhi santi ca bahavaḥ kevalinaḥ. te hi trīṇi bandhanāni cchittvā
            kaivalyaṃ prāptā īśvarasya ca tatsaṃbandho na bhūto na bhāvī. yathā muktasya pūrvā
            bandhakoṭiḥ prajñāyate naivam īśvarasya. yathā vā prakṛtilīnasyottarā bandhakoṭiḥ
            saṃbhāvyate naivam īśvarasya. sa tu sadaiva muktaḥ sadaiveśvara iti.
children.translated_text: But then, since isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>) has been attained, there are indeed many isolated ones; they, having cut the three bonds, have attained <s>kaivalya</s>, and with <s>Īśvara</s> there is neither past nor future connection of that sort. Just as for one liberated the prior series of bondage is cognized, not so for <s>Īśvara</s>; or just as for one merged into <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) a subsequent series of bondage is conceivable, not so for <s>Īśvara</s>. But he is ever liberated, ever the Lord

children.text:
yo 'sau prakṛṣṭasattvopādānād īśvarasya śāśvatika utkarṣaḥ sa kiṃ sanimitta āhosvin
            nirnimitta iti. tasya śāstraṃ nimittam.
children.translated_text: Now, the perpetual excellence of <s>Īśvara</s>, arising from the adoption of exceedingly pure <s>sattva</s> (lucidity), is that with a cause or without a cause? Its cause is scripture (<s>śāstra</s>)
And what is the cause of scripture? The cause is exceedingly pure <s>sattva</s>

children.text:
etayoḥ śāstrotkarṣayor īśvarasattve vartamānayor anādiḥ saṃbandhaḥ. etasmād etad
            bhavati sadaiveśvaraḥ sadaiva mukta iti. tac ca tasyaiśvaryaṃ sāmyātiśayavinirmuktam. na
            tāvad aiśvaryāntareṇa tad atiśayyate. yad evātiśayi syāt tad eva tat syāt. tasmād yatra
            kāṣṭhāprāptir aiśvaryasya sa īśvara iti. na ca tatsamānam aiśvaryam asti. kasmāt, dvayos
            tulyayor ekasmin yugapatkāmite+arthe navam idam astu purāṇam idam astv ity ekasya
            siddhāv itarasya prākāmyavighātād ūnatvaṃ prasaktam. dvayoś ca tulyayor
            yugapatkāmitārthaprāptir nāsti. arthasya viruddhatvāt. tasmād yasya sāmyātiśayair
            vinirmuktam aiśvaryaṃ sa eveśvaraḥ. sa ca puruṣaviśeṣa iti.
children.translated_text: Between these two—excellence of scripture and the presence of <s>Īśvara</s>—there is a beginningless relation. From this it follows: he is ever the Lord, ever liberated. And that lordship of his is free from superiority and from parity; by no other lordship is that surpassed, for whatever would surpass it would itself be that very thing. Therefore, he in whom there is the extremity of attainment of lordship is <s>Īśvara</s>. Nor is there lordship equal to that. Why? For two equals, if, with respect to one and the same object simultaneously desired, one were to have “let this be new, let that be old,” then, upon the success of the one, because of the obstruction of the other’s prerogative, inferiority would result. And for two equals there is no simultaneous attainment of an object simultaneously desired, because the object is mutually opposed. Therefore, he whose lordship is free from parity and superiority—he alone is <s>Īśvara</s>; and he is a special <s>puruṣa</s>
Moreover—
There, the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed

children.text:
yad idam atītānāgatapratyutpannapratyekasamuccayātīndriyagrahaṇam alpaṃ bahv iti
            sarvajñabījam etad vivardhamānaṃ yatra niratiśayaṃ sa sarvajñaḥ. asti kāṣṭhāprāptiḥ
            sarvajñabījasya sātiśayatvāt parimāṇavad iti. yatra kāṣṭhāprāptir jñānasya sa sarvajñaḥ.
            sa ca puruṣaviśeṣa iti.
children.translated_text: This grasping—beyond the senses—of each and every collection of past, future, and present, whether little or much, this is the seed of omniscience; where this, growing, is unsurpassed, he is omniscient. There is an extremity of attainment of the seed of omniscience, since, having superiority, it is measurable; where there is the extremity of attainment of knowledge, he is omniscient; and he is a special <s>puruṣa</s>

children.text:
sāmānyamātropasaṃhāre ca kṛtopakṣayam anumānaṃ na viśeṣapratipattau samartham iti.
            tasya saṃjñādiviśeṣapratipattir āgamataḥ paryanveṣyā. tasyātmānugrahābhāve+api
            bhūtānugrahaḥ prayojanam. jñānadharmopadeśena kalpapralayamahāpralayeṣu saṃsāriṇaḥ
            puruṣān uddhariṣyāmīti. tathā coktam --- ādividvān nirmāṇacittam adhiṣṭhāya kāruṇyād
            bhagavān paramarṣir āsuraye jijñāsamānāya tantraṃ provāceti.
children.translated_text: And moreover, where there is only a general summative conclusion, inference, having accomplished the removal of [ignorance] to that extent, is not capable with respect to the ascertainment of the particular; therefore, the ascertainment of his particular designations and the like is to be traced from scripture (<s>āgama</s>), even though there is no benefaction to himself, the benefaction to beings is the purpose, “By instructing in the dharma of knowledge I shall lift up the transmigrating <s>puruṣas</s> at the [periodic] dissolution of a cycle and at the great dissolution,” and thus it has been said—“the knower of the beginning (<s>ādi-vidvān</s>), having assumed a mind created by will (<s>nirmāṇa-citta</s>), out of compassion, the Blessed Supreme Seer (<s>bhagavān paramarṣi</s>) spoke a scripture (<s>tantra</s>) to <s>Āsuri</s>, who was desiring to know,”
He is this one—
He is also the teacher of the former ones, because he is not delimited by time

children.text:
pūrve hi guravaḥ kālenāvacchidyante. yatrāvacchedārthena kālo nopāvartate sa eṣa
            pūrveṣām api guruḥ. yathāsya sargasyādau prakarṣagatyā siddhas tathātikrāntasargādiṣv
            api pratyetavyaḥ.
children.translated_text: For the former teachers indeed are limited by time; he, with respect to whom time does not recur as a delimiter, this very one is the teacher even of the former ones; as at the beginning of this creation he is to be understood as perfected through the excellence of his course, so also in creations that have passed beyond, and so forth
His denotative word is the <s>praṇava</s> (the syllable Om)

children.text:
vācya īśvaraḥ praṇavasya. kim asya saṃketakṛtaṃ vācyavācakatvam atha pradīpaprakāśavad
            avasthitam iti.
children.translated_text: The denoted is <s>Īśvara</s> of the <s>praṇava</s>; now, is the relation of denoted and denotative for this established by convention, or is it as established as the illumination of a lamp?

children.text:
sthito+asya vācyasya vācakena saha saṃbandhaḥ. saṃketas tv īśravasya sthitam evārtham
            abhinayati. yathāvasthitaḥ pitṛputrayoḥ saṃbandhaḥ saṃketenāvadyotyate, ayam asya pitā,
            ayam asya putra iti. sargāntareṣv api vācyavācakaśaktyapekṣas tathaiva saṃketaḥ kriyate.
            saṃpratipattinityatayā nityaḥ śabdārthasaṃbandha ity āgaminaḥ pratijānate.
children.translated_text: The relation of the denoted, which is established, with the denotative, is established; and convention, for <s>Īśvara</s>, indicates precisely the already-established meaning; as the relation of father and son, being as it is, is indicated by convention—“this is his father, this is his son”; so too, even in other creations, the convention is made with regard to the powers of denoted and denotative; those who rely on scripture assert that the relation of word and meaning is eternal by reason of the constant mutual apprehension
For the yogin who has understood the denoted-and-denotative relationship—
Its recitation and the contemplation of its meaning

children.text:
praṇavasya japaḥ praṇavābhidheyasya ceśvarasya bhāvanam. tad asya yoginaḥ praṇavaṃ
            japataḥ praṇavārthaṃ ca bhāvayataś cittam ekāgraṃ saṃpadyate. tathā coktam ---
children.translated_text: The recitation of the <s>praṇava</s>, and the contemplation of <s>Īśvara</s> who is signified by the <s>praṇava</s>; then, for this yogin who recites the <s>praṇava</s> and contemplates the meaning of the <s>praṇava</s>, the mind becomes one-pointed; and so it has been said—

children.text:
svādhyāyād yogam āsīta yogāt svādhyāyam āmanet / svādhyāyayogasaṃpattyā
              paramātmā prakāśate //
children.translated_text: From self-recitation (<s>svādhyāya</s>) one should enter into <s>yoga</s>, and from <s>yoga</s> one should undertake self-recitation; by the accomplishment of self-recitation and <s>yoga</s>, the Supreme Self (<s>paramātman</s>) becomes manifest
And further, what accrues to him—
Thence, the attainment of inward consciousness and also the absence of obstacles

children.text:
ye tāvad antarāyā vyādhiprabhṛtayas te tāvad īśvarapraṇidhānān na bhavanti.
            svarūpadarśanam apy asya bhavati. yathaiveśvaraḥ puruṣaḥ śuddhaḥ prasannaḥ
            kevalo+anupasargas tathāyam api buddheḥ pratisaṃvedī yaḥ puruṣas tam adhigacchati.
children.translated_text: Those obstacles beginning with illness do not occur at all because of devotion to <s>Īśvara</s>; likewise, there is for him the vision of his own nature; just as <s>Īśvara</s>, the <s>puruṣa</s>, is pure, serene, alone, untouched by affliction, so this one too attains that <s>puruṣa</s> who, being self-cognizant over against the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), is his own self

children.text: atha ke+antarāyā ye cittasya vikṣepāḥ. ke punas te kiyanto veti ---
children.translated_text: Now then, which are the obstacles—those perturbations of the mind? And what are they, and how many—
Illness, stagnation, doubt, carelessness, laziness, non-abstinence, false seeing, non-attainment of a level, and instability—these are the distractions of the mind; those are the obstacles

children.text:
navāntarāyāś cittasya vikṣepāḥ. sahaite cittavṛttibhir bhavanti. eteṣām abhāve na
            bhavanti pūrvoktāś cittavṛttayaḥ. vyādhir dhāturasakaraṇavaiṣamyam. styānam akarmaṇyatā
            cittasya. saṃśaya ubhayakoṭispṛg vijñānaṃ syād idam evaṃ naivaṃ syād iti. pramādaḥ
            samādhisādhanānām abhāvanam. ālasyaṃ kāyasya cittasya ca gurutvād apravṛttiḥ. aviratiś
            cittasya viṣayasaṃprayogātmā gardhaḥ. bhrāntidarśanaṃ viparyayajñānam.
            alabdhabhūmikatvaṃ samādhibhūmer alābhaḥ. anavasthitatvaṃ yal labdhāyāṃ bhūmau
            cittasyāpratiṣṭhā. samādhipratilambhe hi sati tadavasthitaṃ syād iti. ete cittavikṣepā
            nava yogamalā yogapratipakṣā yogāntarāyā ity abhidhīyante.
children.translated_text: The distractions of the mind are nine obstacles; these occur together with mental modifications, and in the absence of these, the previously mentioned mental modifications do not occur; illness is the inequality of the elements that compose the body; stagnation is the mind’s incapacity for action; doubt is a cognition that grasps both alternatives—“thus it is,” “thus it is not”; carelessness is the non-cultivation of the means to <s>samādhi</s>; laziness is the non-activity of body and mind due to heaviness; non-abstinence is greed, consisting in the mind’s conjunction with objects; false seeing is cognition as error (<s>viparyaya-jñāna</s>); non-attainment of a level is the non-attainment of the level of <s>samādhi</s>; instability is the non-establishment of the mind upon a level that has been attained—for, when the attainment of <s>samādhi</s> has indeed been secured, it should be established in that state; these nine—distractions of the mind—are called the impurities of <s>yoga</s>, the adversaries of <s>yoga</s>, the obstacles to <s>yoga</s>
Suffering, dejection, trembling of the limbs, and inhalation-exhalation are concomitants of distraction

children.text:
duḥkham ādhyātmikam ādhibhautikam ādhidaivikaṃ ca. yenābhihatāḥ prāṇinas tadapaghātāya
            prayatante tad duḥkham. daurmanasyam icchāvighātāc cetasaḥ kṣobhaḥ. yad aṅgāny ejayati
            kampayati tad aṅgamejayatvam. prāṇo yad bāhyaṃ vāyum ācāmati sa śvāsaḥ. yat kauṣṭhyaṃ
            vāyuṃ niḥsārayati sa praśvāsaḥ. ete vikṣepasahabhuvo vikṣiptacittasyaite bhavanti.
            samāhitacittasyaite na bhavanti.
children.translated_text: Suffering is threefold: pertaining to oneself (<s>ādhyātmika</s>), pertaining to beings/external elements (<s>ādhibhautika</s>), and pertaining to the divine (<s>ādhidaivika</s>). That by which living beings are struck, for the removal of which they strive—that is suffering. Dejection (<s>daurmanasya</s>) is an agitation of the mind due to the frustration of desire. That which makes the limbs tremble and shake—that is trembling of the limbs (<s>aṅgamejayatva</s>). When <s>Prāṇa</s> sips in the external air, that is inhalation (<s>śvāsa</s>); when it expels the air from the mouth, that is exhalation (<s>praśvāsa</s>). These are concomitants of distraction; these occur for one whose mind is distracted. For one whose mind is enstatically collected, these do not occur

children.text:
athaite vikṣepāḥ samādhipratipakṣās tābhyām evābhyāsavairāgyābhyāṃ niroddhavyāḥ.
            tatrābhyāsasya viṣayam upasaṃharann idam āha ---
children.translated_text: Now, these distractions are opposed to <s>samādhi</s>; they are to be suppressed by these two—by practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>) and dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>). Thereupon, bringing to a conclusion the scope of practice, he says this—
For the prevention of that, the practice of one-tattva (one principle) [is to be undertaken],

children.text:
vikṣepapratiṣedhārtham ekatattvāvalambanaṃ cittam abhyaset. yasya tu pratyarthaniyataṃ
            pratyayamātraṃ kṣaṇikaṃ ca cittaṃ tasya sarvam eva cittam ekāgraṃ nāsty eva vikṣiptam.
            yadi punar idaṃ sarvataḥ pratyāhṛtyaikasminn arthe samādhīyate tadā bhavaty ekāgram ity
            ato na pratyarthaniyatam.
children.translated_text: For the prevention of distraction, one should practice fixing the mind upon a single principle (<s>ekatattva-avalambana</s>). But for one whose mind is only a momentary cognition, fixed upon a specifically opposed object and restricted to it, for him the entire mind is not one-pointed at all but distracted. If, on the contrary, withdrawing this [mind] from everything, it is collected upon a single object, then it becomes one-pointed, and therefore it is not to be restricted to an opposed object

children.text:
yo+api sadṛśapratyayapravāhena cittam ekāgraṃ manyate tasyaikāgratā yadi
            pravāhacittasya dharmas tadaikaṃ nāsti pravāhacittaṃ kṣaṇikatvāt. atha pravāhāṃśasyaiva
            pratyayasya dharmaḥ, sa sarvaḥ sadṛśapratyayapravāhī vā visadṛśapratyayapravāhī vā
            pratyarthaniyatatvād ekāgra eveti vikṣiptacittānupapattiḥ. tasmād ekam anekārtham
            avasthitaṃ cittam iti.
children.translated_text: And if someone thinks the mind is one-pointed by a stream of similar cognitions—if his one-pointedness is a property of a stream-mind, then there is no one [mind], for a stream-mind is momentary; or if it is a property of only a portion of the stream, then whether the stream of similar cognitions or of dissimilar cognitions, being restricted to an opposed object, it would be one-pointed—thus the consequence that a distracted mind would be untenable. Therefore, the mind is one, established with respect to many objects

children.text:
yadi ca cittenaikenānanvitāḥ svabhāvabhinnāḥ pratyayā jāyerann atha katham
            anyapratyayadṛṣṭasyānyaḥ smartā bhavet. anyapratyayopacitasya ca karmāśayasyānyaḥ
            pratyaya upabhoktā bhavet. kathaṃcit samādhīyamānam apy etad gomayapāyasīyanyāyam ākṣi.
children.translated_text: And if cognitions, not connected with one and the same mind, differing in their own natures, were to arise, then how would one who has seen one cognition remember another cognition? And for the heap of karmic deposits (<s>karmāśaya</s>) accrued by one cognition, some other cognition would be the enjoyer. Even if in some way this were being collected in <s>samādhi</s>, behold the fallacy of the maxim of cow-dung and milk (gomaya–pāyasī)—[an incongruous mixture]

children.text:
kiṃ ca svātmānubhavāpahnavaś cittasyānyatve prāpnoti. katham, yad aham adrākṣaṃ tat
            spṛśāmi yac cāsprākṣaṃ tat paśyāmīty aham iti pratyayaḥ sarvasya pratyayasya bhede sati
            pratyayiny abhedenopasthitaḥ. ekapratyayaviṣayo+ayam abhedātmāham iti pratyayaḥ katham
            atyantabhinneṣu citteṣu vartamānaḥ sāmānyam ekaṃ pratyayinam āśrayet. svānubhavagrāhyaś
            cāyam abhedātmāham iti pratyayaḥ. na ca pratyakṣasya māhātmyaṃ pramāṇāntareṇābhibhūyate.
            pramāṇāntaraṃ ca pratyakṣabalenaiva vyavahāraṃ labhate. tasmād ekam anekārtham
            avasthitaṃ ca cittam.
children.translated_text: What is more, the otherness of mind would result in a denial of one’s own experience. How so? The cognition “I touch what I have seen, and I see what I have not touched,” the ‘I’-cognition, though every cognition is distinct, is presented as non-distinct in the cognizer. This cognition ‘I’, whose nature is non-difference within the scope of a single cognition—how, existing in minds absolutely distinct, would it rely upon one single common cognizer? And this non-different ‘I’-cognition, grasped in one’s own experience, is not overruled in its supremacy by another means of knowledge; and another means of knowledge gains its very operation by the power of perception. Therefore, the mind is one and is established with respect to many objects

children.text: yasya cittasyāvasthitasyedaṃ śāstreṇa parikarma nirdiśyate tat katham ---
children.translated_text: For the one whose mind is thus established, what purification is indicated in scripture? How so—
By the cultivation of friendliness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward those who are the subjects of happiness, suffering, merit, and demerit, there is clarity of mind

children.text:
tatra sarvaprāṇiṣu sukhasaṃbhogāpanneṣu maitrīṃ bhāvayet. duḥkhiteṣu karuṇām.
            puṇyātmakeṣu muditām. apuṇyaśīleṣūpekṣām. evam asya bhāvayataḥ śuklo dharma upajāyate.
            tataś ca cittaṃ prasīdati. prasannam ekāgraṃ sthitipadaṃ labhate.
children.translated_text: Therein, toward all beings who have come into the enjoyment of happiness, one should cultivate friendliness (<s>maitrī</s>); toward those who are suffering, compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>); toward those possessed of merit, sympathetic joy (<s>muditā</s>); toward those of unmeritorious conduct, equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>). Thus, for one who cultivates in this way, a white (pure) <s>dharma</s> arises; thereafter the mind becomes serene, and being serene, one-pointed, it attains the abiding state
Or, by exhalation and retention of the <s>Prāṇa</s>,

children.text:
kauṣṭhyasya vāyor nāsikāpuṭābhyāṃ prayatnaviśeṣād vamanaṃ pracchardanam, vidhāraṇaṃ
            prāṇāyāmas tābhyāṃ vā manasaḥ sthitiṃ saṃpādayet.
children.translated_text: The vomiting forth (expulsion) of the air of the mouth, through the nostrils by a special exertion—this is exhalation (<s>pracchardana</s>); retention (<s>vidhāraṇa</s>) is <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath-regulation); by these two one should bring about the steadiness of the mind

children.text: viṣayavatī vā pravṛttir utpannā manasaḥ sthitinibandhanī
children.translated_text: Or the arising activation furnished with an object becomes a fetter (support) for the steadiness of the mind,

children.text:
nāsikāgre dhārayato+asya yā divyagandhasaṃvit sā gandhapravṛttiḥ. jihvāgre rasasaṃvit.
            tāluni rūpasaṃvit. jihvāmadhye sparśasaṃvit. jihvāmūle śabdasaṃvid ity etā vṛttaya
            utpannāś cittaṃ sthitau nibadhnanti, saṃśayaṃ vidhamanti, samādhiprajñāyāṃ ca
            dvārībhavantīti. etena candrādityagrahamaṇipradīparaśmyādiṣu pravṛttir utpannā
            viṣayavaty eva veditavyā yady api hi tattacchāstrānumānācāryopadeśair avagatam
            arthatattvaṃ sadbhūtam eva bhavati. eteṣāṃ yathābhūtārthapratipādanasāmarthyāt, tathāpi
            yāvad ekadeśo+api kaścin na svakaraṇasaṃvedyo bhavati tāvat sarvaṃ parokṣam
            ivāpavargādiṣu sūkṣmeṣv artheṣu na dṛḍhāṃ buddhim utpādayati. tasmāc
            chāstrānumānācāryopadeśopodbalanārtham evāvaśyaṃ kaścid arthaviśeṣaḥ pratyakṣīkartavyaḥ.
            tatra tadupadiṣṭārthaikadeśapratyakṣatve sati sarvaṃ sūkṣmaviṣayam api āpavargāc
            chraddhīyate. etadartham evedaṃ cittaparikarma nirdiśyate. aniyatāsu vṛttiṣu
            tadviṣayāyāṃ vaśīkārasaṃjñāyām upajātāyāṃ samarthaṃ syāt tasya tasyārthasya
            pratyakṣīkaraṇāyeti. tathā ca sati śraddhāvīryasmṛtisamādhayo+asyāpratibandhena
            bhaviṣyantīti.
children.translated_text: For one who holds (fixes) at the tip of the nose, the consciousness-of-scent that is divine—this is the activation of scent; at the tip of the tongue, consciousness-of-taste; on the palate, consciousness-of-form; in the middle of the tongue, consciousness-of-touch; at the root of the tongue, consciousness-of-sound—these activations, having arisen, bind the mind to steadiness, dispel doubt, and become doorways to <s>samādhi-prajñā</s> (enstatic insight). From this it is to be understood that, when an activation arises with respect to moons, suns, planets, jewels, lamp-rays, and so on, it is indeed endowed with an object; for although the true nature of a given object, grasped by scripture (<s>śāstra</s>), inference, and the instruction of the teacher, is indeed existent as real by reason of their capacity to present the object as it is, nevertheless, so long as even a single portion of that [object] is not apprehended by one’s own organ, the whole remains, as it were, indirect, and with respect to subtle objects such as liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) and the like, it does not produce firm understanding. Therefore, solely for the fortifying of scripture, inference, and the teacher’s instruction, some particular object must necessarily be made directly perceptible. Then, when even a single portion of the object taught has been made perceptible, everything—even what has a subtle object, beginning from liberation—is trusted. It is for this very purpose that this mind-preparation is prescribed: when, among the non-fixed activations, mastery over their respective objects has arisen, one becomes competent to render this or that object directly perceptible. And when that is so, his faith (<s>śraddhā</s>), energy (<s>vīrya</s>), memory (<s>smṛti</s>), and enstasy (<s>samādhi</s>) will come to be without hindrance
Or, free from sorrow (<s>viśokā</s>), and luminous (<s>jyotiṣmatī</s>),

children.text:
pravṛttir utpannā manasaḥ sthitinibandhanīty anuvartate. hṛdayapuṇḍarīke dhārayato yā
            buddhisaṃvit, buddhisattvaṃ hi bhāsvaram ākāśakalpaṃ, tatra sthitivaiśāradyāt pravṛttiḥ
            sūryendugrahamaṇiprabhārūpākāreṇa vikalpate. tathāsmitāyāṃ samāpannaṃ cittaṃ
            nistaraṅgamahodadhikalpaṃ śāntam anantam asmitāmātraṃ bhavati. yatredam uktam ---
              ``
tam aṇumātram ātmānam anuvidyāsmīty evaṃ tāvat saṃprajānīte
children.translated_text: “Having followed the self as minute as an atom, ‘I am this’—thus far, he is conscious,”

children.text:
'' iti.
            eṣā dvayī viśokā viṣayavatī, asmitāmātrā ca pravṛttir jyotiṣmatīty ucyate. yayā yoginaś
            cittaṃ sthitipadaṃ labhata iti.
children.translated_text: Thus. These two—free from sorrow and endowed with an object—and the activation that is mere <s>asmitā</s>, are called luminous (<s>jyotiṣmatī</s>). By these the yogin’s mind attains the abiding state

The earlier statement continues: an activation that has arisen is a fetter (support) for the establishment of the mind. For one who holds (fixes) in the lotus of the heart there is consciousness of intellect (<s>buddhi</s>); for the <s>buddhi-sattva</s> (the lucidity of the intellect) is radiant, like space; there, by excellence in steadiness, the activation is diversified in the form of the effulgence of sun, moon, planets, and jewels. Likewise, when the mind has entered into <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness), it becomes calm, infinite, consisting of mere <s>asmitā</s>, like a great ocean without waves. Regarding this it is said—
Or the mind whose object is one who is free from passion (<s>vītarāga</s>),

children.text: vītarāgacittālambanoparaktaṃ vā yoginaś cittaṃ sthitipadaṃ labhata iti.
children.translated_text: Or the yogin’s mind, tinged by reliance upon the mind of one who is free from passion, attains the abiding state
Or reliance upon the cognition of dream or of sleep,

children.text:
svapnajñānālambanaṃ vā nidrājñānālambanaṃ vā tadākāraṃ yoginaś cittaṃ sthitipadaṃ
            labhata iti.
children.translated_text: Either reliance upon dream-cognition or reliance upon sleep-cognition—of that form, the yogin’s mind attains the abiding state
Or by meditation on whatever is esteemed,

children.text:
yad evābhimataṃ tad eva dhyāyet. tatra labdhasthitikam anyatrāpi sthitipadaṃ labhata
            iti.
children.translated_text: Whatever indeed is esteemed, let him meditate upon just that; there, having obtained steadiness, he attains an abiding state elsewhere as well
His mastery extends up to the limit of the minute atom and of the greatest magnitude,

children.text:
sūkṣme niviśamānasya paramāṇvantaṃ sthitipadaṃ labhata iti. sthūle niviśamānasya
            paramamahattvāntaṃ sthitipadaṃ cittasya. evaṃ tām ubhayīṃ koṭim anudhāvato
            yo+asyāpratīghātaḥ sa paro vaśīkāraḥ. tadvaśīkārāt paripūrṇaṃ yoginaś cittaṃ na punar
            abhyāsakṛtaṃ parikarmāpekṣata iti.
children.translated_text: For one settling into the subtle, the abiding state extends up to the limit of the minute atom; for one settling into the gross, the abiding state of the mind extends up to the limit of the greatest magnitude. Thus, as he pursues both extremes, the absence of obstruction for him—this is supreme mastery. Through that mastery, the yogin’s mind becomes complete, and no longer requires preparation brought about by practice

children.text:
atha labdhasthitikasya cetasaḥ kiṃsvarūpā kiṃviṣayā vā samāpattir iti, tad ucyate
            ---
children.translated_text: Now, for a mind that has obtained steadiness, what is the nature of samāpatti (enstatic attainment), and what is its object? This is explained—

children.text: kṣīṇavṛtter abhijātasyeva maṇer grahītṛgrahaṇagrāhyeṣu tatsthatadañjanatā samāpattiḥ
children.translated_text: For one whose activations are diminished, the samāpatti is the taking-on of the coloration of that [object] in the apprehender, the apprehension, and the apprehended, as of a flawless gem, standing upon that [object] and tinged by that

children.text:
kṣīṇavṛtter iti pratyastamitapratyayasyety arthaḥ. abhijātasyeva maṇer iti
            dṛṣṭāntopādānam. yathā sphaṭika upāśrayabhedāt tattadrūpoparakta upāśrayarūpākāreṇa
            nirbhāsate tathā grāhyālambanoparaktaṃ cittaṃ grāhyasamāpannaṃ grāhyasvarūpākāreṇa
            nirbhāsate. bhūtasūkṣmoparaktaṃ bhūtasūkṣmasamāpannaṃ bhūtasūkṣmasvarūpābhāsaṃ bhavati.
            tathā sthūlālambanoparaktaṃ sthūlarūpasamāpannaṃ sthūlarūpābhāsaṃ bhavati. tathā
            viśvabhedoparaktaṃ viśvabhedasamāpannaṃ viśvarūpābhāsaṃ bhavati.
children.translated_text: “Of diminished activations” means “of one whose conceptions have subsided.” “Like a flawless gem”—this is the adducing of an illustration; just as a crystal, due to the difference of its support, appears tinged with the forms corresponding to that support and shines forth in the shape of the support, so the mind, tinged by the support which is the apprehended object, having attained samāpatti on the apprehended, shines forth in the mode of the very form of the apprehended; tinged by subtle elements (<s>bhūta-sūkṣma</s>), having attained samāpatti on the subtle elements, it becomes an appearance of the very nature of the subtle elements; likewise, tinged by a gross support, having attained samāpatti on a gross form, it becomes an appearance of the gross form; likewise, tinged by the differentiations of the universe, having attained samāpatti on the differentiations of the universe, it becomes an appearance of the universal form

children.text:
tathā grahaṇeṣv apīndriyeṣv api draṣṭavyam. grahaṇālambanoparaktaṃ grahaṇasamāpannaṃ
            grahaṇasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate. tathā grahītṛpuruṣālambanoparaktaṃ
            grahītṛpuruṣasamāpannaṃ grahītṛpuruṣasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate. tathā
            muktapuruṣālambanoparaktaṃ muktapuruṣasamāpannaṃ muktapuruṣasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsata
            iti. tad evam abhijātamaṇikalpasya cetaso grahītṛgrahaṇagrāhyeṣu puruṣendriyabhūteṣu yā
            tatsthatadañjanatā teṣu sthitasya tadākārāpattiḥ sā samāpattir ity ucyate.
children.translated_text: So too it should be understood in respect of the instruments of apprehension, namely the senses; tinged by the support which is apprehension, having attained samāpatti on apprehension, it shines forth in the mode of the very nature of apprehension; likewise, tinged by the support which is the apprehender-<s>puruṣa</s>, having attained samāpatti on the apprehender-<s>puruṣa</s>, it shines forth in the mode of the very nature of the apprehender-<s>puruṣa</s>; likewise, tinged by the support which is the liberated <s>puruṣa</s>, having attained samāpatti on the liberated <s>puruṣa</s>, it shines forth in the mode of the very nature of the liberated <s>puruṣa</s>. Thus, for a mind likened to a flawless gem, in respect of apprehender, apprehension, and apprehended—being <s>puruṣa</s>, senses, and elements—its being colored by whatever each of those is, and the assumption of the form of that in which it is established, that is what is called samāpatti
Therein, the samāpatti accompanied by conceptual differentiations of word, meaning, and cognition is savitarkā

children.text:
tadyathā gaur iti śabdo gaur ity artho gaur iti jñānam ity avibhāgena vibhaktānām api
            grahaṇaṃ dṛṣṭam. vibhajyamānāś cānye śabdadharmā anye+arthadharmā anye vijñānadharmā ity
            eteṣāṃ vibhaktaḥ panthāḥ. tatra samāpannasya yogino yo gavādyarthaḥ samādhiprajñāyāṃ
            samārūḍhaḥ sa cec chabdārthajñānavikalpānuviddha upāvartate sā saṃkīrṇā samāpattiḥ
            savitarkety ucyate.
children.translated_text: For example, one perceives, without distinction, even of things that are distinct, “the word ‘cow’,” “the meaning ‘cow’,” “the cognition ‘cow’”; and when distinguished, there are other properties belonging to word, others belonging to meaning, others belonging to cognition—these have distinct pathways. There, if for the yogin who has entered samāpatti, the object such as “cow,” mounted in enstatic insight (<s>samādhi-prajñā</s>), nevertheless returns accompanied by conceptual differentiations of word, meaning, and cognition, that mixed samāpatti is called savitarkā

children.text:
yadā punaḥ śabdasaṃketasmṛtipariśuddhau śrutānumānajñānavikalpaśūnyāyāṃ
            samādhiprajñāyāṃ svarūpamātreṇāvasthito 'rthas tatsvarūpākāramātratayaivāvacchidyate. sā
            ca nirvitarkā samāpattiḥ. tat paraṃ pratyakṣam. tac ca śrutānumānayor bījam. tataḥ
            śrutānumāne prabhavataḥ. na ca śrutānumānajñānasahabhūtaṃ tad darśanam. tasmād
            asaṃkīrṇaṃ praṃmāṇāntareṇa yogino nirvitarkasamādhijaṃ darśanam iti. nirvitarkāyāḥ
            samāpatter asyāḥ sūtreṇa lakṣaṇaṃ dyotyate ---
children.translated_text: But when, upon the purification of the memory of the conventional association of word, in enstatic insight devoid of the conceptual constructions of hearing and inference, the object stands by its own nature alone, it is delimited solely as the mode of its own form; and that is nirvitarkā samāpatti—this is the supreme perception, and it is the seed of hearing and inference; thereafter hearing and inference arise from it; nor is that seeing conjoined with the knowledge of hearing and inference; therefore, the yogin’s seeing born of nirvitarka-samādhi is unmixed and not via another means of knowledge. By this sūtra the definition of nirvitarkā samāpatti is indicated—
When memory is purified, with the own-form appearing as if absent, there is a shining-forth of the mere object alone—this is nirvitarkā

children.text:
yā śabdasaṃketaśrutānumānajñānavikalpasmṛtipariśuddhau grāhyasvarūpa.uparaktā prajñā
            svam iva prajñāsvarūpaṃ grahaṇātmakaṃ tyaktvā padārthamātrasvarūpā grāhyasvarūpāpanneva
            bhavati sā tadā nirvitarkā samāpattiḥ.
children.translated_text: That insight which, upon the purification of the memory of conceptual constructions arising from word-convention, hearing, and inference, having abandoned its own form as if it were its own insight-nature consisting in grasping, and being of the mere nature of the object alone, appears as if it had become the very form of the apprehended—that then is nirvitarkā samāpatti

children.text:
tathā ca vyākyātaṃ tasyā ekabuddhyupakramo hy arthātmāṇupracayaviśeṣātmā gavādir
            ghaṭādir vā lokaḥ.
children.translated_text: And thus it has been explained: its initiation is by a single cognition; indeed, the world beginning with “cow” or with “pot” is of the nature of a particular accumulation of <s>artha</s>-atoms (object-atoms)

children.text:
sa ca saṃsthānaviśeṣo bhūtasūkṣmāṇāṃ sādhāraṇo dharma ātmabhūtaḥ phalena
            vyaktenānumitaḥ svavyañjakāñjanaḥ prādurbhavati. dharmāntarasya kapālāder udaye ca
            tirobhavati. sa eṣa dharmo+avayavīty ucyate. yo+asāv ekaś ca mahāṃś cāṇīṃyaś ca
            sparśavāṃś ca kriyādharmakaś cānityaś ca tenāvayavinā vyavahārāḥ kriyante.
children.translated_text: And that particular configuration, a common property of the subtle elements, being inferred by an effect that is manifest, appears along with its own revealing adjuncts; and when another property, like “pot-shard” and the like, arises, it disappears; this property is called the whole (avayavin). It is by that whole, which is one, great, minute, possessing contact, action-qualified, and impermanent, that dealings are carried on

children.text:
yasya punar avastukaḥ sa pracayaviśeṣaḥ. sūkṣmaṃ ca kāraṇam anupalabhyam avikalpasya
            tasyāvayavyabhāvād atadrūpapratiṣṭhaṃ mithyājñānam iti prāyeṇa sarvam eva prāptaṃ
            mithyājñānam iti. tadā ca samyagjñānam api kiṃ syād viṣayābhāvāt. yad yad upalabhyate
            tat tad avayavitvenāmnātam. tasmād asty avayavī yo mahattvādivyavahārāpannaḥ samāpatter
            nirvitarkāyā viṣayī bhavati.
children.translated_text: But if, on the other hand, that particular accumulation is without a substrate (object), and the subtle cause is unapprehended for the non-conceptual, then, due to the absence of the whole (avayavin), the cognition not established in that very form is false cognition; thus, for the most part, everything would end up being false cognition. And then, would there even be right cognition, given the absence of an object? Whatever is apprehended is designated as a whole (avayavin). Therefore, there exists a whole which incurs ordinary dealings such as largeness, and it becomes the object of nirvitarkā samāpatti

children.text: etayaiva savicārā nirvicārā ca sūkṣmaviṣayā vyākhyātā
children.translated_text: By this very account, the savicārā and the nirvicārā, having subtle objects, have been explained

children.text:
tatra bhūtasūkṣmakeṣv abhivyaktadharmakeṣu deśakālanimittānubhavāvacchinneṣu yā
            samāpattiḥ sā savicārety ucyate. tatrāpy ekabuddhinirgrāhyam evoditadharmaviśiṣṭaṃ
            bhūtasūkṣmam ālambanībhūtaṃ samādhiprajñāyām upatiṣṭhate.
children.translated_text: There, the samāpatti which is upon subtle elements (<s>bhūta-sūkṣma</s>) whose properties are manifest, yet bounded by the experience of place, time, and occasion, is called savicāra; and there too, that subtle element, endowed with manifest properties and graspable by a single intellect alone, becomes the support (ālambana) in enstatic insight (<s>samādhi-prajñā</s>)

children.text:
yā punaḥ sarvathā sarvataḥ śāntoditāvyapadeśyadharmānavacchinneṣu sarvadharmānupātiṣu
            sarvadharmātmakeṣu samāpattiḥ sā nirvicārety ucyate. evaṃsvarūpaṃ hi tadbhūtasūkṣmam
            etenaiva svarūpeṇālambanībhūtam eva samādhiprajñāsvarūpam uparañjayati.
children.translated_text: But the samāpatti which, in every way and from every side, is upon those whose properties of quiescence and arising are inexpressible, not delimited, which accompany all properties, which are of the nature of all properties—that is called nirvicāra; for just such is that subtle element, and by this very its own form, having become the support, it tinges (imbues) the very nature of enstatic insight

children.text:
prajñā ca svarūpaśūnyevārthamātrā yadā bhavati tadā nirvicārety ucyate. tatra
            mahadvastuviṣayā savitarkā nirvitarkā ca, sūkṣmavastuviṣayā savicārā nirvicārā ca. evam
            ubhayor etayaiva nirvitarkayā vikalpahānir vyākhyāteti.
children.translated_text: And when the insight, being as if devoid of its own form, becomes mere object, then it is called nirvicāra. There, with a great object as its field, there are savitarkā and nirvitarkā; with a subtle object as its field, there are savicārā and nirvicārā; thus, for both, by this very nirvitarkā, the removal of conceptual construction (vikalpa) has been explained
And the condition of having a subtle object culminates in the unmarked (<s>aliṅga</s>)

children.text:
pārthivasyāṇor gandhatanmātraṃ sūkṣmo viṣayaḥ. āpyasya rasatanmātram. taijasasya
            rūpatanmātram. vāyavīyasya sparśatanmātram. ākāśasya śabdatanmātram iti. teṣām
            ahaṃkāraḥ. asyāpi liṅgamātraṃ sūkṣmo viṣayaḥ. liṅgamātrasyāpy aliṅgaṃ sūkṣmo viṣayaḥ. na
            cāliṅgāt paraṃ sūkṣmam asti. nanv asti puruṣaḥ sūkṣma iti satyam. yathā liṅgāt param
            aliṅgasya saukṣmyaṃ na caivaṃ puruṣasya. kiṃtu, liṅgasyānvayikāraṇaṃ puruṣo na bhavati,
            hetus tu bhavatīti. ataḥ pradhāne saukṣmyaṃ niratiśayaṃ vyākhyātam.
children.translated_text: For the earthy atom, the subtle object is the tanmātra of scent; for the aqueous, the tanmātra of taste; for the fiery, the tanmātra of form; for the airy, the tanmātra of touch; for the ākāśic, the tanmātra of sound. Their <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (I-maker); and for this too, the mere-mark (<s>liṅga-mātra</s>) is the subtle object; and for the mere-mark, the unmarked (<s>aliṅga</s>) is the subtle object. And beyond the unmarked there is no subtler. But is there not the <s>puruṣa</s> as subtle? True; yet, whereas beyond the marked the subtlety of the unmarked is affirmed, it is not so for the <s>puruṣa</s>; rather, the <s>puruṣa</s> does not become the concomitant cause (anvayi-kāraṇa) of the marked, though he is indeed a reason (hetu) [for its operation as an end]; therefore, unsurpassed subtlety is explained to be in <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter)
Those themselves are the seeded samādhi

children.text:
tāś catasraḥ samāpattayo bahirvastubījā iti samādhir api sabījaḥ. tatra sthūle+arthe
            savitarko nirvitarkaḥ, sūkṣme+arthe savicāro nirvicāra iti caturdhopasaṃkhyātaḥ samādhir
            iti.
children.translated_text: Those four samāpattis have external objects as seeds; therefore samādhi too is with seed. Therein, with a gross object, there are savitarka and nirvitarka; with a subtle object, there are savicāra and nirvicāra—thus samādhi is enumerated in four ways
With skill (mastery) in nirvicāra, there is clarity of the inner self (<s>adhyātma-prasāda</s>)

children.text:
aśuddhyāvaraṇamalāpetasya prakāśātmano buddhisattvasya rajastamobhyām anabhibhūtaḥ
            svacchaḥ sthitipravāho vaiśāradyam. yadā nirvicārasya samādher vaiśāradyam idaṃ jāyate
            tadā yogino bhavaty adhyātmaprasādo bhūtārthaviṣayaḥ kramānanurodhī sphuṭaḥ prajñālokaḥ.
            tathā coktam --- ``

children.translated_text: Ascending to the serenity of insight, the wise one, not to be sorrowed over, beholds the sorrowing people,
like one standing upon a mountain beholds those on the ground

The lucidity (vaiśāradyam) is the clear, steady flow of the luminous nature of the <s>buddhi-sattva</s>, from which impurity, veil, and stain have been removed, not overpowered by rajas and tamas; when this mastery in nirvicāra-samādhi arises, then for the yogin there is clarity of the inner self—namely, a bright light of insight, concerning real things, explicit, and in conformity with the sequence
There, the insight is truth-bearing (<s>ṛtaṃbharā</s>)

children.text:
tasmin samāhitacittasya yā prajñā jāyate tasyā ṛtaṃbhareti saṃjñā bhavati. anvarthā ca
            sā, satyam eva bibharti na ca tatra viparyāsajñānagandho+apy astīti. tathā coktam ---
children.translated_text: In that one whose mind is enstatically collected, the insight that arises has the designation ‘truth-bearing’; and it is apt to its name, for it bears only truth, and there is not even a scent of erroneous cognition therein
By scripture, by inference, and by the sap of meditative practice,

children.text: tridhā prakalpayan prajñāṃ labhate yogam uttamam
children.translated_text: fashioning insight in three ways, one attains the highest <s>yoga</s>
That, moreover—
Is of a different object than the insights from hearing and inference, because it has a specific object

children.text:
śrutam āgamavijñānaṃ tat sāmānyaviṣayam. na hy āgamena śakyo viśeṣo+abhidhātum, kasmāt,
            na hi viśeṣeṇa kṛtasaṃketaḥ śabda iti. tathānumānaṃ sāmānyaviṣayam eva. yatra prāptis
            tatra gatir yatrāprāptis tatra na bhavati gatir ity uktam. anumānena ca
            sāmānyenopasaṃhāraḥ. tasmāc chrutānumānaviṣayo na viśeṣaḥ kaścid astīti.
children.translated_text: Hearing is scripture-based cognition; that has a general object. For a specification cannot be expressed by scripture—why? because a word is not fixed by a convention made with respect to a specification. Likewise, inference too has only a general object; it is said, “Where there is presence, there is going; where there is absence, there is no going.” And by inference there is a general conclusion. Therefore, no specification at all is the object of hearing and inference,

children.text:
na cāsya sūkṣmavyavahitaviprakṛṣṭasya vastuno lokapratyakṣeṇa grahaṇam asti. na cāsya
            viśeṣasyāpramāṇakasyābhāvo+astīti samādhiprajñānirgrāhya eva sa viśeṣo bhavati
            bhūtasūkṣmagato vā puruṣagato vā. tasmāc chrutānumānaprajñābhyām anyaviṣayā sā prajñā
            viśeṣārthatvād iti.
children.translated_text: Nor is there apprehension of this exceedingly subtle, obstructed, and remote entity by ordinary perception. Nor does the absence of this specification, which lacks a means of valid cognition, obtain; thus, it is only graspable by enstatic insight (<s>samādhi-prajñā</s>)—that specification occurs either pertaining to subtle elements (<s>bhūta-sūkṣma</s>) or pertaining to <s>puruṣa</s>. Therefore, that insight has a different object than hearing-based and inference-based insights, because it has a specific object,

children.text: samādhiprajñāpratilambhe yoginaḥ prajñākṛtaḥ saṃskāro navo navo jāyate ---
children.translated_text: Upon the obtaining of enstatic insight (<s>samādhi-prajñā</s>), for the yogin, a disposition fashioned by insight is born ever anew—
The disposition born from that restrains other dispositions

children.text:
samādhiprajñāprabhavaḥ saṃskāro vyutthānasaṃskārāśayaṃ bādhate.
            vyutthānasaṃskārābhibhavāt tatprabhavāḥ pratyayā na bhavanti. pratyayanirodhe samādhir
            upatiṣṭhate. tataḥ samādhijā prajñā, tataḥ prajñākṛtāḥ saṃskārā iti navo navaḥ
            saṃskārāśayo jāyate. tataś ca prajñā, tataś ca saṃskārā iti. katham asau saṃskārātiśayaś
            cittaṃ sādhikāraṃ na kariṣyatīti. na te prajñākṛtāḥ saṃskārāḥ kleśakṣayahetutvāc cittam
            adhikāraviśiṣṭaṃ kurvanti. cittaṃ hi te svakāryād avasādayanti. khyātiparyavasānaṃ hi
            cittaceṣṭitam iti.
children.translated_text: The disposition that arises from enstatic insight (<s>samādhi-prajñā</s>) suppresses the bed of dispositions produced by emergence. Because of overpowering the emergence-dispositions, the ideations originating from them do not occur; when ideations are restrained, samādhi is established; then there is insight born of samādhi, then dispositions fashioned by insight—thus an ever-new bed of dispositions is produced. Then again insight, then again dispositions, and so on; how then will that excess of dispositions not render the mind endowed with eligibility for action? Those dispositions fashioned by insight do not render the mind possessed of eligibility for action, because they are causes of the destruction of the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>); indeed, they bring the mind down from its own activity. For the activity of the mind culminates in discriminative knowledge (<s>khyāti</s>)—so it is,
Moreover, what comes of this—
Upon the restraint of even that, owing to the restraint of all, there is seedless samādhi

children.text:
sa na kevalaṃ samādhiprajñāvirodhī prajñākṛtānām api saṃskārāṇāṃ pratibandhī bhavati.
            kasmāt, nirodhajaḥ saṃskāraḥ samādhijān saṃskārān bādhata iti.
children.translated_text: That does not merely oppose enstatic insight (<s>samādhi-prajñā</s>); it also restrains even the dispositions fashioned by insight. Why? Because the disposition born of restraint suppresses the dispositions born of samādhi,

children.text:
nirodhasthitikālakramānubhavena nirodhacittakṛtasaṃskārāstitvam anumeyam.
            vyutthānanirodhasamādhiprabhavaiḥ saha kaivalyabhāgīyaiḥ saṃskāraiś cittaṃ svasyāṃ
            prakṛtāv avasthitāyāṃ pravilīyate. tasmāt te saṃskārāś cittasyādhikāravirodhino na
            sthitihetavo bhavantīti. yasmād avasitādhikāraṃ saha kaivalyabhāgīyaiḥ saṃskāraiś cittaṃ
            nivartate, tasmin nivṛtte puruṣaḥ svarūpamātrapratiṣṭho+ataḥ śuddhaḥ kevalo mukta ity
            ucyata iti.
children.translated_text: From the experience of the temporal sequence of the abiding of restraint, the existence of dispositions produced by the mind-in-restraint is to be inferred. Together with the dispositions produced by emergence, restraint, and samādhi, as well as those that partake of isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>), the mind dissolves into its own nature when it is established therein; therefore, those dispositions, being opposed to the mind’s eligibility-for-action, do not become causes of its continuance. Since the mind, having completed its function, together with the dispositions that partake of isolation, turns back, when that has turned back, the <s>puruṣa</s>, established only in his own form, is therefore called pure, alone, liberated,

children.text:
iti śrīpātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre śrīmadvyāsabhāṣye prathamaḥ
            samādhipādaḥ 1.
children.translated_text: Thus, in the venerable Yoga treatise, the Sāṃkhya exposition of <s>Śrī</s><s>Patañjali</s>, in the venerable <s>Vyāsa</s>’s Bhāṣya, the first book, the Samādhi-pāda, [is concluded],
Sādhanapādaḥ

children.text:
uddiṣṭaḥ samāhitacittasya yogaḥ. kathaṃ vyutthitacitto+api yogayuktaḥ syād ity etad
          ārabhyate ---
children.translated_text: The yoga for one whose mind is collected has been taught. How should one whose mind is outwardly active nevertheless be yoked to yoga?—this is begun—
Austerity (<s>tapas</s>), self-recitation (<s>svādhyāya</s>), and dedication to <s>Īśvara</s> (<s>Īśvara-praṇidhāna</s>) are the <s>kriyā-yoga</s>

children.text:
nātapasvino yogaḥ sidhyati. anādikarmakleśavāsanācitrā pratyupasthitaviṣayajālā
            cāśuddhir nāntareṇa tapaḥ saṃbhedam āpadyata iti tapasa upādānam. tac ca cittaprasādanam
            abādhamānam anenāsevyam iti manyate.
