children.translated_text: Without austerity (<s>tapas</s>), yoga does not succeed; for the impurity—variegated by beginningless karma, afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), and impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), and by the nets of objects that present themselves—does not come to be broken up without austerity—therefore the adoption of austerity. And that, being a pacifier of the mind, unobstructive, is to be practiced by him—so he holds,

children.text:
svādhyāyaḥ praṇavādipavitrāṇāṃ japo mokṣaśāstrādhyayanaṃ vā. īśvarapraṇidhānaṃ
            sarvakriyāṇāṃ paramagurāv arpaṇaṃ tatphalasaṃnyāso vā.
children.translated_text: Self-recitation (<s>svādhyāya</s>) is the japa of purifiers such as the syllable Om (<s>praṇava</s>), or the study of the scriptures of liberation; dedication to <s>Īśvara</s> (<s>Īśvara-praṇidhāna</s>) is the offering of all actions to the supreme Teacher and the renunciation of their fruits,
For that indeed, the <s>kriyā-yoga</s>—
Is for cultivating samādhi and for attenuating the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>)

children.text:
sa hy āsevyamānaḥ samādhiṃ bhāvayati kleśāṃś ca pratanūkaroti. pratanūkṛtān kleśān
            prasaṃkhyānāgninā dagdhabījakalpān aprasavadharmiṇaḥ kariṣyatīti. teṣāṃ tanūkaraṇāt
            punaḥ kleśair aparāmṛṣṭā sattvapuruṣānyatāmātrakhyātiḥ sūkṣmā prajñā samāptādhikārā
            pratiprasavāya kalpiṣyata iti.
children.translated_text: For, when cultivated, that [kriyā-yoga] fosters samādhi and attenuates the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>). The afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) having been made thin become, as it were, seeds scorched by the fire of discriminative cognition (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), of the nature of non-germination, so that they will not produce [future fruition]. Because of the attenuation of those, a mere discriminative knowledge of the difference between <s>Sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> (<s>sattva-puruṣa-anyatā-mātra-khyāti</s>), a subtle insight whose mandate (scope) has been completed, is contrived for reversal (return-flow, <s>pratiprasava</s>)
Now then, which are the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) and how many are they—
Ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), I-notion (<s>asmitā</s>), attachment (<s>rāga</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), and clinging-to-life (<s>abhiniveśa</s>) are the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>)

children.text:
kleśā iti pañca viparyayā ity arthaḥ. te spandamānā guṇādhikāraṃ draḍhayanti, pariṇāmam
            avasthāpayanti, kāryakāraṇasrota unnamayanti, parasparānugrahatantrībhūtvā karmavipākaṃ
            cābhinirharantīti.
children.translated_text: Afflictions—there are five; that is to say, they are misapprehensions (viparyaya). As they vibrate, they consolidate the jurisdiction of the <s>guṇa</s>-s, establish transformation, raise up the current of cause and effect, and, having become a system of mutual favoring of one another, they also bring about karma and its ripening
Ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is the field for the others—whether dormant, thinned, interrupted, or fully manifest

children.text:
atrāvidyā kṣetraṃ prasavabhūmir uttarareṣām asmitādīnāṃ caturvidhavikalpānāṃ
            prasuptatanuvicchinnodārāṇām. tatra kā prasuptiḥ. cetasi śaktimātrapratiṣṭhānāṃ
            bījabhāvopagamaḥ. tasya prabodha ālambane saṃmukhībhāvaḥ. prasaṃkhyānavato
            dagdhakleśabījasya saṃmukhībhūte+apy ālambane nāsau punar asti, dagdhabījasya kutaḥ
            praroha iti. ataḥ kṣīṇakleśaḥ kuśalaś caramadeha ity ucyate. tatraiva sā dagdhabījabhāvā
            pañcamī kleśāvasthā nānyatreti. satāṃ kleśānāṃ tadā bījasāmarthyaṃ dagdham iti viṣayasya
            saṃmukhībhāve+api sati na bhavaty eṣāṃ prabodha ity uktā prasuptir dagdhabījānām
            aprarohaś ca.
children.translated_text: Here, ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is the field, the generative ground, for the subsequent ones beginning with <s>asmitā</s>, in their fourfold modes of dormancy, thinness, interruption, and manifestness. There, what is dormancy? The coming to have seed-nature, consisting in mere potency established in the mind. Its awakening, upon the presence of a support (object), is the coming into the forefront. For one who possesses discriminative cognition (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), even when the support has come to the forefront for the one whose affliction-seeds are burnt, that [affliction] is no longer there—how could there be a sprouting of a burnt seed? Therefore, he whose afflictions are exhausted is a skillful person in his final body, so it is said. Right there, that state of burnt-seed-ness is the fifth stage of the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), not elsewhere. When the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) yet exist, then their seed-capability is burnt—hence, even when the object is present to view, there is no awakening of these; thus dormancy is explained as the non-sprouting of burnt seeds

children.text:
tanutvam ucyate --- pratipakṣabhāvanopahatāḥ kleśās tanavo bhavanti. tathā vicchidya
            vicchidya tena tenātmanā punaḥ punaḥ samudācarantīti vicchinnāḥ. kathaṃ, rāgakāle
            krodhasyādarśanāt. na hi rāgakāle krodhaḥ samudācarati. rāgaś ca kvacid dṛśyamāno na
            viṣayāntare nāsti. naikasyāṃ striyāṃ caitro rakta ity anyāsu strīṣu viraktaḥ, kiṃtu
            tatra rāgo labdhavṛttir anyatra tu bhaviṣyadvṛttir iti. sa hi tadā prasuptatanuvicchinno
            bhavati.
children.translated_text: Thinness is stated thus: afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) struck down by cultivating the opposite (pratipakṣa-bhāvanā) become thin. Likewise, being cut off again and again, they arise repeatedly each in their own fashion—hence they are ‘interrupted.’ How so? Because, at the time of attachment (<s>rāga</s>), hatred (<s>krodha</s>) is not seen; for, at the time of attachment, hatred does not arise. And attachment, though seen in some case, is not present with respect to another object. It is not that because <s>Caitra</s> is infatuated with one woman he is dispassionate toward other women; rather, there the attachment has obtained operative status, whereas elsewhere it will have to-be-operative status. Thus at that time it becomes dormant, thin, and interrupted

children.text:
viṣaye yo labdhavṛttiḥ sa udāraḥ. sarva evaite kleśaviṣayatvaṃ nātikrāmanti. kas tarhi
            vicchinnaḥ prasuptas tanur udāro vā kleśa iti, ucyate --- satyam evaitat, kiṃtu
            viśiṣṭānām evaiteṣāṃ vicchinnāditvam. yathaiva pratipakṣabhāvanāto nivṛttas tathaiva
            svavyañjakāñjanenābhivyakta iti. sarva evāmī kleśā avidyābhedāḥ. kasmāt, sarveṣv
            avidyaivābhiplavate. yad avidyayā vastv ākāryate tad evānuśerate kleśā
            viparyāsapratyayakāla upalabhyante kṣīyamāṇāṃ cāvidyām anu kṣīyanta iti.
children.translated_text: That which has obtained operative status with respect to its object is ‘manifest.’ All of these, indeed, do not transgress being afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) with respect to an object. Which, then, is an affliction—interrupted, dormant, thinned, or manifest? It is said: this is indeed true; but these modes of interruption and so on belong only to the particular ones [present]. Just as that which has ceased through the cultivation of the opposite becomes manifest again by its own revealers, so it is. All these afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) are divisions of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). Why? Because ignorance floods into all. Whatever is made to appear as the real by ignorance—that alone the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) adhere to; they are encountered at the time of a cognitional inversion (viparyāsa-pratyaya), and, as ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is being attenuated, they too are attenuated along with it
There, the nature of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is stated—
Ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is the ascription of permanence, purity, happiness, and selfhood to what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self

children.text:
anitye kārye nityakhyātiḥ. tadyathā --- dhruvā pṛthivī, dhruvā sacandratārakā dyauḥ,
            amṛtā divaukasa iti. tathāśucau paramabībhatse kāye, ---
children.translated_text: Permanence is ascribed to the impermanent—i.e., to an effect; for example: “The earth is constant,” “The heaven with moon and stars is constant,” “The dwellers in heaven are immortal,” likewise, purity is ascribed to the body, which is supremely loathsome—

children.text: sthānād bījād upaṣṭambhān niḥsyandān nidhanād api /
children.translated_text: Because of its position, its seed, its supports, its discharges, and its very perishing,

children.text: kāyam ādheyaśaucatvāt paṇḍitā hy aśuciṃ viduḥ//
children.translated_text: the body, being only something to be placed down, is known by the learned to be impure,”

children.text:
iti aśucau śucikhyātir dṛśyate. naveva śaśāṅkalekhā kamanīyeyaṃ kanyā
            madhvamṛtāvayavanirmiteva candraṃ bhittvā niḥsṛteva jñāyate, nīlotpalapatrāyatākṣī
            hāvagarbhābhyāṃ locanābhyāṃ jīvalokam āśvāsayantīveti kasya kenābhisaṃbandhaḥ. bhavati
            caivam aśucau śuciviparyāsapratyaya iti. etenāpuṇye puṇyapratyayas tathaivānarthe
            cārthapratyayo vyākhyātaḥ.
children.translated_text: Thus, the apprehension of purity is seen in what is impure. “She—charming like a fresh crescent of the moon, as though fashioned from honey and nectar, as if having burst through the moon and come forth—is perceived; with eyes long like the petals of a blue lotus, with the two gaze-organs pregnant with coquettish play, as if she were comforting the world of living beings”—what relation does there exist of whom with whom? And so it is that, in the impure, there is a cognition inverted as purity. By this, a cognition of merit (virtue) is likewise explained in what is demerit (vice), and a cognition of value (meaning) in what is non-value (non-meaning),

children.text:
pariṇāmatāpasaṃskāraduḥkhair
              guṇavṛttivirodhāc ca duḥkham eva sarvaṃ vivekinaḥ
children.translated_text: “Because of the pains of transformation, ardor (burning), and saṃskāra, and because of the mutual opposition of the functions of the <s>guṇa</s>-s, all is pain indeed for the discerning,”

children.text:
'' iti. tatra sukhakhyātir
            avidyā. tathānātmany ātmakhyātir bāhyopakaraṇeṣu cetanācetaneṣu bhogādhiṣṭhāne vā śarīre
            puruṣopakaraṇe vā manasy anātmany ātmakhyātir iti. tathaitad atroktam ---
              ``
children.translated_text: Thus there, the cognition as happiness is ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). Likewise, the cognition as self in what is non-self—whether in external implements, conscious or non-conscious; or in the body as the seat of enjoyment; or in the mind as an instrument of <s>puruṣa</s>—the cognition as self in the non-self, indeed. Likewise, this has been said here—

children.text:
vyaktam avyaktaṃ vā sattvam ātmatvenābhipratītya tasya saṃpadam anu nandaty
              ātmasaṃpadaṃ manvānas tasya vyāpadam anu śocaty ātmavyāpadaṃ manvānaḥ sa
              sarvo+apratibuddhaḥ
children.translated_text: “Manifest or unmanifest, <s>Sattva</s>, being apprehended as the self, he delights in its success, thinking it the success of the self; he sorrows at its misfortune, thinking it the misfortune of the self; he is entirely unawakened,”

children.text:
'' iti. eṣā catuṣpadā bhavaty avidyā mūlam asya
            kleśasaṃtānasya karmāśayasya ca savipākasyeti.
children.translated_text: And this ignorance has four feet (aspects), and is the root of this continuum of afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) and of the karmic deposit (<s>karmāśaya</s>) together with its ripening,
Likewise, regarding pain, he will state the cognition as happiness—

children.text:
tasyāś cāmitrāgoṣpadavadvastusatattvaṃ vijñeyam. yathā nāmitro mitrābhāvo na
            mitramātraṃ kiṃtu tadviruddhaḥ sapatnaḥ. yathā vāgoṣpadaṃ na goṣpadābhāvo na
            goṣpadamātraṃ kiṃtu deśa eva tābhyām anyad vastvantaram. evam avidyā na pramāṇaṃ na
            pramāṇābhāvaḥ kiṃtu vidyāviparītaṃ jñānāntaram avidyeti.
children.translated_text: And its real nature is to be understood by the examples of ‘non-friend’ and ‘cattle-footprint.’ Just as ‘non-friend’ is not merely the absence of a friend, nor merely something friend-like, but rather an enemy opposed to that; and just as a cattle-footprint is not the absence of a cattle-footprint nor merely a cattle-footprint, but a distinct entity—namely, a patch of ground other than those two; so ignorance is neither a means of valid cognition nor the absence of a means of valid cognition, but rather a different kind of cognition opposed to knowledge—this is ignorance,
The seeming unity of the power of the seer and the power of seeing is <s>asmitā</s> (I-notion),

children.text:
puruṣo dṛkśaktir buddhir darśanaśaktir ity etayor ekasvarūpāpattir ivāsmitā kleśa
            ucyate. bhoktṛbhogyaśaktyor atyantavibhaktayor atyantāsaṃkīrṇayor avibhāgaprāptāv iva
            satyāṃ bhogaḥ kalpate. svarūpapratilambhe tu tayoḥ kaivalyam eva bhavati kuto bhoga iti.
            tathā coktam --- ``

buddhitaḥ paraṃ puruṣam ākāraśīlavidyādibhir vibhaktam apaśyan
              kuryāt tatrātmabuddhiṃ mohena
children.translated_text: “Not perceiving the <s>puruṣa</s> as distinct from the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) by forms, dispositions, knowledge, and the like, one would, through delusion, impute self-notion there,”

The <s>puruṣa</s> is the power of seeing (seer-power), the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) is the power of seeing (instrumental power); the seeming attainment of one-form-ness of these two is called the affliction (<s>kleśa</s>) ‘<s>asmitā</s>.’ When, as it were, there occurs the non-discrimination (fusion) of the enjoyer and the enjoyable powers, which are absolutely distinct and utterly unmingled, then experience (enjoyment) is contrived. But when their own nature is recovered, there is only isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>) of the two—whence, then, enjoyment? Thus it is also said—
Attachment (<s>rāga</s>) is that which accompanies pleasure,

children.text:
sukhābhijñasya sukhānusmṛtipūrvaḥ sukhe tatsādhane vā yo gardhas tṛṣṇā lobhaḥ sa rāga
            iti.
children.translated_text: For one acquainted with pleasure, that greed, craving, covetousness—preceded by the recollection of pleasure—in regard to pleasure or to its means, that is <s>rāga</s> (attachment),
Aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) is that which accompanies pain,

children.text:
duḥkhābhijñasya duḥkhānusmṛtipūrvo duḥkhe tatsādhane vā yaḥ pratigho manyur jighāṃsā
            krodhaḥ sa dveṣaḥ.
children.translated_text: For one acquainted with pain, that repulsion, resentment, desire-to-destroy, anger—preceded by the recollection of pain—in regard to pain or to its means, that is <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion),
Clinging-to-life (<s>abhiniveśa</s>) flows along with the taste (instinct), and is established even in the learned,

children.text:
sarvasya prāṇina iyam ātmāśīr nityā bhavati mā na bhūvaṃ bhūyāsam iti. na
            cānanubhūtamaraṇadharmakasyaiṣā bhavaty ātmāśīḥ. etayā ca pūrvajanmānubhavaḥ pratīyate.
            sa cāyam abhiniveśaḥ kleśaḥ svarasavāhī kṛmer api jātamātrasya pratyakṣānumānāgamair
            asaṃbhāvito maraṇatrāsa ucchedadṛṣṭyātmakaḥ pūrvajanmānubhūtaṃ maraṇaduḥkham
            anumāpayati.
children.translated_text: In all living beings there is this perpetual wish-of-the-self: “May I not cease to be; may I be again.” And this wish-of-the-self does not belong to one who has not experienced the property of death. And by this, experience in a previous birth is inferred. And this <s>abhiniveśa</s> is an affliction (<s>kleśa</s>) that flows with the native taste (instinct); the fear of death, not supportable by perception, inference, or scripture even in a newborn worm, being of the nature of a view of annihilation, makes it to be inferred that the pain of death experienced in a previous birth [now] manifests,

children.text:
yathā cāyam atyantamūḍheṣu dṛśyate kleśas tathā viduṣo+api vijñātapūrvāparāntasya
            rūḍhaḥ. kasmāt samānā hi tayoḥ kuśalākuśalayor maraṇaduḥkhānubhavād iyaṃ vāsaneti.
children.translated_text: And just as this affliction is seen in the utterly deluded, so too is it established even in the learned, who know the before-and-after; why? Because in both the skillful and the unskillful alike, there is this impression from experiencing the pain of death,
They, subtle, are to be overcome by return-flow (<s>pratiprasava</s>)

children.text:
te pañca kleśā dagdhabījakalpā yoginaś caritādhikāre cetasi pralīne saha tenaivāstaṃ
            gacchanti.
children.translated_text: Those five afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), like seeds scorched, once dissolved in the mind of the yogin who has traversed the stages of practice, depart together with that very mind when it sets,
But of those that remain, having come into the state of seed-nature—
Their activities are to be removed by meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>)

children.text:
kleśānāṃ yā vṛttayaḥ sthūlās tāḥ kriyāyogena tanūkṛtāḥ satyaḥ prasaṃkhyānena dhyānena
            hātavyā yāvat sūkṣmīkṛtā yāvad dagdhabījakalpā iti. yathā vastrāṇāṃ sthūlo malaḥ pūrvaṃ
            nirdhūyate paścāt sūkṣmo yatnenopāyena cāpanīyate tathā svalpapratipakṣāḥ sthūlā
            vṛttayaḥ kleśānāṃ, sūkṣmās tu mahāpratipakṣā iti.
children.translated_text: The coarse activities of the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), those which, being made thin by <s>kriyā-yoga</s>, indeed are to be abandoned by discriminative cognition (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), by meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>), until they are subtilized, until they become like scorched seeds; just as, of garments, the gross dirt is first shaken off, thereafter the subtle [dirt] is removed by effort and by a means, so the coarse activities of the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) have slight opposers, whereas the subtle [activities] have great opposers,
The karmic deposit (<s>karmāśaya</s>), rooted in the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), is to be experienced in seen and unseen births

children.text:
tatra puṇyāpuṇyakarmāśayaḥ kāmalobhamohakrodhabhavaḥ. sa dṛṣṭajanmavedanīyaś
            cādṛṣṭajanmavedanīyaś ca. tatra tīvrasaṃvegena mantratapaḥsamādhibhir nirvartita
            īśvaradevatāmaharṣimahānubhāvānām ārādhanād vā yaḥ pariniṣpannaḥ sa sadyaḥ paripacyate
            puṇyakarmāśaya iti. tathā tīvrakleśena bhītavyādhitakṛpaṇeṣu viśvāsopagateṣu vā
            mahānubhāveṣu vā tapasviṣu kṛtaḥ punaḥ punar apakāraḥ sa cāpi pāpakarmāśayaḥ sadya eva
            paripacyate. yathā nandīśvaraḥ kumāro manuṣyapariṇāmaṃ hitvā devatvena pariṇataḥ. tathā
            nahuṣo+api devānām indraḥ svakaṃ pariṇāmaṃ hitvā tiryaktvena pariṇata iti. tatra
            nārakāṇāṃ nāsti dṛṣṭajanmavedanīyaḥ karmāśayaḥ. kṣīṇakleśānām api nāsty
            adṛṣṭajanmavedanīyaḥ karmāśaya iti.
children.translated_text: There, the deposit of meritorious and demeritorious karma (<s>puṇya</s>-<s>apuṇya karmāśaya</s>) arises from lust, greed, delusion, anger; that one is to be experienced in a seen birth and is also to be experienced in an unseen birth. There, that which, through intense urgency, having been accomplished by mantra, austerity, and samādhi (<s>mantra</s>, <s>tapas</s>, <s>samādhi</s>), or by the propitiation of deities beginning with <s>Īśvara</s>, of great-souled ones, of great-powerful ones, is brought to perfection—that is the deposit of meritorious karma (<s>puṇya-karmāśaya</s>) which ripens immediately; likewise, the repeated injury done to those who are intensely afflicted—terrified, diseased, wretched—or to those who have attained trust, or to great-souled ones, or to ascetics, that too is the deposit of demerit (<s>pāpa-karmāśaya</s>) which ripens immediately. Thus <s>Nandīśvara</s>, the boy, having abandoned a human transformation, was transformed into a deity; likewise <s>Nahuṣa</s>, even though [becoming] the <s>Indra</s> of the gods, having abandoned his own transformation, was transformed into an animal—so it is. There, for the denizens of hell there is no deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>) to be experienced in a seen birth; and for those whose afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) are exhausted, there is also no deposit of karma to be experienced in an unseen birth,
When the root exists, its fruition is birth, lifespan, and experience (enjoyment-suffering)

children.text:
satsu kleśeṣu karmāśayo vipākārambhī bhavati nocchinnakleśamūlaḥ. yathā tuṣāvanaddhāḥ
            śālitaṇḍulā adagdhabījabhāvāḥ prarohasamarthā bhavanti, nāpanītatuṣā dagdhabījabhāvā vā
            tathā kleśāvanaddhaḥ karmāśayo vipākaprarohī bhavati, nāpanītakleśo na
            prasaṃkhyānadagdhakleśabījabhāvo veti. sa ca vipākas trividho jātir āyur bhoga iti.
children.translated_text: When the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) are present, the deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>) undertakes (initiates) fruition, but not when the root of the afflictions has been cut off; just as rice-grains encased in husk, being of the nature of unburnt seeds, are capable of sprouting, whereas not [so] when the husk is removed or when they are of the nature of burnt seeds, so the deposit of karma, encased in afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), becomes sprouting in fruition, not when the afflictions have been removed, not when it is of the nature of affliction-seeds scorched by discriminative cognition (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), that is; and that fruition is threefold—birth, lifespan, and experience,

children.text:
tatredaṃ vicāryate --- kim ekaṃ karmaikasya janmanaḥ kāraṇam athaikaṃ karmānekaṃ
            janmākṣipatīti. dvitīyā vicāraṇā --- kim anekaṃ karmānekaṃ janma nirvartayati athānekaṃ
            karmaikaṃ janma nirvartayatīti. na tāvad ekaṃ karmaikasya janmanaḥ kāraṇam. kasmāt,
            anādikālapracitasyāsaṃkhyeyasyāvaśiṣṭasya karmaṇaḥ sāṃpratikasya ca phalakramāniyamād
            anāśvāso lokasya prasaktaḥ, sa cāniṣṭa iti. na caikaṃ karmānekasya janmanaḥ kāraṇam.
            kasmāt, anekeṣu karmasu ekaikam eva karmānekasya janmanaḥ kāraṇam ity avaśiṣṭasya
            vipākakālābhāvaḥ prasaktaḥ, sa cāpy aniṣṭa iti. na cānekaṃ karmānekasya janmanaḥ
            kāraṇam. kasmāt, tad anekaṃ janma yugapan na saṃbhavatīti krameṇaiva vācyam. tathā ca
            pūrvadoṣānuṣaṅgaḥ.
children.translated_text: Here this is to be considered—does a single karma cause a single birth, or does a single karma propel many births? A second consideration—does many karma bring about many births, or does many karma bring about a single birth? To begin with, a single karma is not the cause of a single birth; why? Because, given the countless remainder of karma accumulated from beginningless time and also contemporary, due to the non-fixity of the order of results there would ensue for the world a lack of assurance, and that is undesirable; nor is a single karma the cause of many births; why? Because, if in many karma each single karma were the cause of many births, then the absence of a time for the remainder to ripen would ensue, and that too is undesirable; nor is many karma the cause of many births; why? Because those many births cannot occur simultaneously, and it would have to be stated that they occur only in sequence, and thus the previous defects would persist,

children.text:
tasmāj janmaprāyaṇāntare kṛtaḥ puṇyāpuṇyakarmāśayapracayo vicitraḥ
            pradhānopasarjanabhāvenāvasthitaḥ prāyaṇābhivyakta ekapraghaṭṭakena maraṇaṃ prasādhya
            saṃmūrchita ekam eva janma karoti. tac ca janma tenaiva karmaṇā labdhāyuṣkaṃ bhavati.
            tasminn āyuṣi tenaiva karmaṇā bhogaḥ saṃpadyata iti. asau karmāśayo
            janmāyurbhogahetutvāt trivipāko+abhidhīyata iti. ata ekabhavikaḥ karmāśaya ukta iti.
children.translated_text: Therefore, the variegated accumulation of meritorious and demeritorious deposits of karma (<s>puṇya</s>-<s>apuṇya karmāśaya</s>) performed between birth and death, remaining with the status of principal-and-subsidiary, manifests at death, and, having been compacted into a single striking-together, brings about a swoon, produces one single birth; and that birth has a lifespan obtained by that very karma, and within that lifespan, by that very karma, experience (enjoyment-suffering) is accomplished; this deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>), being the cause of birth, lifespan, and experience, is said to have threefold fruition; therefore, a deposit of karma belonging to a single existence (one-lifetime) is stated

children.text:
dṛṣṭajanmavedanīyas tv ekavipākārambhī bhogahetutvād dvivipākārambhī vāyurbhogahetutvān
            nandīśvaravan nahuṣavad veti. kleśakarmavipākānubhavanirvartitābhis tu vāsanābhir
            anādikālasaṃmūrchitam idaṃ cittaṃ vicitrīkṛtam iva sarvato matsyajālaṃ granthibhir
            ivātatam ity etā anekabhavapūrvikā vāsanāḥ. yas tv ayaṃ karmāśaya eṣa evaikabhavika ukta
            iti. ye saṃskārāḥ smṛtihetavas tā vāsanās tāś cānādikālīnā iti.
children.translated_text: That which is to be experienced in a seen birth is a single-fruition-initiator, since it is the cause of experience (enjoyment-suffering); or, like the wind, which is a two-fruition-initiator, since it is the cause of experience—as in the case of <s>Nandīśvara</s>, and as in the case of <s>Nahuṣa</s>, thus. But through impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) that are produced by the undergoing of afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), karma (<s>karma</s>), and fruition (<s>vipāka</s>), this mind (<s>citta</s>), condensed from beginningless time, is made variegated, as it were, being spread out everywhere like a net of fish, like being stretched with knots; these are impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) having many previous births. As for this deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>), this very one has been stated to belong to a single existence; and the formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>) that are the causes of memory (<s>smṛti</s>)—those are impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), and they are from beginningless time

children.text:
yas tv asāv ekabhavikaḥ karmāśayaḥ sa niyatavipākaś cāniyatavipākaś ca. tatra
            dṛṣṭajanmavedanīyasya niyatavipākasyaivāyaṃ niyamo na tv
            adṛṣṭajanmavedanīyasyāniyatavipākasya kasmāt. yo hy adṛṣṭajanmavedanīyo+aniyatavipākas
            tasya trayī gatiḥ --- kṛtasyāvipakvasya nāśaḥ, pradhānakarmaṇy āvāpagamanaṃ vā,
            niyatavipākapradhānakarmaṇābhibhūtasya vā ciram avasthānam iti.
children.translated_text: Now, that deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>) belonging to a single existence is of fixed fruition and of non-fixed fruition. There, for that which is to be experienced in a seen birth and has fixed fruition, this rule alone holds, not for that which is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has non-fixed fruition—why? For that which is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has non-fixed fruition, there is a threefold course: the destruction, here itself, of what has been done but has not ripened; or a descent and going-into a principal karma; or, being overpowered by a principal karma of fixed fruition, a long remaining

children.text:
tatra kṛtasyāvipakvasya nāśo yathā śuklakarmodayād ihaiva nāśaḥ kṛṣṇasya. yatredam
            uktam --- ``

dve dve ha vai karmaṇī veditavye pāpakasyaiko rāśiḥ
              puṇyakṛto+apahanti tad icchasva karmāṇi sukṛtāni kartum ihaiva te karma kavayo
              vedayante.
children.translated_text: “Two, two indeed, are the karmas to be understood: one heap of the evil-doer’s [acts]. The acts of the doer of merit remove that—desire, then, to perform auspicious deeds; even here the sages make known your karma,”

There, the destruction, here itself, of what has been done but has not ripened—just as, upon the rise of white (meritorious) karma, there is here itself the destruction of black (demeritorious) [karma]; as where this has been said—

children.text:
syāt svalpaḥ saṃkaraḥ
              saparihāraḥ sapratyavamarṣaḥ kuśalasya nāpakarṣāyālam. kasmāt, kuśalaṃ hi me bahv
              anyad asti yatrāyam āvāpaṃ gataḥ svarge+apy apakarṣam alpaṃ kariṣyati
children.translated_text: “There may be a slight admixture, with remedy, with counter-consideration, not sufficient to drag down what is skillful. Why? For I have much other skillful [karma] in which this one has gone into descent; even in heaven it will make only slight diminution,”
thus.
The descent and going-into a principal karma; as where this has been said—

children.text:
niyatavipākapradhānakarmaṇābhibhūtasya vā ciram avasthānam. katham iti,
            adṛṣṭajanmavedanīyasyaiva niyatavipākasya karmaṇaḥ samānaṃ maraṇam abhivyaktikāraṇam
            uktam. na tv adṛṣṭajanmavedanīyasyāniyatavipākasya. yat tv adṛṣṭajanmavedanīyaṃ
            karmāniyatavipākaṃ tan naśyed āvāpaṃ vā gacched abhibhūtaṃ vā ciram apy upāsīta, yāvat
            samānaṃ karmābhivyañjakaṃ nimittam asya na vipākābhimukhaṃ karotīti. tadvipākasyaiva
            deśakālanimittānavadhāraṇād iyaṃ karmagatiś citrā durvijñānā ceti. na cotsargasyāpavādān
            nivṛttir ity ekabhavikaḥ karmāśayo+anujñāyata iti.
children.translated_text: Or, being overpowered by a principal karma of fixed fruition, a long remaining. How so? It has been stated that equal death is the manifesting cause for the karma which is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has fixed fruition, but not for that which is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has non-fixed fruition. Now, that karma which is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has non-fixed fruition—let it be destroyed, or let it go into descent, or, being overpowered, let it remain even a long time, so long as an equal manifesting occasion for karma does not make it face toward fruition. Because the place-time-occasion for the fruition of that [karma] is not determined, this course of karma is variegated and hard to discern. Nor is there a cessation of exceptions to the general rule; thus, the deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>) belonging to a single existence is admitted
Their fruits are delight and burning (pleasure and pain), since they are caused by merit and demerit (<s>puṇya</s>-<s>apuṇya</s>)

children.text:
te janmāyurbhogāḥ puṇyahetukāḥ sukhaphalā apuṇyahetukā duḥkhaphalā iti. yathā cedaṃ
            duḥkhaṃ pratikūlātmakam evaṃ viṣayasukhakāle+api duḥkham asty eva pratikūlātmakaṃ
            yoginaḥ.
children.translated_text: Those—birth, lifespan, and experience—are produced by merit in the case of the cause being merit and have pleasure as fruit, and produced by demerit in the case of the cause being demerit and have pain as fruit. And just as this pain has the nature of contrariety, so too, at the time of sense-object pleasure there certainly exists pain of a contrarious nature for the yogin
How? This is demonstrated—

children.text: pariṇāmatāpasaṃskāraduḥkhair guṇavṛttivirodhāc ca duḥkham eva sarvaṃ vivekinaḥ
children.translated_text: “Because of the pains of transformation, burning (ardor), and formation-impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), and because of the opposition of the functions of the <s>guṇa</s>-s, all is truly pain for the discerning,”

children.text:
sarvasyāyaṃ rāgānuviddhaś cetanācetanasādhanādhīnaḥ sukhānubhava iti tatrāsti rāgajaḥ
            karmāśayaḥ. tathā ca dveṣṭi duḥkhasādhanāni muhyati ceti dveṣamohakṛto+apy asti
            karmāśayaḥ. tathā coktam --- ``

nānupahatya bhūtāny upabhogaḥ saṃbhavatīti
              hiṃsākṛto+apy asti śarīraḥ karmāśayaḥ
children.translated_text: “Since enjoyment does not occur without injuring beings, therefore there also exists a bodily deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>) born of violence,”
thus. And sense-object pleasure has been said to be ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>)

For everyone, the experience of pleasure depends on means both conscious and non-conscious, pierced by attachment (<s>rāga</s>); thus there exists a deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>) born of attachment. Likewise, one hates the means of pain and is deluded—thus there also exists a deposit of karma born of aversion and delusion. And so it is said—

children.text:
yā bhogeṣv indriyāṇāṃ tṛpter upaśāntis tat sukham. yā laulyād anupaśāntis tad duḥkham.
            na cendriyāṇāṃ bhogābhyāsena vaitṛṣṇyaṃ kartuṃ śakyam. kasmāt, yato bhogābhyāsam anu
            vivardhante rāgāḥ kauśalāni cendriyāṇām iti. tasmād anupāyaḥ sukhasya bhogābhyāsa iti.
            sa khalv ayaṃ vṛścikaviṣabhīta ivāśīviṣeṇa daṣṭo yaḥ sukhārthī viṣayānuvāsito mahati
            duḥkhapaṅke nimagna iti. eṣā pariṇāmaduḥkhatā nāma pratikūlā sukhāvasthāyām api yoginam
            eva kliśnāti.
children.translated_text: That pacification (cessation) of the senses in enjoyments which is the satisfaction of the senses, that is pleasure; that non-pacification due to restlessness (greediness), that is pain. Nor can non-thirst (dispassion, <s>vaitṛṣṇyā</s>) be brought about by habituation to sense-enjoyment. Why? Because, following upon habituation to enjoyment, attachments (<s>rāga</s>-s) and the skills of the senses increase, thus. Therefore, habituation to enjoyment is not a means to pleasure. Indeed, this one, like a man afraid of a scorpion’s poison, bitten by a cobra, who, seeking pleasure, being perfumed by (steeped in) sense-objects, is sunk in a great mire of pain—this is the so-called pain-of-transformation (<s>pariṇāma-duḥkhatā</s>) which, even in a state apparently of pleasure, afflicts only the yogin,

children.text:
atha kā tāpaduḥkhatā, sarvasya dveṣānuviddhaś cetanācetanasādhanādhīnas tāpānubhava iti
            tatrāsti dveṣajaḥ karmāśayaḥ. sukhasādhanāni ca prārthayamānaḥ kāyena vācā manasā ca
            parispandate tataḥ param anugṛhṇāty upahanti ceti parānugrahapīḍābhyāṃ dharmādharmāv
            upacinoti. sa karmāśayo lobhān mohāc ca bhavatīty eṣā tāpaduḥkhatocyate. kā punaḥ
            saṃskāraduḥkhatā, sukhānubhavāt sukhasaṃskārāśayo duḥkhānubhavād api duḥkhasaṃskārāśaya
            iti. evaṃ karmabhyo vipāke+anubhūyamāne sukhe duḥkhe vā punaḥ karmāśayapracaya iti.
children.translated_text: Now, what is pain-of-ardor (burning, <s>tāpa-duḥkhatā</s>)? For everyone, the experience of ardor (torment) depends on means, conscious and non-conscious, pierced by aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>); thus there exists a karmic deposit (<s>karmāśaya</s>) born of aversion. And, desiring the means of pleasure, one agitates by body, speech, and mind; thereafter one benefits and injures others—thus, by benefiting and harming others one accumulates merit and demerit (<s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>). That karmic deposit arises from greed (<s>lobha</s>) and delusion (<s>moha</s>); this is what is called pain-of-ardor (<s>tāpa-duḥkhatā</s>). And what then is pain-of-formations (<s>saṃskāra-duḥkhatā</s>)? From the experience of pleasure, there is a deposit of pleasurable formations (<s>sukha-saṃskāra-āśaya</s>), and from the experience of pain, a deposit of painful formations (<s>duḥkha-saṃskāra-āśaya</s>). Thus, when, from karma, upon ripening, pleasure or pain is experienced, there is again an accumulation of karmic deposit (<s>karmāśaya</s>),

children.text:
evam idam anādi duḥkhasroto viprasṛtaṃ yoginam eva pratikūlātmakatvād udvejayati.
            kasmāt, akṣipātrakalpo hi vidvān iti. yathorṇātantur akṣipātre nyastaḥ sparśena
            duḥkhayati na cānyeṣu gātrāvayaveṣu, evam etāni duḥkhāny akṣipātrakalpaṃ yoginam eva
            kliśnanti netaraṃ pratipattāram. itaraṃ tu svakarmopahṛtaṃ duḥkham upāttam upāttaṃ
            tyajantaṃ tyaktaṃ tyaktam upādadānam anādivāsanāvicitrayā cittavṛttyā samantato
            'nuviddham ivāvidyayā hātavya evāhaṃkāramamakārānupātinaṃ jātaṃ jātaṃ
            bāhyādhyātmikobhayanimittās triparvāṇas tāpā anuplavante. tad evam anādinā duḥkhasrotasā
            vyuhyamānam ātmānaṃ bhūtagrāmaṃ ca dṛṣṭvā yogī sarvaduḥkhakṣayakāraṇaṃ samyagdarśanaṃ
            śaraṇaṃ prapadyata iti.
children.translated_text: Thus this beginningless stream of pain, having been sent forth, perturbs the yogin alone because of its contrarious nature. Why? Because the knower is like an eye-cup (eyelid) receptacle. Just as the spider’s thread placed upon an eye-cup causes pain by touch, and not upon the other members of the body, so these pains afflict only the yogin who is like an eye-cup, not another knower. But the other, whose pain is brought on by his own karma (<s>karma</s>), taking up what is taken up, casting off what is cast off, and taking up again what is cast off, being everywhere pierced, as it were, by ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) through the manifold, beginningless impression-nature of the mind’s activities (<s>citta-vṛtti</s>), necessarily accompanies I-notion and mine-notion (<s>ahaṃkāra</s> and <s>mamakāra</s>); ever and again the threefold burns—having external, internal, and both causes—flood him. Therefore, seeing himself and the multitude of beings being buffeted by the beginningless stream of pain, the yogin takes refuge in right-seeing (<s>samyag-darśana</s>) as the means to the exhaustion of all pain,

children.text:
guṇavṛttivirodhāc ca duḥkham eva sarvaṃ vivekinaḥ. prakhyāpravṛttisthitirūpā
            buddhiguṇāḥ parasparānugrahatantrī bhūtvā śāntaṃ ghoraṃ mūḍhaṃ vā pratyayaṃ triguṇam
            evārabhante. calaṃ ca guṇavṛttam iti kṣiprapariṇāmi cittam uktam. rūpātiśayā
            vṛttyatiśayāś ca paraspareṇa virudhyante, sāmānyāni tv atiśayaiḥ saha pravartante. evam
            ete guṇā itaretarāśrayeṇopārjitasukhaduḥkhamohapratyayāḥ sarve sarvarūpā bhavantīti,
            guṇapradhānabhāvakṛtas tv eṣāṃ viśeṣa iti. tasmād duḥkham eva sarvaṃ vivekina iti.
children.translated_text: And because of the opposition of the activities of the <s>guṇa</s>-s, all is truly pain for the discerning. The qualities (<s>buddhi-guṇa</s>-s), of the forms luminosity, activity, and fixity (clarity, motion, inertia), becoming mutually dependent in conferring benefit upon one another, set in motion a three-<s>guṇa</s> cognition that is serene, terrible, or stupefied. And since the activity of the <s>guṇa</s>-s is unsteady, the mind (<s>citta</s>) is said to be quickly transformed. Excess of form (intensity of a quality) and excess of activity (function) oppose one another, whereas the commonalities proceed together with the excesses. Thus these <s>guṇa</s>-s, by mutual dependence, becoming cognitions of pleasure, pain, and delusion, all become of every sort; yet their specificities are due to the predominance of a particular <s>guṇa</s>. Therefore, all is truly pain for the discerning,

children.text:
tad asya mahato duḥkhasamudāyasya prabhavabījam avidyā. tasyāś ca samyagdarśanam
            abhāvahetuḥ. yathā cikitsāśāstraṃ caturvyūham --- rogo rogahetur ārogyaṃ bhaiṣajyam iti.
            evam idam api śāstram caturvyūham eva. tadyathā --- saṃsāraḥ saṃsārahetur mokṣo
            mokṣopāya iti. tatra duḥkhabahulaḥ saṃsāro heyaḥ. pradhānapuruṣayoḥ saṃyogo heyahetuḥ.
            saṃyogasyātyantikī nivṛttir hānam. hānopāyaḥ samyagdarśanam.
children.translated_text: Now, the originating seed of this great aggregate of pain is ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), and right-seeing (<s>samyag-darśana</s>) is its cause of absence. Just as the medical science has a fourfold array—disease, cause of disease, health, remedy—so this scripture too is indeed fourfold. Namely: transmigration (<s>saṃsāra</s>), the cause of transmigration, liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>), and the means to liberation. There, the transmigration abounding in pain is to be abandoned; the conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) and <s>puruṣa</s> (spirit) is the cause to be abandoned; the final cessation of conjunction is abandonment; the means of abandonment is right-seeing (<s>samyag-darśana</s>)

children.text:
tatra hātuḥ svarūpam upādeyaṃ vā heyaṃ vā na bhavitum arhatīti hāne
            tasyocchedavādaprasaṅga upādāne ca hetuvādaḥ. ubhayapratyākhyāne śāśvatavāda ity etat
            samyagdarśanam.
children.translated_text: There, neither is the own-nature of the agent-of-abandonment to be adopted nor is it to be cast away—else, in abandoning it there would follow the fault of advocating annihilation, and in adopting it, the doctrine of causes; in denying both, there would be the doctrine of eternalism—that is right-seeing (<s>samyagdarśana</s>)

children.text: tad etac chāstraṃ caturvyūham ity abhidhīyate ---
children.translated_text: Accordingly, this scripture is designated as having a fourfold array—
What is to be abandoned is the pain that is not yet arisen

children.text:
duḥkham atītam upabhogenātivāhitaṃ na heyapakṣe vartate. vartamānaṃ ca svakṣaṇe
            bhogārūḍham iti na tat kṣaṇāntare heyatām āpadyate. tasmād yad evānāgataṃ duḥkhaṃ tad
            evākṣipātrakalpaṃ yoginaṃ kliśnāti netaraṃ pratipattāram. tad eva heyatām āpadyate.
children.translated_text: The past pain, having been carried beyond by enjoyment, does not fall under the side of what is to be abandoned; and the present [pain], having mounted upon enjoyment in its own moment, does not, in the next moment, come into the state of being to-be-abandoned. Therefore, that very pain which is not yet arisen afflicts the yogin, who is like an eye-cup (eyelid receptacle), and not another experiencer; that alone comes into the state of being to-be-abandoned

children.text: tasmād yad eva heyam ity ucyate tasyaiva kāraṇaṃ pratinirdiśyate ---
children.translated_text: Therefore, for that very thing which is said to be to-be-abandoned, its cause is precisely indicated—
The conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) of the seer and the seen is the cause of what is to be abandoned

children.text:
draṣṭā buddheḥ pratisaṃvedī puruṣaḥ. dṛśyā buddhisattvopārūḍhāḥ sarve dharmāḥ. tad etad
            dṛśyam ayaskāntamaṇikalpaṃ saṃnidhimātropakāri dṛśyatvena svaṃ bhavati puruṣasya
            dṛśirūpasya svāminaḥ, anubhavakarmaviṣayatām āpannaṃ yataḥ. anyasvarūpeṇa
            pratilabdhātmakaṃ svatantram api parārthatvāt paratantram.
children.translated_text: The seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>) is the <s>puruṣa</s>, the one who is re-cognizer with respect to the <s>buddhi</s>; the seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) are all dharmas mounted upon the clarity (<s>sattva</s>) of the <s>buddhi</s>. This seen, like a magnet-stone, by mere proximity renders service and, as the seen, becomes its own (belonging) of the <s>puruṣa</s>, who is of the nature of seeing and is the master, inasmuch as it comes into the condition of being the field of experience and action; though it has recovered its own nature and is independent, yet, because it is for-another, it is dependent

children.text:
tayor dṛgdarśanaśaktyor anādir arthakṛtaḥ saṃyogo heyahetur duḥkhasya kāraṇam ity
            arthaḥ. tathā coktam --- tatsaṃyogahetuvivarjanāt syād ayam ātyantiko duḥkhapratīkāraḥ.
            kasmāt, duḥkhahetoḥ parihāryasya pratīkāradarśanāt. tadyathā --- pādatalasya bhedyatā,
            kaṇṭakasya bhettṛtvaṃ, parihāraḥ kaṇṭakasya pā(pa)dānadhiṣṭhānaṃ pādatrāṇavyavahitena
            vādhiṣṭhānam, etat trayaṃ yo veda loke sa tatra pratīkāram ārabhamāṇo bhedajaṃ duḥkhaṃ
            nāpnoti. kasmāt, tritvopalabdhisāmarthyād iti. atrāpi tāpakasya rajasaḥ sattvam eva
            tapyam. kasmāt, tapikriyāyāḥ karmasthatvāt, sattve karmaṇi tapikriyā nāpariṇāmini
            niṣkriye kṣetrajñe, darśitaviṣayatvāt. sattve tu tapyamāne tadākārānurodhī puruṣo+apy
            anutapyata iti.
children.translated_text: Of these two powers, the power of seeing and the power of being seen, their beginningless conjunction, caused by the object (purpose), is the cause of what is to be abandoned—the cause of pain; thus the meaning. And so it is said—“From the removal of the cause of that conjunction, there would be this absolute remedy of pain.” Why? Because one sees the remedy of that which is to be avoided, namely the cause of pain. For example—the vulnerableness-to-piercing of the sole of the foot, the thorn’s capacity-to-pierce, the avoidance is the establishing of a base for the thorn in the giving of a shoe, or the establishing of a base for the foot separated by a foot-covering; whoever in the world knows this triad, when setting about the remedy there, does not obtain the pain born of piercing. Why? Because of the capacity to apprehend the threefoldness, that is. Here too, it is the <s>sattva</s> that is heated by the heat of <s>rajas</s>. Why? Because the act of heating abides in karma; the act of heating does not abide in the field-knower (<s>kṣetrajña</s>), who is untransformed, actionless, having the domain of what has been shown; but when the <s>sattva</s> is heated, the <s>puruṣa</s>, conforming to that form, also appears to be heated
The own-nature of the seen is stated—
The seen is of the character of illumination, activity, and stability; consisting of elements and senses; for the sake of enjoyment and release (<s>apavarga</s>)

children.text:
prakāśaśīlaṃ sattvam. kriyāśīlaṃ rajaḥ sthitiśīlaṃ tama iti. ete guṇāḥ
            parasparoparaktapravibhāgāḥ pariṇāminaḥ saṃyogaviyogadharmāṇa
            itaretaropāśrayeṇopārjitamūrtayaḥ parasparāṅgāṅgitve+apy asaṃbhinnaśaktipravibhāgās
            tulyajātīyātulyajātīyaśaktibhedānupātinaḥ pradhānavelāyām upadarśitasaṃnidhānā
            guṇatve+api ca vyāpāramātreṇa pradhānāntarṇītānumitāstitāḥ puruṣārthakartavyatayā
            prayuktasāmarthyāḥ saṃnidhimātropakāriṇo+ayaskāntamaṇikalpāḥ pratyayam
            antareṇaikatamasya vṛttim anuvartamānāḥ pradhānaśabdavācyā bhavanti. etad dṛśyam ity
            ucyate.
children.translated_text: That whose character is illumination is <s>sattva</s>, that whose character is activity is <s>rajas</s>, that whose character is stability is <s>tamas</s>. These <s>guṇa</s>-s, mutually tinctured yet distinguished, are transformative, having the properties of conjunction and disjunction; having forms acquired through mutual dependence upon one another; though being each other’s parts and wholes, they have undisordered divisions of powers; following differences of powers that are of the same kind and of different kinds; at the time of the prominence of the <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter), having their presence shown; though being <s>guṇa</s>-s, by activity alone they are inferred to have existence as included within the <s>Pradhāna</s>; being empowered as to what is to be done for the sake of the <s>puruṣa</s>; by mere proximity, like a magnet-stone; continuing the function of any one of them without the need of a determinate cognition, they are denoted by the term <s>Pradhāna</s>. This is what is called the seen

children.text:
tad etad bhūtendriyātmakaṃ bhūtabhāvena pṛthivyādinā sūkṣmasthūlena pariṇamate.
            tathendriyabhāvena śrotrādinā sūkṣmasthūlena pariṇamata iti. tat tu nāprayojanam api tu
            prayojanam urarīkṛtya pravartata iti bhogāpavargārthaṃ hi tad dṛśyaṃ puruṣasyeti.
            tatreṣṭāniṣṭaguṇasvarūpāvadhāraṇam avibhāgāpannaṃ bhogo bhoktuḥ svarūpāvadhāraṇam
            apavarga iti. dvayor atiriktam anyad darśanaṃ nāsti. tathā coktam --- ayaṃ tu khalu
            triṣu guṇeṣu kartṛṣv akartari ca puruṣe tulyātulyajātīye caturthe tatkriyāsākṣiṇy
            upanīyamānān sarvabhāvān upapannān anupaśyann adarśanam anyac chaṅkata iti.
children.translated_text: This, having the nature of elements and senses (<s>bhūta</s>-<s>indriya</s>-self), transforms in the mode of elements—from earth and the rest—into subtle and gross; likewise, in the mode of senses—from ear and the rest—into subtle and gross it transforms, that is. But it does not proceed without a purpose; rather, having made the purpose prominent it proceeds—for indeed that seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) is for the sake of enjoyment and release (<s>bhoga</s>-<s>apavarga</s>) of the <s>puruṣa</s>. There, enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>) is the ascertainment of the own-forms of desirable and undesirable qualities, fallen-into non-discrimination; release (<s>apavarga</s>) is the ascertainment of the own-form of the experiencer. Other seeing apart from these two does not exist. And thus it is said—“This indeed, when all beings, being brought under observation in the three <s>guṇa</s>-s as agents, and in the <s>puruṣa</s> as non-agent, and in the fourth as of similar and dissimilar kind, and as witnesses of those actions, are examined and found coherent, one who, not seeing, suspects another seeing,”

children.text:
tāv etau bhogāpavargau buddhikṛtau buddhāv eva vartamānau kathaṃ puruṣe vyapadiśyete
            iti. yathā vijayaḥ parājayo vā yoddhṛṣu vartamānaḥ svāmini vyapadiśyate, sa hi
            tatphalasya bhokteti, evaṃ bandhamokṣau buddhāv eva vartamānau puruṣe vyapadiśyete, sa
            hi tatphalasya bhokteti. buddher eva puruṣārthāparisamāptir bandhas tadarthāvasāyo mokṣa
            iti. etena grahaṇadhāraṇohāpohatattvajñānābhiniveśā buddhau vartamānāḥ
            puruṣe+adhyāropitasadbhāvāḥ. sa hi tatphalasya bhokteti.
children.translated_text: Now, these two—enjoyment and release—are wrought by the <s>buddhi</s> and subsist precisely in the <s>buddhi</s>; how are they predicated of the <s>puruṣa</s>? Just as victory or defeat, though present in the combatants, is ascribed to the lord, for he is the enjoyer of that result, so bondage and liberation, though present in the <s>buddhi</s>, are predicated of the <s>puruṣa</s>, for he is the enjoyer of that result. The non-completion of the <s>buddhi</s> itself with respect to the purpose of the <s>puruṣa</s> is bondage; the ascertainment of that purpose is liberation. By this it is indicated that grasping, retention, inference, exclusion, true-knowledge, and attachment, though present in the <s>buddhi</s>, are superimposed upon the <s>puruṣa</s> as having real being—for he is the enjoyer of that result
For the ascertainment of the specific-difference and own-forms of the qualities (<s>guṇa</s>-s) of the seen, this is undertaken—
The stages of the <s>guṇa</s>-s are the particular, the non-particular, the mere mark, and the unmarked

children.text:
tatrākāśavāyvagnyudakabhūmayo bhūtāni śabdasparśarūparasagandhatanmātrāṇām aviśeṣāṇāṃ
            viśeṣāḥ. tathā śrotratvakcakṣurjihvāghrāṇāni buddhīndriyāṇi, vākpāṇipādapāyūpasthāḥ
            karmendriyāṇi, ekādaśaṃ manaḥ sarvārtham, ity etāny asmitālakṣaṇasyāviśeṣasya viśeṣāḥ.
            guṇānām eṣa ṣoḍaśako viśeṣapariṇāmaḥ.
children.translated_text: There, the five—space, air, fire, water, earth—are the elements, the particularizations of the non-particulars—the five subtle essences beginning with sound, namely sound, touch, form, taste, smell. Likewise, the ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose are the cognitive senses (<s>buddhīndriya</s>-s); speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals are the active senses (<s>karmendriya</s>-s); the eleventh is mind (<s>manas</s>), related to all objects—these are the particulars of non-particularity characterized as <s>asmitā</s> (I-ness). This is the sixteenfold particular transformation of the <s>guṇa</s>-s

children.text:
ṣaḍ aviśeṣāḥ. tadyathā --- śabdatanmātraṃ sparśatanmātraṃ rūpatanmātraṃ rasatanmātraṃ
            gandhatanmātraṃ ceti ekadvitricatuḥpañcalakṣaṇāḥ śabdādayaḥ pañcāviśeṣāḥ, ṣaṣṭhaś
            cāviśeṣo+asmitāmātra iti. ete sattāmātrasyātmano mahataḥ ṣaḍaviśeṣapariṇāmāḥ. yat tat
            paramaviśeṣebhyo liṅgamātraṃ mahattattvaṃ tasminn ete sattāmātre mahaty ātmany avasthāya
            vivṛddhikāṣṭhām anubhavanti.
children.translated_text: There are six non-particulars. Namely—the subtle essence of sound, of touch, of form, of taste, and of smell: these five non-particulars, marked as one, two, three, four, five; and the sixth non-particular is mere <s>asmitā</s>. These are the six non-particular transformations of the great self (<s>mahat</s>), whose self is mere being (<s>sattā</s>-mātra). That which, from the supreme particulars, is the mere mark (<s>liṅga</s>-mātra), the great principle (<s>mahat-tattva</s>)—in that, these, abiding in mere being, in the great self, attain the limit of growth

children.text:
pratisaṃsṛjyamānāś ca tasminn eva sattāmātre mahaty ātmany avasthāya yat tan
            niḥsattāsattaṃ niḥsadasan nirasad avyaktam aliṅgaṃ pradhānaṃ tat pratiyanti. eṣa teṣāṃ
            liṅgamātraḥ pariṇāmo niḥsattāsattaṃ cāliṅgapariṇāma iti.
children.translated_text: And being reabsorbed, abiding in that very great self which is mere being, they apprehend that which is devoid of being-of-<s>sattva</s> and non-being-of-<s>sattva</s>, devoid of being and non-being, devoid of essence, unmanifest, unmarked (<s>aliṅga</s>), the <s>Pradhāna</s>. This is their transformation into mere mark (<s>liṅga</s>-mātra), and the transformation into the unmarked which is devoid of being-of-<s>sattva</s> and non-being-of-<s>sattva</s>

children.text:
aliṅgāvasthāyāṃ na puruṣārtho hetur nāliṅgāvasthāyām ādau puruṣārthatā kāraṇaṃ
            bhavatīti. na tasyāḥ puruṣārthatā kāraṇaṃ bhavatīti. nāsau puruṣārthakṛteti
            nityākhyāyate. trayāṇāṃ tv avasthāviśeṣāṇām ādau puruṣārthatā kāraṇaṃ bhavati. sa cārtho
            hetur nimittaṃ kāraṇaṃ bhavatīty anityākhyāyate. guṇās tu sarvadharmānupātino na
            pratyastam ayante nopajāyante. vyaktibhir evātītānāgatavyayāgamavatībhir guṇānvayinībhir
            upajananāpāyadharmakā iva pratyavabhāsante. yathā devadatto daridrāti. kasmāt yato+asya
            mriyante gāva iti, gavām eva maraṇāt tasya daridrāṇaṃ na svarūpahānād iti samaḥ
            samādhiḥ.
children.translated_text: In the unmarked state there is no cause of serving the purpose of the <s>puruṣa</s>; nor, in the initial unmarked state, does purposiveness for the <s>puruṣa</s> become a cause—thus there is no causing of purposiveness for it; since it does not effect the purpose of the <s>puruṣa</s>, it is called eternal. But in the three distinctive states, at the beginning, purposiveness for the <s>puruṣa</s> does become a cause; and that purpose is a cause, an occasion, a reason—therefore it is called non-eternal. But the <s>guṇa</s>-s, being concomitant with all dharmas, neither set, nor arise. Only the particulars, marked as past, future, and present, being accompanied by the <s>guṇa</s>-s, appear as if possessing the properties of production and cessation. As when one says, “Devadatta is impoverished.” Why? “Because his cows are dying”—it is from the death of the cows that he is impoverished, not from a loss of his own essential nature—such is evenness as samādhi

children.text:
liṅgamātram aliṅgasya pratyāsannaṃ, tatra tat saṃsṛṣṭaṃ vivicyate kramān ativṛttayaḥ.
            tathā ṣaḍ aviśeṣā liṅgamātre saṃsṛṣṭā vivicyante pariṇāmakramaniyamāt. tathā teṣv
            aviśeṣeṣu bhūtendriyāṇi saṃsṛṣṭāni vivicyante. tathā coktaṃ purastāt. na viśeṣebhyaḥ
            paraṃ tattvāntaram astīti viśeṣāṇāṃ nāsti tattvāntarapariṇāmaḥ. teṣāṃ tu
            dharmalakṣaṇāvasthāpariṇāmā vyākhyāyiṣyante.
children.translated_text: The mere mark (<s>liṅga-mātra</s>) is adjacent to the unmarked (<s>aliṅga</s>); there, each [stage], being conjoined with that [next], is to be distinguished in sequence, as the overpassings (transitions) proceed. Likewise, the six non-particulars (<s>aviśeṣa</s>-s), being conjoined in the mere mark (<s>liṅga-mātra</s>), are distinguished because of the fixity of the order of transformation; likewise, in those non-particulars, the elements-and-senses (<s>bhūta</s>-<s>indriya</s>) being conjoined are distinguished. And so it was said before: beyond the particulars there is no other principle (no further tattva); therefore, for the particulars there is no transformation into a different principle (no other-tattva transformation). But their transformations as state of property, mark of property, and condition of state (<s>dharma</s>-<s>lakṣaṇa</s>-<s>avasthā</s>-pariṇāma) will be explained

children.text: vyākhyātaṃ dṛśyam atha draṣṭuḥ svarūpāvadhāraṇārtham idam ārabhyate ---
children.translated_text: The seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) has been explained; now, for the purpose of ascertaining the own-form (essential nature) of the seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>), this is undertaken—
The seer is mere seeing (pure vision), though pure, he is an after-observer of cognitions (he observes cognitions)

children.text:
dṛśimātra iti dṛkśaktir eva viśeṣaṇāparāmṛṣṭety arthaḥ. sa puruṣo bhuddheḥ
            pratisaṃvedī. sa buddher na sarūpo nātyantaṃ virūpa iti. na tāvat sarūpaḥ kasmāt.
            jñātājñātaviṣayatvāt pariṇāminī hi buddhiḥ. tasyāś ca viṣayo gavādir ghaṭādir vā jñātaś
            cājñātaś ceti pariṇāmitvaṃ darśayati.
children.translated_text: “Mere seeing” means: only the power of seeing, untouched by any qualifier; that is the sense. He, the <s>puruṣa</s>, is the one who re-cognizes with respect to the <s>buddhi</s>. He is neither identical in form with the <s>buddhi</s> nor completely of different form from it. Not, to be sure, identical in form—why? Because the <s>buddhi</s> has as its domain both what is known and what is unknown, since the <s>buddhi</s> is subject to transformation; and its objects—cow and the like, or pot and the like—are both known and unknown, thus its being-transformable is shown

children.text:
sadājñātaviṣayatvaṃ tu puruṣasyāpariṇāmitvaṃ paridīpayati kasmāt. na hi buddhiś ca nāma
            puruṣaviṣayaś ca syād agṛhītā gṛhītā ceti siddhaṃ puruṣasya sadājñātaviṣayatvaṃ tataś
            cāpariṇāmitvam iti. kiṃ ca parārthā buddhiḥ saṃhatyakāritvāt, svārthaḥ puruṣa iti. tathā
            sarvārthādhyavasāyakatvāt triguṇā buddhis triguṇatvād acetaneti. guṇānāṃ tūpadraṣṭā
            puruṣa ity ato na sarūpaḥ.
children.translated_text: But the fact that the <s>puruṣa</s> has as his domain what is always-known (ever-known) makes manifest his non-transformability—why? For the <s>buddhi</s> cannot be said to have the <s>puruṣa</s> as its object both not-grasped and grasped; thus it is established that the <s>puruṣa</s> has as his domain what is always-known, and hence is non-transformable. Moreover, the <s>buddhi</s> is for-another (<s>parārtha</s>) because it operates as a conglomerate (is a product of conjunction); the <s>puruṣa</s> is for-self (<s>svārtha</s>). Likewise, since it determines all objects, the <s>buddhi</s> is three-<s>guṇa</s>-ed, and because of being three-<s>guṇa</s>-ed it is non-conscious; whereas the <s>puruṣa</s> is the overseer (witness) of the <s>guṇa</s>-s, therefore he is not identical in form

children.text:
astu tarhi virūpa iti. nātyantaṃ virūpaḥ kasmāt. śuddho+apy asau pratyayānupaśyo yataḥ.
            pratyayaṃ bauddham anupaśyati, tam anupaśyann atadātmāpi tadātmaka iva pratyavabhāsate.
            tathā coktam --- apariṇāminī hi bhoktṛśaktir apratisaṃkramā ca pariṇāminy arthe
            pratisaṃkrānteva tadvṛttim anupatati, tasyāś ca prāptacaitanyopagraharūpāyā buddhivṛtter
            anukāramātratayā buddhivṛttyaviśiṣṭā hi jñānavṛttir ity ākhyāyate.
children.translated_text: Then let him be of different form—so be it; yet he is not completely of different form—why? Because, though pure, he is an after-observer of cognitions; he after-observes the cognition that is of the <s>buddhi</s>, and by after-observing it, though he is not of that nature, he appears as if of that very nature. And so it has been said—“The power of enjoying (experiencing) is non-transformable and does not transmigrate, yet, when the transformable object is as if transmigrated (has shifted), it follows its function; and since the cognition-function of the <s>buddhi</s> has the form of having received the accession of manifested consciousness, by mere imitation of that cognition-function, the knowledge-function (in the <s>puruṣa</s>) is spoken of as not distinct from the cognition-function of the <s>buddhi</s>,”
The very self of the seen is for the sake of that [seer]

children.text:
dṛśirūpasya puruṣasya karmarūpatām āpannaṃ dṛśyam iti tadartha eva dṛśyasyātmā bhavati.
            svarūpaṃ bhavatīty arthaḥ. svarūpaṃ tu pararūpeṇa pratilabdhātmakaṃ
            bhogāpavargārthatāyāṃ kṛtāyāṃ puruṣeṇa na dṛśyata iti. svarūpahānād asya nāśaḥ prāpto na
            tu vinaśyati.
children.translated_text: What is of the form of seeing—the <s>puruṣa</s>—when the seen has assumed the form of action (has become the domain of action), then indeed the very self of the seen is for the sake of that [seer]; that is, it becomes its own-form (essential nature) [as-for-another]. Its own-form is acquired in another’s form, when its being for enjoyment and for release (<s>bhoga</s>-<s>apavarga</s>) has been accomplished, it is not seen by the <s>puruṣa</s>; from the loss of its own-form its destruction would be imminent, yet it does not perish
Why so—

children.text: kṛtārthaṃ prati naṣṭam apy anaṣṭaṃ tadanyasādhāraṇatvāt
children.translated_text: Though destroyed with respect to the one for whom the purpose has been accomplished, it is not destroyed, because it is not common to that other (it remains common to others)

children.text:
kṛtārtham ekaṃ puruṣaṃ prati dṛśyaṃ naṣṭam api nāśaṃ prāptam apy anaṣṭaṃ
            tadanyapuruṣasādhāraṇatvāt. kuśalaṃ puruṣaṃ prati nāśaṃ prāptam apy akuśalān puruṣān
            prati na kṛtārtham iti teṣāṃ dṛśeḥ karmaviṣayatām āpannaṃ labhata eva pararūpeṇātmarūpam
            iti. ataś ca dṛgdarśanaśaktyor nityatvād anādiḥ saṃyogo vyākhyāta iti. tathā coktam ---
            dharmiṇām anādisaṃyogād dharmamātrāṇām apy anādiḥ saṃyoga iti.
children.translated_text: With respect to the one <s>puruṣa</s> whose purpose is accomplished, the seen, though destroyed (though having reached destruction), is not destroyed, because it is common to other <s>puruṣa</s>-s. With respect to a skillful (capable) <s>puruṣa</s> it has reached destruction (its purpose is done), but with respect to unskillful <s>puruṣa</s>-s it is not fulfilled; therefore, for those, the seen, having assumed the character of being the field of action, indeed attains, in another’s form, its own-form. And thus, because the powers of seeing and of being seen are eternal, their conjunction has been explained as beginningless. And so it has been said—“Because of the beginningless conjunctions of substrata (bearers of properties), even for properties alone there is a beginningless conjunction,”
With the intention of defining the own-nature of conjunction, this sūtra is set forth—
Conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) is the cause of the apprehension of the own-forms of the power that is one’s own (self) and the power that is the owner (master)

children.text:
puruṣaḥ svāmī dṛśyena svena darśanārthaṃ saṃyuktaḥ. tasmāt saṃyogād dṛśyasyopalabdhir
            yā sa bhogaḥ. yā tu draṣṭuḥ svarūpopalabdhiḥ so+apavargaḥ. darśanakāryāvasānaḥ saṃyoga
            iti darśanaṃ viyogasya kāraṇam uktam. darśanam adarśanasya pratidvandvīty adarśanaṃ
            saṃyoganimittam uktam. nātra darśanaṃ mokṣakāraṇam adarśanābhāvād eva bandhābhāvaḥ sa
            mokṣa iti. darśanasya bhāve bandhakāraṇasyādarśanasya nāśa ity ato darśanaṃ jñānaṃ
            kaivalyakāraṇam uktam.
children.translated_text: The <s>puruṣa</s> (spirit), the master, is conjoined with the seen by his own [power] for the sake of seeing; therefore, from that conjunction there is the apprehension of the seen—that is enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>), whereas the apprehension of the own-form (essential nature) of the seer—that is release (<s>apavarga</s>). The termination of the work of seeing is conjunction—that is to say, seeing is said to be the cause of disjunction; seeing is the counter-opposite of non-seeing, thus non-seeing is said to be the occasion (cause) of conjunction. Here, seeing is not the cause of liberation—since from the mere absence of non-seeing there is the absence of bondage, that is liberation. But when seeing is present, there is the destruction of non-seeing, the cause of bondage; therefore seeing—knowledge—is said to be the cause of <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation)

children.text:
kiṃcedam adarśanaṃ nāma, kiṃ guṇānām adhikāra āhosvid dṛśirūpasya svāmino
            darśitaviṣayasya pradhānacittasyānutpādaḥ. svasmin dṛśye vidyamāne yo darśanābhāvaḥ.
children.translated_text: And what is this so-called non-seeing? Is it the jurisdiction (operative scope) of the <s>guṇa</s>-s, or else the non-arising of the <s>pradhāna</s>-mind (<s>pradhāna-citta</s>)—which is of the form of the seen and has its objects shown—of the master who is of the form of seeing? It is the absence of seeing when the seen is present in itself

children.text:
kim arthavattā guṇānām. athāvidyā svacittena saha niruddhā svacittasyotpattibījam. kiṃ
            sthitisaṃskārakṣaye gatisaṃskārābhivyaktiḥ. yatredam uktaṃ pradhānaṃ sthityaiva
            vartamānaṃ vikārākaraṇād apradhānaṃ syāt.
children.translated_text: What purposiveness (use) do the <s>guṇa</s>-s have? Or is it that ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), restrained together with its own mind, is the seed of the arising of its own mind? Is it, when the formation-impressions of stability are exhausted, that the formation-impressions of motion become manifest? Where it has been said: if the <s>Pradhāna</s> abides solely in stability, then, because it does not effect transformation, it would be non-<s>Pradhāna</s>

children.text:
tathā gatyaiva vartamānaṃ vikāranityatvād apradhānaṃ syāt. ubhayathā cāsya vṛttiḥ
            pradhānavyavahāraṃ labhate nānyathā. kāraṇāntareṣv api kalpiteṣv eva samānaś carcaḥ.
            darśanaśaktir evādarśanam ity eke, ``

children.translated_text: The activity of the <s>Pradhāna</s> is for the purpose of making known its own self,”
thus it is heard

Likewise, if it abides solely in motion, then, because of transformation’s being constant, it would be non-<s>Pradhāna</s>; and in both ways its operation acquires the usage (designation) “<s>Pradhāna</s>,” not otherwise. Even when other causes are posited, the same discussion applies. Some say: the very power of seeing is non-seeing, on the authority of [the scriptural statement], “

children.text:
sarvabodhyabodhasamarthaḥ prākpravṛtteḥ puruṣo na paśyati sarvakāryakaraṇasamarthaṃ
            dṛśyaṃ tadā na dṛśyata iti. ubhayasyāpy adarśanaṃ dharma ity eke. tatredaṃ dṛśyasya
            svātmabhūtam api puruṣapratyayāpekṣaṃ darśanaṃ dṛśyadharmatvena bhavati. tathā
            puruṣasyānātmabhūtam api dṛśyapratyayāpekṣaṃ puruṣadharmatvenevādarśanam avabhāsate.
            darśanaṃ jñānam evādarśanam iti kecid abhidadhati. ity ete śāstragatā vikalpāḥ. tatra
            vikalpabahutvam etat sarvapuruṣāṇāṃ guṇānāṃ saṃyoge sādhāraṇaviṣayam.
children.translated_text: The <s>puruṣa</s>, capable of every cognition of every knowable, does not see, prior to the activity, the seen which is capable of every function and instrument; at that time it is not seen—thus. Others say: the non-seeing of both is a property (dharma). Here, then, this: even though seeing belongs to the seen as its own-self, being dependent upon the notion of the <s>puruṣa</s>, it becomes a property of the seen; likewise, even though non-seeing does not belong to the <s>puruṣa</s> as his own-self, being dependent upon the notion of the seen, it appears as if a property of the <s>puruṣa</s>. Some declare that seeing is knowledge, and non-seeing likewise. Such are the alternatives found in the scripture. Among these, this multiplicity of alternatives has as its common subject the conjunction of the <s>guṇa</s>-s with all <s>puruṣa</s>-s
But as for the conjunction of one whose consciousness is turned inward (<s>pratyak-cetana</s>) with his own <s>buddhi</s>—
Its cause is ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>)

children.text:
viparyayajñānavāsanety arthaḥ. viparyayajñānavāsanāvāsitā ca na kāryaniṣṭhāṃ
            puruṣakhyātiṃ buddhiḥ prāpnoti sādhikārā punar āvartate. sā tu puruṣakhyātiparyavasānāṃ
            kāryaniṣṭhāṃ prāpnoti, caritādhikārā nivṛttādarśanā bandhakāraṇābhāvān na punar
            āvartate.
children.translated_text: That is to say, the latent impression (residual potency) of erroneous knowledge (<s>viparyaya-jñāna-vāsanā</s>). And when perfumed by the latent impression of erroneous knowledge, the <s>buddhi</s> does not attain steadfastness in the recognition of the <s>puruṣa</s> (puruṣa-discernment); being still qualified for action, it returns again. But that [same <s>buddhi</s>] attains steadfastness which culminates in recognition of the <s>puruṣa</s>; having fulfilled its task, with non-seeing ceased, and in the absence of the cause of bondage, it does not return again

children.text:
atra kaścit paṇḍakopākhyānenodghāṭayati --- mugdhayā bhāryayābhidhīyate ---
            paṇḍakāryaputra, apatyavatī me bhaginī kimarthaṃ nāma nāham iti, sa tām āha --- mṛtas
            te+aham apatyam utpādayiṣyāmīti. tathedaṃ vidyamānaṃ jñānaṃ cittanivṛttiṃ na karoti,
            vinaṣṭaṃ kariṣyatīti kā pratyāśā. tatrācāryadeśīyo vakti --- nanu buddhinivṛttir eva
            mokṣo+adarśanakāraṇābhāvād buddhinivṛttiḥ. tac cādarśanaṃ bandhakāraṇaṃ darśanān
            nivartate. tatra cittanivṛttir eva mokṣaḥ, kimartham asthāna evāsya mativibhramaḥ.
children.translated_text: Here someone opens [the matter] with the anecdote called “The Eunuch” (Paṇḍaka): he is addressed by his foolish wife—“O son of a eunuch, my sister is with child: for what reason, pray, am I not?” He says to her—“I am dead; I shall beget offspring,” thus. So too, this present knowledge does not effect the cessation of the mind, while [one says that] when destroyed it will do so—what expectation is that? Thereupon a teacher of the lineage says—“But surely the cessation of the <s>buddhi</s> itself is liberation; and the cessation of the <s>buddhi</s> comes about from the absence of the cause of non-seeing. And that non-seeing, the cause of bondage, is turned back by seeing. Therefore, the cessation of the mind is precisely liberation—why this confusion of judgment in a matter that is not apt?”

children.text:
heyaṃ duḥkhaṃ heyakāraṇaṃ ca saṃyogākhyaṃ sanimittam uktam ataḥ paraṃ hānaṃ vaktavyam
            ---
children.translated_text: What is to be abandoned is pain, and its cause to be abandoned has been said to be conjunction, which has an occasion (cause); after this, cessation (abandonment) is to be stated—
From the absence of that, there is the absence of conjunction—abandonment; for that seer, <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation)

children.text:
tasyādarśanasyābhāvād buddhipuruṣasaṃyogābhāva ātyantiko bandhanoparama ity arthaḥ.
            etad dhānam. taddṛśeḥ kaivalyaṃ puruṣasyāmiśrībhāvaḥ punar asaṃyogo guṇair ity arthaḥ.
            duḥkhakāraṇanivṛttau duḥkhoparamo hānam, tadā svarūpapratiṣṭhaḥ puruṣa ity uktam.
children.translated_text: From the absence of that non-seeing, there is the absence of the conjunction of <s>buddhi</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>—an absolute cessation of bondage; this is the meaning. This is abandonment. <s>Kaivalya</s> (isolation) for that seer is the unmixing of the <s>puruṣa</s>, a renewed non-conjunction with the <s>guṇa</s>-s; this is the meaning. When the cause of pain has ceased, the cessation of pain is abandonment; at that time, the <s>puruṣa</s>, established in his own-form, this has been said
Now, what is the means of attainment for abandonment—
Unfaltering <s>viveka-khyāti</s> (discernment-knowledge) is the means to abandonment

children.text:
sattvapuruṣānyatāpratyayo vivekakhyātiḥ. sā tv anivṛttamithyājñānā plavate. yadā
            mithyājñānaṃ dagdhabījabhāvaṃ vandhyaprasavaṃ saṃpadyate tadā vidhūtakleśarajasaḥ
            sattvasya pare vaiśāradye parasyāṃ vaśīkārasaṃjñāyāṃ vartamānasya vivekapratyayapravāho
            nirmalo bhavati. sā vivekakhyātir aviplavā hānopāyaḥ. tato mithyājñānasya
            dagdhabījabhāvopagamaḥ punaś cāprasava ity eṣa mokṣasya mārgo hānasyopāya iti.
children.translated_text: The ascertainment that <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> are other (mutually distinct) is <s>viveka-khyāti</s>. And that, while false-knowledge has not ceased, wavers. When false-knowledge attains the condition of a burned seed, a barren production, then, for one whose <s>sattva</s>, with afflictions and <s>rajas</s> shaken off, abides in the supreme clarity, in the supreme mastery called subjugation, the stream of discernment-cognitions becomes stainless. That unfaltering <s>viveka-khyāti</s> is the means to abandonment. From that, there is the coming-to the state of a burned seed for false-knowledge, and further a non-production—this is the path of liberation, the means of abandonment
Its culminating-ground (<s>prāntabhūmi</s>) of insight is sevenfold

children.text:
tasyeti pratyuditakhyāteḥ pratyāmnāyaḥ. saptadheti aśuddhyāvaraṇamalāpagamāc cittasya
            pratyayāntarānutpāde sati saptaprakāraiva prajñā vivekino bhavati.
children.translated_text: “Its” means: of the discernment just declared—this is a restatement. “Sevenfold”: when, through the removal of the impurities that are the defilements, coverings, and stains, while there is no arising of other cognitions in the mind (<s>citta</s>), the insight of the discerner (<s>vivekin</s>) is only of seven kinds

children.text:
tadyathā --- parijñātaṃ heyaṃ nāsya punaḥ parijñeyam asti. kṣīṇā heyahetavo na punar
            eteṣāṃ kṣetavyam asti. sākṣātkṛtaṃ nirodhasamādhinā hānam. bhāvito vivekakhyātirūpo
            hānopāya iti. eṣā catuṣṭayī kāryā vimuktiḥ prajñāyāḥ. cittavimuktis tu trayī
            caritādhikārā buddhiḥ. guṇā giriśikharataṭacyutā iva grāvāṇo niravasthānāḥ svakāraṇe
            pralayābhimukhāḥ saha tenāstaṃ gacchanti. na caiṣāṃ pravilīnānāṃ punar asty utpādaḥ
            prayojanābhāvād iti. etasyām avasthāyāṃ guṇasaṃbandhātītaḥ svarūpamātrajyotir amalaḥ
            kevalī puruṣa iti. etāṃ saptavidhāṃ prāntabhūmiprajñām anupaśyan puruṣaḥ kuśala ity
            ākhyāyate. pratiprasave pi cittasya muktaḥ kuśala ity eva bhavati guṇātītatvād iti.
children.translated_text: As follows—The to-be-abandoned is fully known; for him there is nothing to be known again as to-be-abandoned. The causes of what is to be abandoned are exhausted; there is nothing further to be exhausted for these. Abandonment has been directly realized by the samādhi of cessation. The means of abandonment in the form of <s>viveka-khyāti</s> has been cultivated. This fourfold accomplishing is the liberation with respect to insight; but the liberation of the mind (<s>citta</s>) is threefold—the <s>buddhi</s> whose entitlement to conduct has been carried through. The <s>guṇa</s>-s, like stones fallen from the edge of a mountain peak, having no foothold, heading toward dissolution into their own cause, set along with it. And for those that have dissolved, there is no re-arising again, because of the absence of purpose—so it is. In this state, beyond connection with the <s>guṇa</s>-s, pure as the mere light of his own-form, the <s>puruṣa</s> is solitary (<s>kevalī</s>). One who contemplates this sevenfold culminating insight (<s>prāntabhūmi-prajñā</s>) is called skillful (<s>kuśala</s>). Even at the reversal (return) of the <s>citta</s> into its source, he is released and indeed skillful, because he is beyond the <s>guṇa</s>-s

children.text:
siddhā bhavati vivekakhyātir hānopāya iti, na ca siddhir antareṇa sādhanam ity etad
            ārabhyate ---
children.translated_text: That <s>viveka-khyāti</s> is established as the means to abandonment; and there is no accomplishment without a means—this is begun—
From the practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s>, with the destruction of impurity, there is the illumination of knowledge up to <s>viveka-khyāti</s>

children.text:
yogāṅgāny aṣṭāv abhidhāyiṣyamāṇāni. teṣām anuṣṭhānāt pañcaparvaṇo
            viparyayasyāśuddhirūpasya kṣayo nāśaḥ. tatkṣaye samyagjñānasyābhivyaktiḥ. yathā yathā ca
            sādhanāny anuṣṭhīyante tathā tathā tanutvam aśuddhir āpadyate. yathā yathā ca kṣīyate
            tathā tathā kṣayakramānurodhinī jñānasyāpi dīptir vivardhate. sā khalv eṣā vivṛddhiḥ
            prakarṣam anubhavatyā vivekakhyāteḥ, ā guṇapuruṣasvarūpavijñānād ity arthaḥ.
            yogāṅgānuṣṭhānam aśuddher viyogakāraṇam. yathā paraśuś chedyasya. vivekakhyātes tu
            prāptikāraṇaṃ yathā dharmaḥ sukhasya nānyathā kāraṇam. kati caitāni kāraṇāni śāstre
            bhavanti. navaivety āha. tadyathā ---
children.translated_text: The eight limbs of <s>yoga</s> are about to be stated. From their practice, there is the destruction, the annihilation, of the impurity that is of the form of error, which has five segments. Upon that destruction, there is the manifestation of right-knowledge. And the more the means are practiced, the more thinness—impurity—comes to be obtained. And as it is worn away, in correspondence with the sequence of its wearing-away, the brilliance of knowledge also increases. This growth indeed reaches the excellence of <s>viveka-khyāti</s>, up to the knowledge of the own-forms of <s>guṇa</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>—that is the meaning. The practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s> is the cause of separation from impurity, as an axe is of what is to be cut. But it is the cause of the attainment of <s>viveka-khyāti</s>, as <s>dharma</s> is the cause of happiness, and not otherwise. And how many such causes are there in the scripture? “Only nine”—so he says. Namely—
Origin, continuance, manifestation, transformation, attainment by cognition; separation, otherness, and firmness are the cause, remembered ninefold

children.text:
tatrotpattikāraṇaṃ mano bhavati vijñānasya, sthitikāraṇaṃ manasaḥ puruṣārthatā,
            śarīrasyevāhāra iti. abhivyaktikāraṇaṃ yathā rūpasyālokas tathā rūpajñānam,
            vikārakāraṇaṃ manaso viṣayāntaram. yathāgniḥ pākyasya. pratyayakāraṇaṃ dhūmajñānam
            agnijñānasya. prāptikāraṇaṃ yogāṅgānuṣṭhānaṃ vivekakhyāteḥ.
children.translated_text: There, the cause of production for cognition is the mind; the cause of continuance for the mind is purposiveness-for-the-<s>puruṣa</s> (<s>puruṣārthatā</s>), just as for the body it is nourishment. The cause of manifestation is, as light is for form, so is form-cognition; the cause of transformation for the mind is a different object, as fire is for what is to be cooked. The cause by way of a ground-for-cognition (inferential sign) is smoke-cognition for fire-cognition; the cause of attainment is the practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s> for <s>viveka-khyāti</s> (discernment-knowledge)

children.text:
viyogakāraṇaṃ tad evāśuddheḥ. anyatvakāraṇaṃ yathā suvarṇasya suvarṇakāraḥ. evam ekasya
            strīpratyayasyāvidyā mūḍhatve dveṣo duḥkhatve rāgaḥ sukhatve tattvajñānaṃ mādhyasthye.
            dhṛtikāraṇaṃ śarīram indriyāṇām. tāni ca tasya. mahābhūtāni śarīrāṇām, tāni ca
            parasparaṃ sarveṣāṃ tairyagyaunamānuṣadaivatāni ca parasparārthatvād ity evaṃ nava
            kāraṇāni. tāni ca yathāsaṃbhavaṃ padārthāntareṣv api yojyāni. yogāṅgānuṣṭhānaṃ tu
            dvidhaiva kāraṇatvaṃ labhata iti.
children.translated_text: The cause of separation is that very impurity; the cause of otherness is, as for gold, the goldsmith. Likewise, for a single cognition of “woman,” ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is [its] delusion-as-foolishness, aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) [is its function] in the state of pain, attachment (<s>rāga</s>) in the state of pleasure, true-knowledge (<s>tattva-jñāna</s>) in neutrality. The cause of firmness is the body for the senses, and they are for it; the great elements (<s>mahābhūta</s>-s) are for bodies, and they, mutually for one another, are for all—beast, bird, human, and divine—because of being for one another’s sake. Thus there are nine causes; and these are to be applied, as the case allows, also to other categories. But the practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s> attains a twofold causality
Therein the limbs of <s>yoga</s> are determined—
<s>Yama</s>, <s>niyama</s>, <s>āsana</s>, <s>prāṇāyāma</s>, <s>pratyāhāra</s>, <s>dhāraṇā</s>, <s>dhyāna</s>, <s>samādhi</s>—the eight limbs

children.text: yathākramam eṣām anuṣṭhānaṃ svarūpaṃ ca vakṣyāmaḥ.
children.translated_text: In due order we shall state their practice and their own-forms (essential definitions)
There—
Non-injury (<s>ahiṃsā</s>), truth (<s>satya</s>), non-stealing (<s>asteya</s>), celibacy (<s>brahmacarya</s>), and non-acceptance (<s>aparigraha</s>) are the restraints (<s>yamāḥ</s>)

children.text:
tatrāhiṃsā sarvathā sarvadā sarvabhūtānām anabhidrohaḥ. uttare ca yamaniyamās tanmūlās
            tatsiddhiparatayaiva tatpratipādanāya pratipādyante. tadavadātarūpakaraṇāyaivopādīyante.
