children.translated_text: The entire operation of the senses, characterized as the breaths beginning with <s>Prāṇa</s>, is life; its functions are fivefold: <s>Prāṇa</s> has the course in the mouth and nose, its activity being toward the heart; from distributing equally, <s>Samāna</s>, with activity in the navel; from moving downward, <s>Apāna</s>, with activity in the soles of the feet; from moving upward, <s>Udāna</s>, with activity in the head; all-pervading is <s>Vyāna</s>. Among these, the chief is <s>Prāṇa</s>. From the mastery of <s>Udāna</s> there is non-contact with water, mud, thorns, and the like, and also ascension at the time of departure (death); he attains that as lordship (control)
From the mastery of <s>Samāna</s>, kindling (of fire)
One who has conquered <s>Samāna</s>, having performed fanning of the fire by heat, causes it to blaze
From <s>saṃyama</s> on the connection of the ear and space (<s>ākāśa</s>), divine hearing

children.text:
sarvaśrotrāṇām ākāśaṃ pratiṣṭhā sarvaśabdānāṃ ca yathoktam --- tulyadeśaśravaṇānām
            ekadeśaśrutitvaṃ sarveṣāṃ bhavatīti tac caitad ākāśasya liṅgam.
children.translated_text: For the support of all ears is <s>ākāśa</s>, and so too of all sounds, as has been said—because, when sounds are heard in the same place, there is the hearing of a single locality for them all—this is the mark of <s>ākāśa</s>

children.text:
anāvaraṇaṃ coktam. tathāmūrtasyānāvaraṇadarśanād vibhutvam api prakhyātam ākāśasya.
            śabdagrahaṇānumitaṃ śrotram. badhirābadhirayor ekaḥ śabdaṃ gṛhṇāty aparo na gṛhṇātīti
            tasmāc chrotram eva śabdaviṣayam śrotrākāśayoḥ saṃbandhe kṛtasaṃyamasya yogino divyaṃ
            śrotraṃ pravartate.
children.translated_text: And its non-obstruction has been stated; likewise, from the seeing of the non-obstruction of the formless, the all-pervasiveness of <s>ākāśa</s> is well-known. The ear is inferred from the apprehension of sound: between two, one who is hard of hearing and one who is deaf, one apprehends sound, the other does not—therefore the ear alone has sound as its object. For the yogin who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on the connection of ear and <s>ākāśa</s>, divine hearing proceeds
From <s>saṃyama</s> on the connection of body and space, and from attainment of lightness like that of cotton, movement through <s>ākāśa</s> (space)

children.text:
yatra kāyas tatrākāśaṃ tasyāvakāśadānāt kāyasya tena saṃbandhaḥ prāptis tatra
            kṛtasaṃyamo jitvā tatsaṃbandhaṃ laghuṣu vā tūlādiṣv ā paramāṇubhyaḥ samāpattiṃ labdhvā
            jitasaṃbandho laghur bhavati. laghutvāc ca jale pādābhyāṃ viharati tatas
            tūrṇanābhitantumātre vihṛtya raśmiṣu viharati tato yatheṣṭam ākāśagatir asya
            bhavatīti.
children.translated_text: Where the body is, there is space, by its granting an opening (room) to the body; by that, there is the body’s connection with it. Having performed <s>saṃyama</s> there, and having conquered that connection, or having attained absorption in light things such as cotton, down to atoms, having conquered the connection, one becomes light; and by lightness he moves upon water with his feet; then, having sported swiftly within a wheel’s-nave’s measure, he moves upon rays; thereafter he has movement through <s>ākāśa</s> as he desires

children.text: bahir akalpitā vṛttir mahāvidehā tataḥ prakāśāvaraṇakṣayaḥ
children.translated_text: External, non-conceptual operation—[that is] the great incorporeality (<s>mahā-videha</s>); from that, the destruction of the covering of light

children.text:
śarīrād bahir manaso vṛttilābho videhā nāma dhāraṇā. sā yadi śarīrapratiṣṭhasya manaso
            bahirvṛttimātreṇa bhavati sā kalpitety ucyate. yā tu śarīranirapekṣā bahirbhūtasyaiva
            manaso bahirvṛttiḥ sā khalv akalpitā tatra kalpitayā sādhayanty akalpitāṃ mahāvidehām
            iti. yayā paraśarīrāṇy āviśanti yoginaḥ, tataś ca dhāraṇātaḥ prakāśātmano
            buddhisattvasya yadāvaraṇaṃ kleśakarmavipākatrayaṃ rajastamomūlaṃ tasya ca kṣayo
            bhavati.
children.translated_text: Outside the body, the obtaining of a mental operation—this concentration is called ‘incorporeal’ (<s>videhā</s>); if that occurs for a mind established in the body merely as an external operation, it is said to be constructed (imagined), whereas the external operation of a mind that is in fact external, independent of the body, that indeed is unconstructed; by means of the constructed one they accomplish the unconstructed great incorporeality (<s>mahā-videhā</s>). By that, yogins enter other bodies; and from that concentration, the triple covering of the luminosity-nature of the intellect (<s>buddhi-sattva</s>)—defilements, karmas, and their ripenings, whose root is rajas and tamas—there is the cessation of that covering.
From <s>saṃyama</s> on grossness, essential-nature, subtlety, conjunction (anvaya), and meaningfulness (arthavattva), mastery over the elements (<s>bhūta</s>-s)

children.text:
tatra pārthivādyāḥ śabdādayo viśeṣāḥ sahākārādibhir dharmaiḥ sthūlaśabdena paribhāṣitāḥ
            etad bhūtānāṃ prathamaṃ rūpam. dvitīyaṃ rūpaṃ svasāmānyaṃ mūrtir bhūmiḥ sneho jalaṃ
            vahnir uṣṇatā vāyuḥ praṇāmī sarvatogatir ākāśa ity etat svarūpaśabdenocyate.
children.translated_text: Therein, the particular qualities beginning with sound and so on pertaining to earth and the rest, along with properties such as co-operation (mutual assistance), are designated by the term ‘gross’; this is the first form of the elements. The second form is their own generality, their essential-nature: solidity is earth, liquidity is water, heat is fire, motion is wind, all-pervasiveness is space—this is what is called by the term ‘essential-nature’.

children.text:
asya sāmānyasya śabdādayo viśeṣāḥ tathā coktam --- ekajātisamanvitānām eṣāṃ
            dharmamātravyāvṛttir iti.
children.translated_text: Of this generality, the particular qualities beginning with sound and so on [are its differentiations]; thus it is said: ‘For those endowed with one genus, the mere exclusion by way of properties [marks out their differences].’

children.text:
sāmānyaviśeṣasamudāyo+atra dravyam. dviṣṭho hi samūhaḥ pratyastamitabhedāvayavānugataḥ
            śarīraṃ vṛkṣo yūthaṃ vanam iti.
children.translated_text: Here, the aggregation of generality and particularity is substance (dravya). A group rests in two ways: following (pervading) members whose differences are suppressed—‘body,’ ‘tree,’ ‘troop,’ ‘forest’, thus.

children.text:
śabdenopāttabhedāvayavānugataḥ samūha ubhaye devamanuṣyāḥ samūhasya devā eko bhāgo
            manuṣyā dvitīyo bhāgas tābhyām evābhidhīyate samūhaḥ.
children.translated_text: A group that follows members whose differences have been grasped by a word—‘both gods and humans’; of the group, gods are one part, humans a second part; by these two the group itself is denoted.

children.text:
sa ca bhedābhedavivakṣitaḥ. āmrāṇāṃ vanaṃ brāhmaṇānāṃ saṃgha āmravaṇaṃ brāhmaṇasaṃgha
            iti.
children.translated_text: And it is spoken of with difference or non-difference intended: ‘a grove of mango trees,’ ‘an assembly of <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>-s’—‘a mango-grove,’ ‘a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>-assembly’, thus.

children.text:
sa punar dvividho yutasiddhāvayavo+ayutasiddhāvayavaś ca. yutasiddhāvayavaḥ samūho
            vanaṃ saṃgha iti ayutasiddhāvayavaḥ saṃghātaḥ śarīraṃ vṛkṣaḥ paramāṇur iti.
            ayutasiddhāvayavabhedānugataḥ samūho dravyam iti patañjaliḥ etat svarūpam ity uktam.
children.translated_text: And further, it is twofold: having conjointly accomplished parts (yuta-siddha-avayava) and having non-conjointly accomplished parts (ayuta-siddha-avayava). A group with conjointly accomplished parts is ‘forest,’ ‘assembly’; with non-conjointly accomplished parts it is ‘aggregate,’ ‘body,’ ‘tree,’ ‘atom.’ ‘A group that follows divisions of non-conjointly accomplished parts is substance’—so says <s>Patañjali</s>; this was stated as the essential-nature.

children.text:
atha kim eṣāṃ sūkṣmarūpaṃ, tanmātraṃ bhūtakāraṇaṃ, tasyaiko+avayavaḥ paramāṇuḥ
            sāmānyaviśeṣātmāyutasiddhāvayavabhedānugataḥ samudāya ity evaṃ sarvatanmātrāṇy etat
            tṛtīyam. atha bhūtānāṃ caturthaṃ rūpaṃ khyātikriyāsthitiśīlā guṇāḥ
            kāryasvabhāvānupātino+anvayaśabdenoktāḥ. athaiṣāṃ pañcamaṃ rūpam arthavattvaṃ,
            bhogāpavargārthatā guṇeṣv evānvayinī, guṇās tanmātrabhūtabhautikeṣv iti sarvam arthavat.
            teṣv idānīṃ bhūteṣu pañcasu pañcarūpeṣu saṃyamāt tasya tasya rūpasya svarūpadarśanaṃ
            jayaś ca prādurbhavati. tatra pañca bhūtasvarūpāṇi jitvā bhūtajayī bhavati tajjayād
            vatsānusāriṇya iva gāvo+asya saṃkalpānuvidhāyinyo bhūtaprakṛtayo bhavanti.
children.translated_text: Now, what is their subtle form? The <s>tanmātra</s>-s, the causes of the elements; of that, a single part is the atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>); an aggregation that follows divisions whose nature is generality-and-particularity and non-conjointly accomplished parts; in this way, all the <s>tanmātra</s>-s—this is the third [form]. Next, the fourth form of the elements is the qualities (<s>guṇa</s>-s) of manifestation, activity, stability—following their functional natures—which are indicated by the term ‘conjunction’ (anvaya). Next, their fifth form is meaningfulness (arthavattva), the being-for-experience-and-release (enjoyment and emancipation), which inheres indeed in the <s>guṇa</s>-s; and the <s>guṇa</s>-s in the subtle, elemental, and gross composites—thus all is meaningful. Now, from <s>saṃyama</s> on these five elements in their five forms, there arises the seeing of the essential-nature of each respective form, and mastery. There, having conquered the five essential-natures of the elements, one becomes a master of the elements; by that mastery, the elemental natures become obedient to his resolve, like cows following their calves.
Then the manifestation of the powers beginning with minuteness (<s>aṇimā</s>), perfection of the body, and non-impediment by the properties of that [body]

children.text:
tatrāṇimā bhavaty aṇuḥ laghimā laghur bhavati mahimā mahān bhavati. prāptir
            aṅgulyagreṇāpi spṛśati candramasam. prākāmyam icchānabhighātaḥ bhūmāv unmajjati
            nimajjati yathodake. vaśitvaṃ bhūtabhautikeṣu vaśī bhavaty avaśyaś cānyeṣām īśitṛtvaṃ
            teṣāṃ prabhavāpyayavyūhānām īṣṭe. yatra kāmāvasāyitvaṃ satyasaṃkalpatā yathā saṃkalpas
            tathā bhūtaprakṛtīnām avasthānam. na ca śakto+api padārthaviparyāsaṃ karoti kasmāt
            anyasya yatra kāmāvasāyinaḥ pūrvasiddhasya tathā bhūteṣu saṃkalpād iti. etāny aṣṭāv
            aiśvaryāṇi.
children.translated_text: Therein, <s>aṇimā</s> is ‘he becomes minute like an atom’; lightness (<s>laghimā</s>) is ‘he becomes light’; greatness (<s>mahimā</s>) is ‘he becomes great.’ ‘Reach’ (<s>prāpti</s>) is: with even a fingertip he touches the moon. ‘Pervasion’ (<s>prākāmya</s>) is the non-impediment of will—on earth he emerges and submerges as in water. ‘Mastery’ (<s>vaśitva</s>) is: he becomes lord over elemental and composite things; and ‘lordship’ (<s>īśitṛtva</s>) over their productions, dissolutions, and arrangements is desired. Where there is determination according to desire (<s>kāmāvasāyitva</s>), there is truth of resolve: just as the resolve, so the state of the elemental natures. Nor, though capable, does he effect a reversal of the categories—why? Because for another who has the determination according to desire previously accomplished, thus the arrangement of the elements is by his resolve. These are the eight <s>aiśvarya</s>-s (lordly powers).

children.text:
kāyasaṃpad vakṣyamāṇā taddharmānabhighātaś ca pṛthvī mūrtyā na niruṇaddhi yoginaḥ
            śarīrādikriyāṃ, śilām apy anuviśatīti. nāpaḥ snigdhāḥ kledayanti nāgnir uṣṇo dahati na
            vāyuḥ praṇāmī vahati anāvaraṇātmake+apy ākāśe bhavaty āvṛtakāyaḥ siddhānām apy adṛśyo
            bhavati.
children.translated_text: The perfection of the body will be stated—non-impediment by its properties as well: the earth-nature does not confine the yogin’s bodily actions such as entering even a rock; waters, though unctuous, do not moisten; fire, though hot, does not burn; wind, though impelling, does not carry away; even in <s>ākāśa</s> (space), whose nature is non-obstruction, he becomes one whose body is veiled, he becomes invisible even to <s>Siddha</s>-s
Beauty of form, loveliness, strength, and adamantine compactness are the perfection of the body
He is handsome to behold, radiant, possessed of exceptional strength, and of adamantine compactness
From <s>saṃyama</s> on apprehension, essential-form, egoity (<s>asmitā</s>), conjunction (anvaya), and meaningfulness (arthavattva), there is mastery over the senses

children.text:
sāmānyaviśeṣātmā śabdādir grāhyaḥ teṣv indriyāṇāṃ vṛttir grahaṇam. na ca
            tatsāmānyamātragrahaṇākāraṃ katham anālocitaḥ sa viṣayaviśeṣa indriyeṇa
            manasānuvyavasīyeteti. svarūpaṃ punaḥ prakāśātmano buddhisattvasya sāmānyaviśeṣayor
            ayutasiddhāvayavabhedānugataḥ samūho dravyam indriyam. teṣāṃ tṛtīyaṃ rūpam
            asmitālakṣaṇo+ahaṃkāraḥ. tasya sāmānyasyendriyāṇi viśeṣāḥ caturthaṃ rūpaṃ
            vyavasāyātmakāḥ prakāśakriyāsthitiśīlā guṇā yeṣām indriyāṇi sāhaṃkārāṇi pariṇāmaḥ.
            pañcamaṃ rūpaṃ guṇeṣu yad anugataṃ puruṣārthavattvam iti. pañcasv eteṣv indriyarūpeṣu
            yathākramaṃ saṃyamas tatra tatra jayaṃ kṛtvā pañcarūpajayād indriyajayaḥ prādurbhavati
            yoginaḥ.
children.translated_text: What is to be apprehended—sound and the rest—whose nature is generality-and-particularity, this is the grāhya; the operation of the senses upon those is apprehension. And not, with respect to that, would the mind subsequently determine a particular object, when the sense has apprehended a mere generality without having attended to it—how so? The essential-form, further, of the luminosity-nature of the intellect (<s>buddhi-sattva</s>) is the sense-organ as substance (dravya), a collection that follows the divisions of non-conjointly accomplished parts of generality and particularity. Their third form is <s>asmitā</s>-characterized <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-maker); of that generality, the senses are the particularizations. The fourth form is the <s>guṇa</s>-s, whose nature is determination, illumination-activity-stability; the senses are transformations of that <s>ahaṃkāra</s>. The fifth form is the being-for-the-<s>Puruṣa</s>-purpose (<s>puruṣārthavattva</s>) that inheres in the <s>guṇa</s>-s. From <s>saṃyama</s>, in due order, on these five forms of the senses, having effected mastery there in each place, from the conquest of the five forms there arises for the yogin mastery of the senses
Then, speed like the mind, the state of being without organs, and mastery of <s>Pradhāna</s>

children.text:
kāyasyānuttamo gatilābho manojavitvam. videhānām indriyāṇām
            abhipretadeśakālaviṣayāpekṣo vṛttilābho vikaraṇabhāvaḥ. sarvaprakṛtivikāravaśitvaṃ
            pradhānajaya ity etās tisraḥ siddhayo madhupratīkā ucyante etāś ca karaṇapañcarūpajayād
            adhigamyante.
children.translated_text: The unsurpassed attainment of speed for the body is speed like the mind. The state of being without organs is the attainment of operations by the disembodied senses, with reference to the desired place, time, and object. Mastery of all modifications of <s>Prakṛti</s> (all nature’s evolutes) is mastery of <s>Pradhāna</s>; these three perfections are called the honey-symbol, and these are attained from mastery of the fivefold forms of the instruments (senses)
Of mere knowledge of the otherness of <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, lordship over all entities and omniscience

children.text:
nirdhūtarajastamomalasya buddhisattvasya pare vaiśāradye parasyāṃ vaśīkārasaṃjñāyāṃ
            vartamānasya sattvapuruṣānyatākhyātimātrarūpapratiṣṭhasya sarvabhāvādhiṣṭhātṛtvam.
            sarvātmāno guṇā vyavasāyavyavaseyātmakāḥ svāminaṃ kṣetrajñaṃ
            pratyaśeṣadṛśyātmatvenopasthitā ity arthaḥ. sarvajñātṛtvaṃ sarvātmanāṃ guṇānāṃ
            śāntoditāvyapadeśyadharmatvena vyavasthitānām akramopārūḍhaṃ vivekajaṃ jñānam ity
            arthaḥ. ity eṣā viśokā nāma siddhir yāṃ prāpya yogī sarvajñaḥ kṣīṇakleśabandhano vaśī
            viharati.
children.translated_text: When the luminosity of intellect (<s>buddhi-sattva</s>), its rajas and tamas shaken off, abides in the highest clarity, in that state called mastery (vaśīkāra), established in the mere form of knowledge of the otherness of <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, there is lordship over all entities—meaning: the <s>guṇa</s>-s, being universal, of the nature of determination and determinables, present themselves to the Lord, the Knower-of-the-field (<s>kṣetrajña</s>), as nothing but the seen. Omniscience is discriminative knowledge, not proceeding in sequence, of the <s>guṇa</s>-s as universal, established with the properties of quiescent, arisen, and inexpressible; this is the siddhi named ‘free from sorrow,’ by attaining which the yogin, having his afflictions and bonds worn away, dwells as a master
From dispassion toward that too, through the destruction of the seed of defects, <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation) [ensues]

children.text:
yadāsyaivaṃ bhavati kleśakarmakṣaye sattvasyāyaṃ vivekapratyayo dharmaḥ sattvaṃ ca
            heyapakṣe nyastaṃ puruṣaś cāpariṇāmī śuddho+anyaḥ sattvād iti. evam asya tato
            virajyamānasya yāni kleśabījāni dagdhaśālibījakalpāny aprasavasamarthāni tāni saha
            manasā pratyastaṃ gacchanti. teṣu pralīneṣu puruṣaḥ punar idaṃ tāpatrayaṃ na bhuṅkte.
            tad eteṣāṃ guṇānāṃ manasi karmakleśavipākasvarūpeṇābhivyaktānāṃ caritārthānāṃ
            pratiprasave puruṣasyātyantiko guṇaviyogaḥ kaivalyaṃ tadā svarūpapratiṣṭhā citiśaktir
            eva puruṣa iti.
children.translated_text: When for him it is thus—the afflictions and karma having been destroyed—this dharma of discriminative discernment of <s>sattva</s> arises, and <s>sattva</s> is consigned to the category to-be-abandoned, while <s>Puruṣa</s>, unchanging, pure, other than <s>sattva</s>, thus; accordingly, as he becomes dispassionate toward that, whatever seeds of afflictions there are, like burnt rice-grains, incapable of sprouting, these, together with the mind, go away, having been cast aside. When these are dissolved, the <s>Puruṣa</s> no longer experiences this triple suffering. Then, when the <s>guṇa</s>-s—manifest in the mind in the form of karma, afflictions, and their ripenings—have fulfilled their purpose and reabsorb, the absolute disconnection of the <s>Puruṣa</s> from the <s>guṇa</s>-s is <s>kaivalya</s>; then the power of awareness, established in its own nature, is the <s>Puruṣa</s> alone
When invited in high places, the non-production of attachment and pride, because of the recurrence of undesired consequences

children.text:
catvāraḥ khalv amī yoginaḥ prāthamakalpiko madhubhūmikaḥ prajñājyotir
            atikrāntabhāvanīyaś ceti. tatrābhyāsī pravṛttamātrajyotiḥ prathamaḥ ṛtaṃbharaprajño
            dvitīyaḥ bhūtendriyajayī tṛtīyaḥ sarveṣu bhāviteṣu bhāvanīyeṣu kṛtarakṣābandhaḥ
            kartavyasādhanād imān. caturtho yas tv atikrāntabhāvanīyas tasya cittapratisarga
            eko+arthaḥ saptavidhāsya prāntabhūmiprajñā.
children.translated_text: Indeed, these four yogins are as follows: the beginner on the path (prāthamakalpika), the one whose ground is honey-like (madhubhūmika), the one whose light is wisdom (prajñājyotis), and the one who has gone beyond what is to be cultivated (atikrāntabhāvanīya); among these, the practitioner (abhyāsin), whose light has just been set in motion, is the first, the one whose knowledge bears truth (<s>ṛtaṃbhara-prajñā</s>) is the second, the conqueror of elements and senses (bhūtendriyajayī) is the third—having secured protection-bonds in all matters that have been cultivated, in what is to be cultivated, these means are to be undertaken; but the fourth, who indeed has gone beyond what is to be cultivated, for him the re-production of the mind (citta-pratisarga) has the single purpose, and his knowledge of the terminal grounds (prānta-bhūmi-prajñā) is sevenfold

children.text:
tatra madhumatīṃ bhūmiṃ sākṣātkurvato brāhmaṇasya sthānino devāḥ sattvaviśuddhim
            anupaśyantaḥ sthānair upanimantrayante bho ihāsyatām iha ramyatāṃ kamanīyo+ayaṃ bhogaḥ
            kamanīyeyaṃ kanyā rasāyanam idaṃ jarāmṛtyuṃ bādhate vaihāyasam idaṃ yānam amī
            kalpadrumāḥ puṇyā mandākinī siddhā maharṣaya uttamā anukūlā apsaraso divye śrotracakṣuṣī
            vajropamaḥ kāyaḥ svaguṇaiḥ sarvam idam upārjitam āyuṣmatā pratipadyatām idam akṣayam
            ajaram amarasthānaṃ devānāṃ priyam iti. evam abhidhīyamānaḥ saṅgadoṣān bhāvayed ghoreṣu
            saṃsārāṅgāreṣu pacyamānena mayā jananamaraṇāndhakāre viparivartamānena kathaṃcid
            āsāditaḥ kleśatimiravināśī yogapradīpas tasya caite tṛṣṇāyonayo viṣayavāyavaḥ
            pratipakṣāḥ. sa khalv ahaṃ labdhālokaḥ katham anayā viṣayamṛgatṛṣṇayā vañcitas tasyaiva
            punaḥ pradīptasya saṃsārāgner ātmānam indhanīkuryām iti. svasti vaḥ svapnopamebhyaḥ
            kṛpaṇajanaprārthanīyebhyo viṣayebhya ity evaṃ niścitamatiḥ samādhiṃ bhāvayet.
children.translated_text: There, when the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> who directly realizes the honeyed ground is seen by the stationed gods, perceiving the purification of his <s>sattva</s>, they invite him from their stations: ‘Come, dwell here, enjoy yourself here; this enjoyment is delightful, this maiden is delightful, this elixir cures old age and death, this is an aerial vehicle; these are wish-fulfilling trees (<s>kalpadruma</s>-s); the sacred <s>Mandākinī</s>; perfected beings and great seers, supreme; the <s>Apsaras</s>-es are favorable; divine ears and eyes; a body like adamant; all this has been acquired by your own virtues; O long-lived one, obtain this imperishable, ageless, immortal station, dear to the gods’—thus; being thus addressed, he should reflect upon the faults of attachment, ‘While the embers of <s>saṃsāra</s> are horrible, I have been roasted; in the darkness of birth-and-death I have been tossed about; somehow attained by me is the lamp of yoga, which destroys the darkness of the afflictions, and these, the winds of objects, sources of thirst (craving), are its opposites; indeed, having obtained the light, how would I be deceived by this mirage of objects? Should I again make myself the fuel of the blazing fire of <s>saṃsāra</s> itself?’—‘Blessings upon you, O sense-objects, akin to dreams, pitiable, things to be begged for by the wretched’—with his mind thus firmly decided, he should cultivate <s>samādhi</s>

children.text:
saṅgam akṛtvā smayam api na kuryād evam ahaṃ devānām api prārthanīya iti smayād ayaṃ
            susthitaṃmanyatayā mṛtyunā keśeṣu gṛhītam ivātmānaṃ na bhāvayiṣyati. tathā cāsya
            cchidrāntaraprekṣī nityaṃ yatnopacaryaḥ pramādo labdhavivaraḥ kleśān uttambhayiṣyati
            tataḥ punar aniṣṭaprasaṅgaḥ. evam asya saṅgasmayāv akurvato bhāvito+artho
            dṛḍhībhaviṣyati bhāvanīyaś cārtho+abhimukhībhaviṣyatīti.
children.translated_text: Without forming attachment, he should not even make self-pleasing pride; thinking, ‘Thus am I one to be besought even by the gods,’ out of such pride, with the complacency of being well-established, he will not consider himself as being, as it were, seized by death by the hair; and accordingly, since lapses and openings are ever to be watched for with diligent care, negligence, having obtained a gap, will prop up the afflictions, then there follows again an undesired consequence; thus, for him who does not make attachment and pride, what has been cultivated will be made firm, and the object to be cultivated will incline into nearness
From <s>saṃyama</s> on instants and their sequence, knowledge born of discrimination (vivekaja) [arises]

children.text:
yathāpakarṣaparyantaṃ dravyaṃ paramāṇur evaṃ paramāpakarṣaparyantaḥ kālaḥ kṣaṇo yāvatā
            vā samayena calitaḥ paramāṇuḥ pūrvadeśaṃ jahyād uttaradeśam upasaṃpadyeta sa kālaḥ
            kṣaṇaḥ. tatpravāhāvicchedas tu kramaḥ kṣaṇatatkramayor nāsti vastusamāhāra iti
            buddhisamāhāro muhūrtāhorātrādayaḥ. sa khalv ayaṃ kālo vastuśūnyo+api buddhinirmāṇaḥ
            śabdajñānānupātī laukikānāṃ vyutthitadarśanānāṃ vastusvarūpa ivāvabhāsate.
children.translated_text: Just as, up to the limit of diminution, a substance is an atom, so up to the limit of utmost diminution, time is an instant; inasmuch as, within whatever time a <s>paramāṇu</s> (atom) having moved would abandon its former place and attain the subsequent place—that is time, the instant; the uninterrupted flow of that is sequence; there is no aggregation of things of instants and of their sequence, thus the aggregation is of cognitions: muhūrtas, days-and-nights, and the like; this time indeed, though devoid of thinghood, is constructed by cognition, accompanied by sound and knowledge, and to those whose view is worldly, arisen from emergence, it appears as though it were the very nature of things

children.text:
kṣaṇas tu vastupatitaḥ kramāvalambī kramaś ca kṣaṇānantaryātmā taṃ kālavidaḥ kāla ity
            ācakṣate yoginaḥ. na ca dvau kṣaṇau saha bhavataḥ kramaś ca na dvayoḥ sahabhuvor
            asaṃbhavāt. pūrvasmād uttarabhāvino yadānantaryaṃ kṣaṇasya sa kramaḥ tasmād vartamāna
            evaikaḥ kṣaṇo na pūrvottarakṣaṇāḥ santīti. tasmān nāsti tatsamāhāraḥ ye tu bhūtabhāvinaḥ
            kṣaṇās te pariṇāmānvitā vyākhyeyāḥ tenaikena kṣaṇena kṛtsno lokaḥ pariṇāmam anubhavati.
            tatkṣaṇopārūḍhāḥ khalv amī sarve dharmāḥ tayoḥ kṣaṇatatkramayoḥ saṃyamāt tayoḥ
            sākṣātkaraṇam. tataś ca vivekajaṃ jñānaṃ prādurbhavati.
children.translated_text: An instant (kṣaṇa), when fallen upon a substance, relies on sequence; and sequence has the nature of the immediate succession of instants—this the knowers of time, the <s>yogin</s>-s, designate as time. Nor do two instants exist together, and there is no sequence of two that co-exist, because co-existence is impossible; the immediacy of the subsequent-becoming with respect to the prior—this immediacy of the instant is sequence; therefore only the present instant alone exists, not past and future instants. Hence, there is no aggregation of that; but the instants that are past and future are to be explained as accompanied by transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>); by that single instant, the entire world undergoes transformation. Indeed, all properties (dharmas) mount upon that very instant; from <s>saṃyama</s> on those two—on the instant and on that sequence—there is direct realization of the two; and then knowledge born of discrimination (<s>vivekaja jñāna</s>) appears
A particular domain of that is briefly presented—
From the non-limitation by difference of genus (jāti), mark (lakṣaṇa), and place (deśa), in two that are alike, there is apprehension (pratipatti) from that

children.text:
tulyayor deśalakṣaṇasārūpye jātibhedo+anyatāyā hetuḥ, gaur iyaṃ baḍaveyam iti.
            tulyadeśajātīyatve lakṣaṇam anyatvakaraṃ kālākṣī gauḥ svastimatī gaur iti. dvayor
            āmalakayor jātilakṣaṇasārūpyād deśabhedo+anyatvakara idaṃ pūrvam idam uttaram iti. yadā
            tu pūrvam āmalakam anyavyagrasya jñātur uttaradeśa upāvartyate tadā tulyadeśatve pūrvam
            etad uttaram etad iti pravibhāgānupapattiḥ. asaṃdigdhena ca tattvajñānena bhavitavyam
            ity ata idam uktaṃ tataḥ pratipattir vivekajajñānād iti.
children.translated_text: When two are alike in place, mark, and essential-form, difference of genus is the cause of otherness: “this is a cow, this is a mare.” When place and genus are the same, a mark effects otherness: “the cow with black eyes; the cow that is auspicious,” thus. For two <s>āmalaka</s> fruits, because of similarity in genus and mark, difference of place effects otherness: “this one is the former, this one the latter.” But when the former <s>āmalaka</s>, for a knower whose attention is otherwise engaged, is turned to the latter place, then, when the place is the same, the division “this is the former, this is the latter” is untenable. And there must be doubtless true knowledge; therefore it is said, “apprehension is from knowledge born of discrimination”

children.text:
kathaṃ, pūrvāmalakasahakṣaṇo deśa uttarāmalakasahakṣaṇād deśād bhinnaḥ te cāmalake
            svadeśakṣaṇānubhavabhinne. anyadeśakṣaṇānubhavas tu tayor anyatve hetur iti. etena
            dṛṣṭāntena paramāṇos tulyajātilakṣaṇadeśasya pūrvaparamāṇudeśasahakṣaṇasākṣātkaraṇād
            uttarasya paramāṇos taddeśānupapattāv uttarasya taddeśānubhavo bhinnaḥ sahakṣaṇabhedāt
            tayor īśvarasya yogino+anyatvapratyayo bhavatīti.
children.translated_text: How so? The place co-instantaneous with the former <s>āmalaka</s> is different from the place co-instantaneous with the latter <s>āmalaka</s>, and the two <s>āmalaka</s>-s have distinct experiences of their own place-instants; but the experience of other place-instants is the cause of their otherness. By this example, in the case of a <s>paramāṇu</s> (atom) whose genus, mark, and place are similar, from the direct realization of the co-instantaneousness of the place of the prior atom, if the place of the later atom is not tenable as that place, then the experience of that place by the later atom is different because of the difference of co-instantaneousness; for the Lord, for the <s>yogin</s>, there arises the cognition of otherness of the two

children.text:
apare tu varṇayanti --- ye+antyā viśeṣās te+anyatāpratyayaṃ kurvantīti tatrāpi
            deśalakṣaṇabhedo mūrtivyavadhijātibhedaś cānyatve hetuḥ. kṣaṇabhedas tu yogibuddhigamya
            eveti ata uktaṃ mūrtivyavadhijātibhedābhāvān nāsti mūlapṛthaktvam iti vārṣagaṇyaḥ.
children.translated_text: Others, however, describe thus—those final particulars (<s>viśeṣa</s>-s) produce the cognition of otherness; there too, difference of place and mark, and difference of genus bounded by corporeal separation (mūrti-vyavadhi), are causes of otherness. But difference of instants is accessible only to the intellect of the <s>yogin</s>; therefore it is said by <s>Vārṣagaṇya</s>: “Because of the absence of difference of corporeal separation, mark, and genus, there is no fundamental distinctness”

children.text: tārakaṃ sarvaviṣayaṃ sarvathāviṣayam akramaṃ ceti vivekajaṃ jñānam
children.translated_text: Knowledge born of discrimination (<s>vivekaja jñāna</s>) is saving (tāraka), pertaining to all objects, in every way pertaining to objects, and non-sequential

children.text:
tārakam iti svapratibhottham anaupadeśikam ity arthaḥ sarvaviṣayaṃ nāsya kiṃcid
            aviṣayībhūtam ity arthaḥ. sarvathāviṣayam atītānāgatapratyutpannaṃ sarvaṃ paryāyaiḥ
            sarvathā jānātīty arthaḥ. akramam ity ekakṣaṇopārūḍhaṃ sarvaṃ sarvathā gṛhṇātīty arthaḥ.
            etad vivekajaṃ jñānaṃ paripūrṇam asyaivāṃśo yogapradīpo madhumatīṃ bhūmim upādāya yāvad
            asya parisamāptir iti.
children.translated_text: “Saving” (tārakam) means: arising from one’s own direct awakening, not derived from instruction; “pertaining to all objects” means: for it nothing is left as a non-object; “in every way pertaining to objects” means: it knows past, future, and present, all, in every mode; “non-sequential” means: it grasps all, in every way, mounted upon a single instant. This knowledge born of discrimination is complete; a portion of just this, having taken up the honeyed ground (<s>madhumatī bhūmi</s>) of the lamp of yoga, continues until its completion
For one who has attained knowledge born of discrimination, or for one who has not yet attained knowledge born of discrimination—
When there is equality of purity of <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, there is <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation)

children.text:
yadā nirdhūtarajastamomalaṃ buddhisattvaṃ puruṣasyānyatāpratītimātrādhikāraṃ
            dagdhakleśabījaṃ bhavati tadā puruṣasya śuddhisārūpyam ivāpannaṃ bhavati, tadā
            puruṣasyopacaritabhogābhāvaḥ śuddhiḥ. etasyām avasthāyāṃ kaivalyaṃ
            bhavatīśvarasyānīśvarasya vā vivekajajñānabhāgina itarasya vā. na hi dagdhakleśabījasya
            jñāne punar apekṣā kācid asti sattvaśuddhidvāreṇaitat samādhijam aiśvaryaṃ jñānaṃ
            copakrāntam. paramārthatas tu jñānād adarśanaṃ nivartate tasmin nivṛtte na santy uttare
            kleśāḥ. kleśābhāvāt karmavipākābhāvaḥ caritādhikārāś caitasyām avasthāyāṃ guṇā na
            puruṣasya punar dṛśyatvenopatiṣṭhante. tatpuruṣasya kaivalyaṃ, tadā puruṣaḥ
            svarūpamātrajyotir amalaḥ kevalī bhavati.
children.translated_text: When the luminosity-nature of the intellect (<s>buddhi-sattva</s>), its rajas and tamas shaken off, becomes one whose sole scope is the cognition of the otherness of <s>Puruṣa</s>, whose seeds of afflictions are burned, then it becomes as though it had assumed the likeness of the purity of <s>Puruṣa</s>; then the absence, by way of figurative attribution, of <s>Puruṣa</s>’s enjoyment is purity. In this state, there is <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation) for the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>) or the non-Lord alike, whether possessed of knowledge born of discrimination (<s>vivekaja-jñāna</s>) or the other. For knowledge in which the seeds of afflictions have been burned has no further need at all; by the door of the purity of <s>sattva</s> this sovereignty born of <s>samādhi</s> and knowledge has been attained. But in the ultimate truth, non-seeing (ignorance) ceases through knowledge; when that is ceased, there are no subsequent afflictions. From the absence of afflictions, there is the absence of karmic ripening; and in this state, the <s>guṇa</s>-s, having exhausted their mandate, do not again present themselves to <s>Puruṣa</s> as the seen. The <s>kaivalya</s> of that <s>Puruṣa</s> [ensues]; then <s>Puruṣa</s>, pure, a mere light of its own essential form, stainless, becomes solitary (kevalin)

children.text:
iti śrīpātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre vyāsabhāṣye vibhūtipādas tṛtīyaḥ
            3.
children.translated_text: Thus ends, in the venerable exposition of <s>Pātañjali</s> on <s>Sāṃkhya</s>, in the Yoga treatise, the third chapter, the Vibhūti-pāda, in the commentary of <s>Vyāsa</s>, 3
Kaivalya-pādaḥ
Perfections (<s>siddhi</s>-s) are born of birth, herbs, mantra, austerity (<s>tapas</s>), or <s>samādhi</s>

children.text:
dehāntaritā janmanā siddhiḥ oṣadhibhir asurabhavaneṣu rasāyanenety evamādiḥ. mantrair
            ākāśagamanāṇimādilābhaḥ. tapasā saṃkalpasiddhiḥ, kāmarūpī yatra tatra kāmaga ity evamādi
            samādhijāḥ siddhayo vyākhyātāḥ.
children.translated_text: Siddhi by birth is being endowed with a body other than the human; by herbs, such as the elixir in the mansions of the Asuras; by mantras, attainment of going through <s>ākāśa</s> and of powers beginning with minuteness (<s>aṇimā</s>); by austerity (<s>tapas</s>), the accomplishment of resolves—assuming forms at will, at any place, enjoying as one desires; and the siddhi-s born of <s>samādhi</s> have been explained in this manner
There, concerning the body and senses, when they have been transformed into a different species—
Transformation into another species is from the filling-up of the nature (<s>prakṛti</s>-s)

children.text:
pūrvapariṇāmāpāya uttarapariṇāmopajanas teṣām apūrvāvayavānupraveśād bhavati.
            kāyendriyaprakṛtayaś ca svaṃ svaṃ vikāram anugṛhṇanty āpūreṇa dharmādinimittam
            apekṣamāṇā iti.
children.translated_text: For them, the cessation of the prior transformation and the arising of the subsequent transformation occurs through the entrance of unprecedented parts; and the natures (<s>prakṛti</s>-s) of the body and senses each support their own modification by a filling-up, while depending on causes such as dharma, and the like

children.text: nimittam aprayojakaṃ prakṛtīnāṃ varaṇabhedas tu tataḥ kṣetrikavat
children.translated_text: The auxiliary cause is not a direct instigator of the natures (<s>prakṛti</s>-s); rather, the removal of the obstruction is from that, like a field-tender

children.text:
na hi dharmādi nimittaṃ tatprayojakaṃ prakṛtīnāṃ bhavati na kāryeṇa kāraṇaṃ pravartyata
            iti kathaṃ tarhi, varaṇabhedas tu tataḥ kṣetrikavat. yathā kṣetrikaḥ kedārād apāṃ pūrṇāt
            kedārāntaraṃ piplāvayiṣuḥ samaṃ nimnaṃ nimnataraṃ vā nāpaḥ pāṇināpakarṣaty āvaraṇaṃ tv
            āsāṃ bhinatti tasmin bhinne svayam evāpaḥ kedārāntaram āplāvayanti tathā dharmaḥ
            prakṛtīnām āvaraṇadharmaṃ bhinatti tasmin bhinne svayam eva prakṛtayaḥ svaṃ svaṃ vikāram
            āplāvayanti. yathā vā sa eva kṣetrikas tasminn eva kedāre na prabhavaty audakān bhaumān
            vā rasān dhānyamūlāny anupraveśayituṃ, kiṃ tarhi mudgagavedhukaśyāmākādīṃs
            tato+apakarṣati. apakṛṣṭeṣu teṣu svayam eva rasā dhānyamūlāny anupraviśanti, tathā
            dharmo nivṛttimātre kāraṇam adharmasya, śuddhyaśuddhyor atyantavirodhāt, na tu
            prakṛtipravṛttau dharmo hetur bhavatīti. atra nandīśvarādaya udāhāryāḥ viparyayeṇāpy
            adharmo dharmaṃ bādhate. tataś cāśuddhipariṇāma iti. tatrāpi nahuṣājagarādaya udāhāryāḥ.
children.translated_text: For causes such as dharma are not an instigator of the natures (<s>prakṛti</s>-s); a cause is not set into motion by its effect—how then? Rather, the removal of the obstruction is from that, like a field-tender. Just as a field-tender, wishing to flood another plot from a plot already filled with water, does not draw the water out with his hands, whether level or lower, but breaks their obstruction; when that is broken, the waters themselves flood the other plot, so dharma breaks the obstructing property of the natures; when that is broken, the natures themselves inundate their own modifications. Or, as that same field-tender, in that very plot, has no power to make watery or earthy juices enter the seeds of grain, what then does he do? He removes mung, millet, black-grain, and the like; when those are removed, the juices themselves enter the seeds of grain. Likewise, dharma is merely a cause of the cessation of adharma, because of the total opposition of purity and impurity, but dharma is not a cause of the activation of the natures (<s>prakṛti</s>-pravṛtti). Here one should cite <s>Nandīśvara</s> and others; conversely, adharma obstructs dharma, hence the transformation into impurity; and there too one should cite <s>Nahuṣa</s> become a serpent, and the like

children.text:
yadā tu yogī bahūn kāyān nirmimīte tadā kim ekamanaskās te bhavanty athānekamanaskā iti
            ---
children.translated_text: But when a yogin fashions many bodies, then are they of one mind, or of many minds?—
Constructed minds arise from mere <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness)

children.text:
asmitāmātraṃ cittakāraṇam upādāya nirmāṇacittāni karoti, tataḥ sacittāni
            bhavantīti.
children.translated_text: Taking mere <s>asmitā</s> as the cause of mind, he makes constructed minds; therefore they become minded (endowed with minds)
In differences of activity, a single mind is the instigator for many

children.text:
bahūnāṃ cittānāṃ katham ekacittābhiprāyapuraḥsarā pravṛttir iti sarvacittānāṃ
            prayojakaṃ cittam ekaṇ nirmimīte, tataḥ pravṛttibhedaḥ.
children.translated_text: How is it that, for many minds, activity proceeds with a single mind’s intention in the forefront?—thus: a single mind fashions the instigator (director) of all the minds, then there is diversity of activities
Among those, the one born of meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>) is without deposit (anāśaya)

children.text:
pañcavidhaṃ nirmāṇacittaṃ janmauṣadhimantratapaḥsamādhijāḥ siddhaya iti. tatra yad eva
            dhyānajaṃ cittaṃ tad evānāśayaṃ tasyaiva nāsty āśayo rāgādipravṛttir nātaḥ
            puṇyapāpābhisaṃbandhaḥ kṣīṇakleśatvād yogina iti itareṣāṃ tu vidyate karmāśayaḥ.
children.translated_text: The constructed mind is fivefold; perfections (<s>siddhi</s>-s) are born of birth, herbs, mantra, austerity (<s>tapas</s>), or <s>samādhi</s>. Among these, that very mind which is born of meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>) is indeed without deposit (anāśaya); for that alone there is no deposit—no activation of passion and the rest, no connection with merit and demerit—because the <s>yogin</s> has afflictions worn away; but for the others there is a karmic deposit (karmāśaya)
Because—
The karma of the <s>yogin</s> is neither white nor black; it is threefold for the others

children.text:
catuṣpadī khalv iyaṃ karmajātiḥ kṛṣṇā śuklakṛṣṇā śuklāśuklākṛṣṇā ceti. tatra kṛṣṇā
            durātmanām, śuklakṛṣṇā bahiḥsādhanasādhyā. tatra parapīḍānugrahadvāreṇaiva
            karmāśayapracayaḥ śuklā tapaḥsvādhyāyadhyānavatām. sā hi kevale manasy āyattatvād
            abahiḥsādhanādhīnā na parān pīḍayitvā bhavati. aśuklākṛṣṇā saṃnyāsināṃ kṣīṇakleśānāṃ
            caramadehānām iti tatrāśuklaṃ yogina eva phalasaṃnyāsād akṛṣṇaṃ cānupādānāt itareṣāṃ tu
            bhūtānāṃ pūrvam eva trividham iti.
children.translated_text: This genus of karma is indeed four-limbed: black, white-and-black, white, and not-white-not-black. There, black is of evil-minded persons; white-and-black is that accomplished by external means. There, by the doorway of harming others and of benefiting (others) alone, there is accumulation of karmic deposit; white belongs to those possessed of austerity (<s>tapas</s>), self-recitation (<s>svādhyāya</s>), and meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>). For that, being dependent on mind alone, not relying on external means, it comes to be without harming others. Not-white-not-black belongs to renouncers whose afflictions are worn away, of the final bodies; therein, not-white is only for the <s>yogin</s> because of the renunciation of the fruit, and not-black is from non-appropriation; but for the other beings, previously, it is threefold
Then, there is manifestation only of those dispositions (vāsanā-s) that are in accordance with the ripenings of that (karma)

children.text:
tata iti trividhāt karmaṇaḥ, tadvipākānuguṇānām eveti yajjātīyasya karmaṇo yo vipākas
            tasyānuguṇā yā vāsanāḥ karmavipākam anuśerate tāsām evābhivyaktiḥ. na hi daivaṃ karma
            vipacyamānaṃ nārakatiryaṅmanuṣyavāsanābhivyaktinimittaṃ saṃbhavati kiṃtu daivānuguṇā
            evāsya vāsanā vyajyante nārakatiryaṅmanuṣyeṣu caivaṃ samānaś carcaḥ.
children.translated_text: Then—namely, from threefold karma—“only of those that are in accordance with the ripenings of that”: whatever kind of karma’s ripening there is, the dispositions that are in accordance with that, which follow upon karmic ripening, only those are manifested. For indeed a divine karma, when ripening, cannot possibly be the occasion for the manifestation of hellish, animal, or human dispositions; rather, only dispositions in accordance with the divine are manifested for it; and likewise in hellish, animal, and human (cases) the discussion is the same
Even for those separated by class (birth), place, and time, there is uninterrupted succession (ānantarya), because memory and latent impression (saṃskāra) have one and the same form

children.text:
vṛṣadaṃśavipākodayaḥ svavyañjakāñjanābhivyaktaḥ. sa yadi jātiśatena vā dūradeśatayā vā
            kalpaśatena vā vyavahitaḥ punaś ca svavyañjakāñjana evodiyād drāg ity evaṃ
            pūrvānubhūtavṛṣadaṃśavipākābhisaṃskṛtā vāsanā upādāya vyajyeta. kasmāt, yato
            vyavahitānām apy āsāṃ sadṛśaṃ karmābhivyajñakaṃ nimittībhūtam ity ānantaryam eva. kutaś
            ca, smṛtisaṃskārayor ekarūpatvāt yathānubhavās tathā saṃskārāḥ. te ca karmavāsanānurūpāḥ
            yathā ca vāsanās tathā smṛtir iti jātideśakālavyavahitebhyaḥ saṃskārebhyaḥ smṛtiḥ.
            smṛteś ca punaḥ saṃskārā ityevam ete smṛtisaṃskārāḥ karmāśayavṛttilābhavaśād vyajyante
            ataś ca vyavahitānām api nimittanaimittikabhāvānucchedād ānantaryam eva siddham iti.
children.translated_text: The arising of the ripening of a bull’s bite (i.e., the sting of a scorpion), manifested by its own manifesters—if that were separated by a hundred births, or by a far-off place, or by a hundred aeons, yet, when it arises again from that very same its-own-manifester, it would arise swiftly—thus, the disposition fashioned by the prior-experienced ripening of the bull’s bite would, taking up (its cause), be manifested. Why? Because, even for things separated, there exists a cause that is similar, a karma-manifester, having become the occasion; therefore there is indeed uninterrupted succession. And why further? Because memory and latent impression have one and the same form: as the experiences, so the impressions; and these are in conformity with karmic dispositions. And as the dispositions, so the memory; thus, from the impressions separated by class (birth), place, and time, there is memory; and again from memory, impressions—thus, these memory-and-impressions, because they are made to obtain the function of karmic deposit, are manifested; and therefore, because the relation of occasion and occasioned is not cut off even for separated things, uninterrupted succession (ānantarya) is indeed established
And their beginninglessness too, because desire (āśiṣ) is eternal

children.text:
tāsāṃ vāsanānām āśiṣo nityatvād anāditvam. yeyam ātmāśīr mā na bhūvaṃ bhūyāsam
            iti.sarvasya dṛśyate sā na svābhāvikī. kasmāt jātamātrasya jantor
            ananubhūtamaraṇadharmakasya dveṣaduḥkhānusmṛtinimitto maraṇatrāsaḥ kathaṃ bhavet na ca
            svābhāvikaṃ vastu nimittam upādatte. tasmād anādivāsanānuviddham idaṃ cittaṃ
            nimittavaśāt kāścid eva vāsanāḥ pratilabhya puruṣasya bhogāyopāvartata iti.
children.translated_text: Of those dispositions, because desire is eternal, there is beginninglessness. This wish of the self—“May I not be; may I be again”—is seen in everyone; it is not innate (by nature). Why? How would there be, in a living being just born, who has not experienced the property of death, fear of death arising from the memory of suffering linked with aversion? And a thing that is by nature does not take up an occasion. Therefore, this mind, pierced by beginningless dispositions, obtains only certain dispositions according to occasion, and turns back toward the enjoyment of <s>Puruṣa</s>

children.text:
ghaṭaprāsādapradīpakalpaṃ saṃkocavikāsi cittaṃ śarīraparimāṇākāramātram ity apare
            pratipannāḥ tathā cāntarābhāvaḥ saṃsāraś ca yukta iti.
children.translated_text: Some, however, have understood: the mind, like a pot, a palace, or a lamp, is contracting and expanding, only of the measure of the body’s size-and-form; and thus, the absence of an inner (self) and <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence) too would be reasonable

children.text:
vṛttir evāsya vibhunaś cittasya saṃkocavikāsinīty ācāryaḥ. tac ca
            dharmādinimittāpekṣam. nimittaṃ ca dvividham --- bāhyam ādhyātmikaṃ ca.
            śarīrādisādhanāpekṣaṃ bāhyaṃ stutidānābhivādanādi, cittamātrādhīnaṃ śraddhādy
            adhyātmikam. tathā coktam --- ye caite maitryādayo dhyāyināṃ vihārās te
            bāhyasādhananiranugrahātmānaḥ prakṛṣṭaṃ dharmam abhinirvartayanti. tayor mānasaṃ
            balīyaḥ. kathaṃ, jñānavairāgye kenātiśayyete, daṇḍakāraṇyaṃ ca cittabalavyatirekeṇa
            śārīreṇa karmaṇā śūnyaṃ kaḥ kartum utsaheta samudram agastyavad vā pibet.
children.translated_text: The activity (vṛtti) alone of this all-pervading mind (<s>vibhu</s>) called <s>citta</s> is contracting-and-expanding—thus the Teacher; and that depends upon conditions such as dharma and the rest. And the condition is twofold—external and internal. External is that which depends on instruments such as body and the rest—praise, giving, salutation, and the like; internal is faith (<s>śraddhā</s>) and so on, dependent on mind alone. And thus it has been said—“And those diversions (vihāra) of meditators consisting of friendliness (<s>maitrī</s>) and so on, being of the nature of not relying on external instruments, effect dharma in an eminent degree.” Of these two, the mental is stronger. How so? By what would knowledge and dispassion be excelled; and who, apart from superiority of mental power, would undertake by bodily action to make the <s>Daṇḍakāraṇya</s> forest empty, or drink the ocean like <s>Agastya</s>?
Because they are bound together by cause, fruit, substratum, and object, with the absence of these, there is the absence of that

children.text:
hetur dharmāt sukham adharmād duḥkhaṃ sukhād rāgo duḥkhād dveṣas tataś ca prayatnas
            tena manasā vācā kāyena vā parispandamānaḥ param anugṛhṇāty upahanti vā tataḥ punar
            dharmādharmau sukhaduḥkhe rāgadveṣāv iti pravṛttam idaṃ ṣaḍaraṃ saṃsāracakram. asya ca
            pratikṣaṇam āvartamānasyāvidyā netrī mūlaṃ sarvakleśānām ity eṣa hetuḥ. phalaṃ tu yam
            āśritya yasya pratyutpannatā dharmādeḥ, na hy apūrvopajanaḥ. manas tu sādhikāram āśrayo
            vāsanānām. na hy avasitādhikāre manasi nirāśrayā vāsanāḥ sthātum utsahante. yad
            abhimukhībhūtaṃ vastu yāṃ vāsanāṃ vyanakti tasyās tadālambanam. evaṃ
            hetuphalāśrayālambanair etaiḥ saṃgṛhītāḥ sarvā vāsanāḥ eṣām abhāve tatsaṃśrayāṇām api
            vāsanānām abhāvaḥ.
children.translated_text: Cause: from dharma, pleasure; from adharma, pain; from pleasure, attachment (<s>rāga</s>); from pain, aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>); and from those, effort (<s>prayatna</s>)—thus, being set into motion by that, with mind, speech, or body, one greatly favors or harms; from that, again, dharma and adharma, pleasure and pain, attachment and aversion—thus is this six-spoked wheel of <s>saṃsāra</s> set in motion. And of this, as it turns at every instant, ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is the leader, the root of all afflictions—this is the cause. As for fruit: that, resorting to which, there is the arising-in-presence of dharma and the rest; for there is no production of what is unprecedented. And the mind is the qualified substratum (<s>āśraya</s>) of dispositions (vāsanā-s); for, in a mind whose qualified function is concluded, dispositions, being without substratum, are not able to remain. That object which has become faced-toward (abhimukhī-bhūta), the disposition that manifests it—of that disposition, that is the object (ālambana). Thus, by these four—cause, fruit, substratum, and object—all dispositions are bound together; with the absence of these, there is the absence of the dispositions that rely upon them

children.text:
nāsty asataḥ saṃbhavaḥ, na cāsti sato vināśa iti dravyatvena saṃbhavantyaḥ kathaṃ
            nivartiṣyante vāsanā iti ---
children.translated_text: “There is no coming-to-be of what is not; nor is there destruction of what is”—if dispositions exist as substances, how will they cease?—
The past and the future exist in their own nature; because of the division of the path (<s>adhvan</s>) of the properties (<s>dharma</s>-s)

children.text:
bhaviṣyadvyaktikam anāgatam anubhūtavyaktikam atītaṃ svavyāpāropārūḍhaṃ vartamānaṃ,
            trayaṃ caitad vastu jñānasya jñeyam. yadi caitat svarūpato nābhaviṣyan nedaṃ nirviṣayaṃ
            jñānam udapatsyata. tasmād atītānāgataṃ svarūpato+astīti. kiṃca bhogabhāgīyasya
            vāpavargabhāgīyasya vā karmaṇaḥ phalam utpitsu yadi nirupākhyam iti taduddeśena tena
            nimittena kuśalānuṣṭhānaṃ na yujyeta. sataś ca phalasya nimittaṃ vartamānīkaraṇe
            samarthaṃ nāpūrvopajanane siddhaṃ nimittaṃ naimittikasya viśeṣānugrahaṇaṃ kurute
            nāpūrvam utpādayatīti.
children.translated_text: The future is particularized as what is-to-become-manifest; the past is particularized as what-has-been-experienced; the present is mounted upon its own operation—this triad is the knowable of knowledge. And if this did not exist in its own nature, this knowledge would not arise as having an object; therefore, the past and the future exist in their own nature. Moreover, if the fruit of karma—whether belonging to enjoyment or belonging to release (<s>apavarga</s>)—that is about to arise were indescribable, then undertaking what is skillful with that as its aim, with that as its condition, would not be reasonable. And a condition with respect to an existent fruit is competent to bring it into presentness, not established for generating the unprecedented; the condition bestows specific favor upon what is conditionally produced, but does not produce the unprecedented

children.text:
dharmī cānekadharmasvabhāvas tasya cādhvabhedena dharmāḥ pratyavasthitāḥ na ca yathā
            vartamānaṃ vyaktiviśeṣāpannaṃ dravyato+asty evam atītam anāgataṃ ca. kathaṃ tarhi,
            svenaiva vyaṅgyena svarūpeṇānāgatam asti. svena cānubhūtavyaktikena svarūpeṇātītam iti
            vartamānasyaivādhvanaḥ svarūpavyaktir iti na sā bhavaty atītānāgatayor adhvanoḥ. ekasya
            cādhvanaḥ samaye dvāv adhvanau dharmisamanvāgatau bhavata eveti nābhūtvā bhāvas trayāṇām
            adhvanām iti.
children.translated_text: And the substratum (<s>dharmin</s>) has the nature of many properties, and its properties are fixed according to the division of the path; and not, as the present, which has attained a particular manifestation, does the past and future exist as a substance in that way. How then? The future exists by its own nature as subtle, by its own suggestive power; and the past, by its own nature as what has been experienced in particular. Thus, manifestation of the form of the path belongs only to the present path; and it does not belong to the past and future paths. And at one and the same time of a single path, two paths, together with the substratum, would arise—that indeed would occur; therefore there is no coming-to-be without having been, of the three paths
They are manifest-and-subtle, having the nature of the <s>guṇa</s>-s

children.text:
te khalv amī tryadhvano dharmā vartamānā vyaktātmāno+atītānāgatāḥ sūkṣmātmānaḥ
            ṣaḍaviśeṣarūpāḥ. sarvam idaṃ guṇānāṃ saṃniveśaviśeṣamātram iti paramārthato guṇātmānaḥ.
            tathā ca śāstrānuśāsanam ---
children.translated_text: These very properties, pertaining to the three paths, are present as manifest in the present, and as subtle in the past and future, having the form of the six particularities; in ultimate truth, this all is merely a particular arrangement of the <s>guṇa</s>-s; and thus the scriptural instruction—

children.text: guṇānāṃ paramaṃ rūpaṃ na dṛṣṭipatham ṛcchati /
children.translated_text: The supreme form of the <s>guṇa</s>-s does not come within the range of vision,

children.text: yat tu dṛṣṭipathaṃ prāptaṃ tan māyeva sutucchakam //
children.translated_text: but whatever has come into the range of vision is, like <s>māyā</s> (illusion), exceedingly trifling
—so it is

children.text: yadā tu sarve guṇāḥ katham ekaḥ śabda ekam indriyam iti ---
children.translated_text: But if all the <s>guṇa</s>-s are [asked about thus:] how is it that one word is one sense-faculty?—
Because of the oneness of transformation, the real nature of the thing (vastu) [is one]

children.text:
prakhyākriyāsthitiśīlānāṃ guṇānāṃ grahaṇātmakānāṃ karaṇabhāvenaikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ śrotram
            indriyaṃ, grāhyātmakānāṃ śabdatanmātrabhāvenaikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ śabdo viṣaya iti, śabdādīnāṃ
            mūrtisamānajātīyānām ekaḥ pariṇāmaḥ pṛthivīparamāṇus tanmātrāvayavas teṣāṃ caikaḥ
            pariṇāmaḥ pṛthivī gaur vṛkṣaḥ parvata ityevamādir bhūtāntareṣv api
            snehauṣṇyapraṇāmitvāvakāśadānāny upādāya sāmānyam ekavikārārambhaḥ samādheyaḥ.
children.translated_text: Since the <s>guṇa</s>-s, whose nature is manifestation, activity, and stability, are of the nature of being apprehended, as instruments there is a single transformation that is the ear as a sense-faculty; and of the nature of being apprehended (as objects), as the subtle-element of sound (<s>śabda-tanmātra</s>), there is a single transformation that is sound as an object; and for sound and the like, which are of the same genus as formed things (gross forms), there is a single transformation that is the earth-atom (<s>pṛthivī-paramāṇu</s>), [namely] the parts of the subtle-element of earth; and for those, there is a single transformation: “earth, cow, tree, mountain,” and so on—likewise, in the other elements too, taking common properties such as viscosity, heat, plasticity (pliability), and capacity to provide space, the commonality as a single inception of modification ought to be established

children.text:
nāsty artho vijñānavisahacaraḥ, asti tu jñānam arthavisahacaraṃ svapnādau kalpitam ity
            anayā diśā ye vastusvarūpam apahnuvate jñānaparikalpanāmātraṃ vastu svapnaviṣayopamaṃ na
            paramārthato+astīti ya āhus te tatheti pratyupasthitam idaṃ svamāhātmyena vastu katham
            apramāṇātmakena vikalpajñānabalena vastusvarūpam utsṛjya tad evāpalapantaḥ
            śraddheyavacanāḥ syuḥ.
children.translated_text: There is no object accompanied by cognition; but cognition accompanied by an object does exist—[yet] in dream and the like it is fabricated: in this manner, those who deny the very nature of a real thing (vastu), saying, “the thing is only a mere construction by cognition, like a dream-object; it does not exist ultimately,”—how would these who, though this real thing has presented itself by its own greatness, abandon the very nature of the real thing by the strength of a non-pramāṇa-type, conceptual cognition, and refute that very thing—be worthy of credence?
And moreover, this is unreasonable—
Because, when the object is the same, from the difference of minds, the two have divergent paths

children.text:
bahucittālambanībhūtam ekaṃ vastu sādhāraṇaṃ, tat khalu naikacittaparikalpitaṃ nāpy
            anekacittaparikalpitaṃ kiṃtu svapratiṣṭham. kathaṃ, vastusāmye cittabhedāt dharmāpekṣaṃ
            cittasya vastusāmye+api sukhajñānaṃ bhavaty adharmāpekṣaṃ tata eva duḥkhajñānam
            avidyāpekṣaṃ tata eva mūḍhajñānaṃ samyagdarśanāpekṣaṃ tata eva mādhyasthyajñānam iti.
            kasya tac cittena parikalpitam. na cānyacittaparikalpitenārthenānyasya cittoparāgo
            yuktaḥ. tasmād vastujñānayor grāhyagrahaṇabhedabhinnayor vibhaktaḥ panthāḥ. nānayoḥ
            saṃkaragandho+apy astīti.
children.translated_text: A single object, which becomes a support for many minds, is common; and indeed it is neither fabricated by one mind nor fabricated by many minds, but rather established in itself. How so? When the object is the same, from the difference of minds: dependent on merit (dharma), even with the object the same, there arises a cognition of pleasure; dependent on demerit (adharma), from that very same [object], a cognition of pain; dependent on ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), from that very same [object], a deluded cognition; dependent on right vision (samyag-darśana), from that very same [object], a neutral cognition—thus. For whom is that fabricated by whose mind? And it is not reasonable that the coloring (modification) of one’s mind should be effected by an object fabricated by another’s mind. Therefore, for the object and for knowledge—distinct by the difference of the grasped and the grasper—their paths are separate; there is not even a scent of intermixture between these two

children.text:
sāṃkhyapakṣe punar vastu triguṇaṃ calaṃ ca guṇavṛttam iti dharmādinimittāpekṣaṃ cittair
            abhisaṃbadhyate. nimittānurūpasya ca pratyayasyotpadyamānasya tena tenātmanā hetur
            bhavati. kecid āhuḥ. jñānasahabhūr evārtho bhogyatvāt sukhādivad iti ta etayā dvārā
            sādhāraṇatvaṃ bādhamānāḥ pūrvottarakṣaṇeṣu vasturūpam evāpahnuvate.
children.translated_text: But, according to the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> position, the object is three-<s>guṇa</s>-ed and unstable—consisting in the activity of the <s>guṇa</s>-s—and, dependent on conditions such as merit and so on, it is connected with minds; and when a cognition arises corresponding to a condition, the condition becomes the cause in that very particular manner. Some say: “the object indeed coexists with cognition, because it is an object of enjoyment, like pleasure and the rest”—and these, by this very doorway, contradicting commonality, deny the very nature of the real thing (vastu) in successive moments,

children.text: na caikacittatantraṃ vastu tadapramāṇakaṃ tadā kiṃ syāt
children.translated_text: Nor is the object dependent on a single mind—for that would lack pramāṇa; what then would it be?

children.text:
ekacittatantraṃ ced vastu syāt tadā citte vyagre niruddhe vāsvarūpam eva tenāparāmṛṣṭam
            anyasyāviṣayībhūtam apramāṇakam agṛhītasvabhāvakaṃ kenacit tadānīṃ kiṃ tat syāt.
            saṃbadhyamānaṃ ca punaś cittena kuta utpadyeta ye cāsyānupasthitā bhāgās te cāsya na
            syur evaṃ nāsti pṛṣṭham ity udaram api na gṛhyeta. tasmāt svatantro+arthaḥ
            sarvapuruṣasādhāraṇaḥ svatantrāṇi ca cittāni pratipuruṣaṃ pravartante tayoḥ saṃbandhād
            upalabdhiḥ puruṣasya bhoga iti.
children.translated_text: If the object were dependent on a single mind, then, when that mind is engaged, restrained, or manifest in its own form and not touching [the object], the object, being not within the scope of another, would be without pramāṇa, having a nature not apprehended by anyone—what then would that be at that time? And, when it becomes connected again with a mind, whence would it arise? And those parts of it that are not present would not belong to it; thus, if “the back does not exist,” then the belly too would not be apprehended. Therefore, the object is independent, common to all persons; and the minds, being independent, operate individually for each person; from the relation of those two there is apprehension, which is the enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>) of <s>Puruṣa</s>
Because the mind depends upon the coloring (adventitious coloration) by that, an object is known or unknown

children.text:
ayaskāntamaṇikalpā viṣayā ayaḥsadharmakaṃ cittam abhisaṃbandhyoparañjayanti. yena ca
            viṣayeṇoparaktaṃ cittaṃ sa viṣayo jñātas tato+anyaḥ punar ajñātaḥ vastuno
            jñātājñātasvarūpatvāt pariṇāmi cittam.
children.translated_text: Objects are like a lodestone-jewel: having connected with the mind, which is of an iron-like nature, they tinge (dye) it; and by whatever object the mind is tinged, that object is known, another, then, is unknown. Since the object has the nature of being known-or-unknown, the mind is that which undergoes transformation

children.text: yasya tu tad eva cittaṃ viṣayas tasya ---
children.translated_text: But for whom that very mind is the object, for him—
The mental activities (<s>citta-vṛtti</s>-s) are always known by the Lord of that (mind), the <s>Puruṣa</s>, because he is unchanging (apariṇāmin)

children.text:
yadi cittavat prabhur api puruṣaḥ pariṇamet tatas tadviṣayāś cittavṛttayaḥ
            śabdādiviṣayavaj jñātājñātāḥ syuḥ sadājñātatvaṃ tu manasas tatprabhoḥ
            puruṣasyāpariṇāmitvam anumāpayati.
children.translated_text: If the Lord, the <s>Puruṣa</s>, were to undergo transformation like the mind (<s>citta</s>), then the mental activities (<s>citta-vṛtti</s>-s) whose object is that (Lord) would be, like objects such as sound, sometimes known and sometimes unknown; but the constant knowability of the mind belongs to it because the Lord of that (mind), the <s>Puruṣa</s>, is unchanging—this is inferred

children.text: syād āśaṅkā cittam eva svābhāsaṃ viṣayābhāsaṃ ca bhaviṣyatīty agnivat ---
children.translated_text: An objection might be raised: the mind itself will be self-luminous and luminous in respect of objects, like fire—
It is not self-luminous, because it is seen

children.text:
yathetarāṇīndriyāṇi śabdādayaś ca dṛśyatvān na svābhāsāni tathā mano+api pratyetavyam.
            na cāgnir atra dṛṣṭāntaḥ na hy agnir ātmasvarūpam aprakāśaṃ prakāśayati prakāśaś cāyaṃ
            prakāśyaprakāśakasaṃyoge dṛṣṭaḥ. na ca svarūpamātre+asti saṃyogaḥ kiṃca svābhāsaṃ cittam
            ity agrāhyam eva kasyacid iti śabdārthaḥ. tadyathā svātmapratiṣṭham ākāśaṃ na
            parapratiṣṭham ity arthaḥ svabuddhipracārapratisaṃvedanāt sattvānāṃ pravṛttir dṛśyate
            --- kruddho+ahaṃ bhīto+aham amutra me rāgo+amutra me krodha iti etat svabuddher agrahaṇe
            na yuktam iti.
children.translated_text: Just as the other senses and also sound and the rest, because they are objects of sight (i.e., are seen), are not self-luminous, so too the mind should be understood; nor is fire an apt example here, for fire does not illuminate its own nature which is non-manifest, and this illumination is observed in the conjunction of illuminable and illuminator; nor is there conjunction with mere own-nature; moreover, “the mind is self-luminous” would mean “it is ungraspable by anyone”—such is the import of the words. For example, “space is grounded in itself, not grounded in another”—the meaning is this: the activities of the intellect (buddhi) are observed from the reflexive awareness of the movement of one’s own cognition—“I am angry, I am afraid, here I have attachment, there I have anger”—this would not be reasonable if there were no apprehension of one’s own cognition
And at one and the same time there is no determination of both

children.text:
na caikasmin kṣaṇe svapararūpāvadhāraṇaṃ yuktaṃ, kṣaṇikavādino yad bhavanaṃ saiva kriyā
            tad eva ca kārakam ity abhyupagamaḥ.
children.translated_text: Nor is it reasonable that, in a single moment, there be determination of one’s own form and another’s form, given the admission by the momentariness-theorists that what is coming-to-be is itself the action and that very thing is the agent

children.text: syān matiḥ svarasaniruddhaṃ cittaṃ cittāntareṇa samanantareṇa gṛhyata iti ---
children.translated_text: One might think: a mind, blocked by its own savor (i.e., engrossed in its own object), is grasped by another mind that is immediately adjacent—
If mind were seen by another mind, there would be an over-proliferation of intellects cognizing intellects, and a confusion of memories

children.text:
atha cittaṃ cec cittāntareṇa gṛhyeta buddhibuddhiḥ kena gṛhyate, sāpy anyayā sāpy
            anyayety atiprasaṅgaḥ. smṛtisaṃkaraś ca, yāvanto buddhibuddhīnām anubhavās tāvatyaḥ
            smṛtayaḥ prāpnuvanti. tatsaṃkarāc caikasmṛtyanavadhāraṇaṃ ca syād ity evaṃ
            buddhipratisaṃvedinaṃ puruṣam apalapadbhir vaināśikaiḥ sarvam evākulīkṛtam. te tu
            bhoktṛsvarūpaṃ yatra kvacana kalpayanto na nyāyena saṃgacchante kecit tu sattvamātram
            api parikalpyāsti sa sattvo ya etān pañca skandhān nikṣipyānyāṃś ca pratisaṃdadhātīty
            uktvā tata eva punas trasyanti. tathā skandhānāṃ mahannirvedāya virāgāyānutpādāya
            praśāntaye guror antike brahmacaryaṃ cariṣyāmīty uktvā sattvasya punaḥ sattvam
            evāpahnuvate. sāṃkhyayogādayas tu pravādāḥ svaśabdena puruṣam eva svāminaṃ cittasya
            bhoktāram upayantīti.
children.translated_text: If the mind were grasped by another mind, by what would the intellect-cognizing-intellect be grasped? By yet another, and that too by yet another—thus an infinite regress. And there would be a confusion of memories: as many as are the experiences of intellects cognizing intellects, so many memories would ensue; from that intermixing there would be non-determination of a single memory. In this way, by those nihilists who repudiate the <s>Puruṣa</s>, the witness of the intellect, everything is thrown into disorder. They, positing a nature of enjoyer (experiencer) somewhere or other, do not accord with reason; some even fabricate a mere “sentience” (sattva-mātra), saying, “There is that sentient one who, depositing these five aggregates (<s>skandha</s>-s) and assembling other parts, [acts],” and then again they shrink back from that very (position). Likewise, having said, “For the great disenchantment, for dispassion, for the non-arising, for the pacification of the aggregates, I will live the celibate life in the presence of a teacher,” they then deny again the very sentience of the sentient. But the doctrines such as <s>Sāṃkhya</s> and <s>Yoga</s>, in their own terms, arrive at the <s>Puruṣa</s> as the master of the mind (<s>citta</s>) and the enjoyer
How—
Because, while consciousness (<s>citi</s>) does not transmigrate, when the mind assumes that form, there is reflexive awareness of one’s own cognition

children.text:
apariṇāminī hi bhoktṛśaktir apratisaṃkramā ca pariṇāminy arthe pratisaṃkrānteva
            tadvṛttim anupatati. tasyāś ca prāptacaitanyopagrahasvarūpāyā buddhivṛtter
            anukārimātratayā buddhivṛttyaviśiṣṭā hi jñānavṛttir ākhyāyate. tathā coktam.
children.translated_text: For the power of the enjoyer is unchanging and non-transmigrating, yet, in the presence of a changing object, as it were transmigrating, it follows that very activity; and of that (power), whose nature is reception of appropriated consciousness when it has been obtained, the cognitive activity of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti), merely as an imitation of it, is designated a cognition-activity not distinct from the intellect-activity. And so it has been said,

children.text: na pātālaṃ na ca vivaraṃ girīṇāṃ naivāndhakāraṃ kukṣayo nodadhīnām /
children.translated_text: Neither the netherworld, nor the clefts of mountains, nor darkness, nor the bellies of the oceans,

children.text: guhā yasyāṃ nihitaṃ brahma śāśvataṃ buddhivṛttim aviśiṣṭāṃ kavayo vedayante
children.translated_text: the cave in which the eternal <s>Brahma</s> is hidden—the sages discover as not distinct from the activity of the intellect”
Therefore this is accepted—
The mind (<s>citta</s>), dyed by seer and seen, is all-purpose (capable of all objects)

children.text:
mano hi mantavyenārthenoparaktaṃ, tat svayaṃ ca viṣayatvād viṣayiṇā puruṣeṇātmīyayā
            vṛttyābhisaṃbaddhaṃ, tad etac cittam eva draṣṭṛdṛśyoparaktaṃ viṣayaviṣayinirbhāsaṃ
            cetanācetanasvarūpāpannaṃ viṣayātmakam apy aviṣayātmakam ivācetanaṃ cetanam iva
            sphaṭikamaṇikalpaṃ sarvārtham ity ucyate.
children.translated_text: For the mind indeed, being tinged by the object to be thought, and that very [mind], because of being an object, being bound to the subject, the <s>Puruṣa</s>, by the mind’s own mode (vṛtti), therefore this very mind (<s>citta</s>), dyed by seer and seen, appearing as object and subject, having assumed the nature of sentient and insentient, though of the nature of object yet as if not of the nature of object, as if insentient though sentient, like a crystal jewel, is said to be all-purpose (capable of all objects)

children.text:
tad anena cittasārūpyeṇa bhrāntāḥ kecit tad eva cetanam ity āhuḥ apare cittamātram
            evedaṃ sarvaṃ nāsti khalv ayaṃ gavādir ghaṭādiś ca sakāraṇo loka iti. anukampanīyās te.
            kasmāt, asti hi teṣāṃ bhrāntibījaṃ sarvarūpākāranirbhāsaṃ cittam iti. samādhiprajñāyāṃ
            prajñeyo+arthaḥ pratibimbībhūtas tasyālambanībhūtatvād anyaḥ. sa ced arthaś cittamātraṃ
            syāt kathaṃ prajñayaiva prajñārūpam avadhāryeta. tasmāt pratibimbībhūto+arthaḥ prajñāyāṃ
            yenāvadhāryate sa puruṣa iti. evaṃ grahītṛgrahaṇagrāhyasvarūpacittabhedāt trayam apy
            etaj jātitaḥ pravibhajante te samyagdarśinas tair adhigataḥ puruṣaḥ.
children.translated_text: Accordingly, through this likeness of mind with [both], some, being deluded, say that very [mind] is the sentient principle; others say, “this all is mere mind only; indeed there is not this world of cow and the like, pot and the like, along with causes,”—they are to be pitied. Why? For they have the seed of their error in this: “the mind has the appearance of all-forms.” In <s>samādhi</s>-wisdom, the knowable object, having become a reflection (pratibimba), is other, because it has become the support (ālambana) of that [wisdom]. If the object were mere mind, how would what is of the nature of cognition be determined by cognition alone? Therefore, the object, having become a reflection in the wisdom, by which it is determined—that [determinant] is the <s>Puruṣa</s>. Thus, due to the distinction of the mind by the natures of grasper, grasping, and grasped, all three are divided by kind; those with right vision (<s>samyag-darśin</s>-s), by these [means], apprehend the <s>Puruṣa</s>
And from what [reason]—

children.text: tad asaṃkhyeyavāsanābhiś citram api parārthaṃ saṃhatyakāritvāt
children.translated_text: Because, although variegated by innumerable dispositions (<s>vāsanā</s>-s), it is for-another’s-sake, since it acts as a conjunction-made (a product of assemblage)

children.text:
tad etac cittam asaṃkhyeyābhir vāsanābhir eva citrīkṛtam api parārthaṃ parasya
            bhogāpavargārthaṃ na svārthaṃ saṃhatyakāritvād gṛhavat. saṃhatyakāriṇā cittena na
            svārthena bhavitavyaṃ, na sukhacittaṃ sukhārthaṃ na jñānaṃ jñānārtham ubhayam apy etat
            parārtham. yaś ca bhogenāpavargeṇa cārthenārthavān puruṣaḥ sa eva paro na paraḥ
            sāmānyamātram. yat tu kiṃcit paraṃ sāmānyamātraṃ svarūpeṇodāhared vaināśikas tat sarvaṃ
            saṃhatyakāritvāt parārtham eva syāt. yas tv asau paro viśeṣaḥ sa na saṃhatyakārī puruṣa
            iti.
children.translated_text: Thus, this mind, even though variegated precisely by innumerable <s>vāsanā</s>-s, is for-another’s-sake—namely for another’s enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>) and liberation (<s>apavarga</s>)—not for its own sake, because it acts as a conjunction-made (like a house). A mind that acts as a conjunction-made ought not to be for its own sake: a pleasurable mind is not for the sake of pleasure [itself], nor is knowledge for the sake of knowledge—both of these are for-another’s-sake. And that person who is rich in purpose by enjoyment and by liberation—that indeed is the Other (the beyond), the <s>Puruṣa</s>, not a mere generality. Whatever the nihilists (<s>vaināśika</s>-s) might adduce as some “other” that is a mere generality in its own nature, all that, because it acts as a conjunction-made, would be for-another’s-sake. But that Other which is a particular (viśeṣa) is not a conjunction-made—[that] is the <s>Puruṣa</s>
For one who sees the Particular (the discerner), cessation of the imagining of selfhood

children.text:
yathā prāvṛṣi tṛṇāṅkurasyodbhedena tadbījasattānumīyate tathā mokṣamārgaśravaṇena yasya
            romaharṣāśrupātau dṛśyete tatrāpy asti viśeṣadarśanabījam apavargabhāgīyaṃ
            karmābhinirvartitam ity anumīyate. tasyātmabhāvabhāvanā svābhāvikī pravartate
            yasyābhāvād idam uktaṃ svabhāvaṃ muktvā doṣādyeṣāṃ pūrvapakṣe rucir bhavaty aruciś ca
            nirṇaye bhavati tatrātmabhāvabhāvanā ko+aham āsaṃ katham aham āsaṃ kiṃsvid idaṃ
            kathaṃsvid idaṃ ke bhaviṣyāmaḥ kathaṃ vā bhaviṣyāma iti. sā tu viśeṣadarśino nivartate
            kutaḥ cittasyaivaiṣa vicitraḥ pariṇāmaḥ, puruṣas tv asatyām avidyāyāṃ śuddhaś
            cittadharmair aparāmṛṣṭa iti. tato+asyātmabhāvabhāvanā kuśalasya nivartata iti.
children.translated_text: Just as, in the rainy season, from the sprouting of a grass-shoot the existence of its seed is inferred, so too, for one in whom, upon hearing the path to liberation, horripilation and tears are seen, there too the seed of vision of the Particular (viśeṣa), belonging to liberation, produced by karma—this is inferred. For him, there naturally proceeds the imagining of selfhood (ātma-bhāva-bhāvanā); in the absence of which, the following has been said: setting aside nature, because of defect and the like, there is fondness in the prima facie view and distaste at the conclusion. There, the imagining of selfhood is [such as:] “Who was I? How was I? What is this? How indeed is this? Who shall we be? Or how shall we be?” But that [imagining] ceases for the one who sees the Particular; why? because this manifold transformation belongs to the mind itself, whereas the <s>Puruṣa</s>, in the non-existence of <s>avidyā</s>, is pure, untouched by the properties of the mind. Therefore the imagining of selfhood ceases for the skillful one
Then the mind is slanted toward discrimination, weighted toward isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>)

children.text:
tadānīṃ yad asya cittaṃ viṣayaprāgbhāram ajñānanimnam āsīt tad asyānyathā bhavati
            kaivalyaprāgbhāraṃ vivekajajñānanimnam iti.
children.translated_text: Then, that mind of his which was previously weighted toward objects and inclined toward ignorance becomes otherwise—namely, weighted toward <s>kaivalya</s> and inclined by knowledge born of discrimination (<s>viveka</s>)
In the gaps of that, other conceptions arise from impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>-s)

children.text:
pratyayavivekanimnasya sattvapuruṣānyatākhyātimātrapravāhiṇaś cittasya tacchidreṣu
            pratyayāntarāṇy asmīti vā mameti vā jānāmīti vā na jānāmīti vā. kutaḥ,
            kṣīyamāṇabījebhyaḥ pūrvasaṃskārebhya iti.
children.translated_text: In the gaps of that mind, which is slanted to discriminative conceptions and flows only with the cognition of the otherness of <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, other conceptions—“I am,” or “mine,” or “I know,” or “I do not know”—[arise]. Why? From prior impressions, whose seeds are being exhausted
The abandonment of these has been stated like the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>-s)

children.text:
yathā kleśā dagdhabījabhāvā na prarohasamarthā bhavanti tathā jñānāgninā
            dagdhabījabhāvaḥ pūrvasaṃskāro na pratyayaprasūr bhavati. jñānasaṃskārās tu
            cittādhikārasamāptim anuśerata iti na cintyante.
children.translated_text: Just as the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>-s), having the condition of seeds burned, are not capable of sprouting, so too the prior impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>-s), having the condition of seeds burned by the fire of knowledge, do not generate further cognitions; whereas the impressions of knowledge, following upon the completion of the mind’s jurisdiction, accompany (only) as an aftermath and therefore are not to be reckoned (as producing new cognitions)

children.text: prasaṃkhyāne+apy akusīdasya sarvathā vivekakhyāter dharmameghaḥ samādhiḥ
children.translated_text: For one who is not complacent even in discriminative contemplation (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), there is, in every way, the cognition of discrimination (<s>viveka-khyāti</s>); [then] the cloud-of-dharma (<s>dharma-megha</s>) <s>samādhi</s>

children.text:
yadāyaṃ brāhmaṇaḥ prasaṃkhyāne+apy akusīdas tato+api na kiṃcit prārthayate. tatrāpi
            viraktasya sarvathā vivekakhyātir eva bhavatīti saṃskārabījakṣayān nāsya pratyayāntarāṇy
            utpadyante tadāsya dharmamegho nāma samādhir bhavati.
children.translated_text: When this <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> is not complacent even in <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>, then he desires nothing even beyond that; for one who is dispassionate even therein, there arises in every way only <s>viveka-khyāti</s>, and because of the exhaustion of the seeds of impressions, no other cognitions arise for him; then for him there is the <s>samādhi</s> named “cloud-of-dharma” (<s>dharma-megha</s>)
Thereupon, cessation of afflictions and karma (<s>kleśa</s>- and <s>karma</s>-cessation)

children.text:
tallābhād avidyādayaḥ kleśāḥ samūlakāṣaṃ kaṣitā bhavanti kuśalākuśalāś ca karmāśayāḥ
            samūlaghātaṃ hatā bhavanti. kleśakarmanivṛttau jīvann eva vidvān vimukto bhavati kasmāt,
            yasmād viparyayo bhavasya kāraṇam. na hi kṣīṇaviparyayaḥ kaścit kenacit kvacij jāto
            dṛśyata iti.
children.translated_text: By the attainment of that, the afflictions beginning with <s>avidyā</s> are cut up by the root, and the stores of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>-s), both wholesome and unwholesome, are struck down by the root; upon the cessation of afflictions and karma, the knower, even while living, becomes liberated—why? because misapprehension (<s>viparyaya</s>) is the cause of becoming (saṃsāra); for no one anywhere is ever seen to be born with misapprehension extinct
